children.title: Marginal Measures
children.top_down_role: Source and target measure data for static transport problems.

assumptions_latex: \(\gamma\) is a probability measure on \(X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The marginal measures of \(\gamma\) are \(\mu=(p_X)_\#\gamma\) and \(\nu=(p_Y)_\#\gamma\).

notation.meaning: Canonical coordinate projections from the product space
Pushforward of a measure by a measurable map

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability marginals on a measurable product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every measurable \(A\subseteq X\) and \(B\subseteq Y\), define
\[
\mu(A):=\gamma(A\times Y),\qquad \nu(B):=\gamma(X\times B).
\]
Equivalently, \(\mu=(p_X)_\#\gamma\) and \(\nu=(p_Y)_\#\gamma\). The measures \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are respectively the first and second marginal measures of \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The marginals of a probability measure on a product space are its pushforwards under the two coordinate projections.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the Marginal Measures leaf and is mathematically standard, but no citation or inspectable locator is supplied. The product measurable space should also be understood as equipped with the product sigma-algebra.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-support approximations of marginal measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic mesh and empirical representations of transport marginals, with the equal-mass two-marginal specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A probability measure \(\mu\) may be approximated by \(\widehat\mu=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}m_i\delta_{x_i}\), where \(m_i\ge 0\) and \(\sum_i m_i=1\). For disjoint measurable cells \(V_i\) covering the support and anchors \(a_i\in V_i\), the mesh approximation is \(\widehat\mu^{\mathrm{mesh}}=\sum_i\mu(V_i)\delta_{a_i}\). For i.i.d. samples \(X_i\sim\mu\), the empirical approximation is \(\widehat\mu_\ell=\ell^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{X_i}\); on \(\mathbb R^d\), \(\widehat\mu_\ell\) converges narrowly to \(\mu\) almost surely. If two marginals are each discretized into the same number \(\ell\) of equal-mass atoms, the resulting two-marginal discrete transport problem admits an optimal permutation coupling and hence a Monge solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A marginal measure can be approximated by finitely many weighted atoms, using either mesh-cell masses or equal-weight empirical samples. Empirical measures on Euclidean space converge narrowly almost surely. Equal-mass discretizations of two marginals with the same number of atoms admit an optimal permutation, and therefore Monge, coupling.
assumptions_latex: V_1,\ldots,V_\ell\ \text{are disjoint measurable cells covering the support and }a_i\in V_i
N=2\ \text{and both discretized marginals have }\ell\text{ atoms of mass }1/\ell\ \text{for the Monge assertion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\mu^{\mathrm{mesh}}=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\mu(V_i)\delta_{a_i},\qquad \widehat\mu_\ell=\frac1\ell\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\delta_{X_i}\rightharpoonup\mu\ \text{a.s.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multi-marginal couplings and map-induced transport plans
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate marginals, multi-marginal couplings, map-induced plans, graph representations, and inverse transport plans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For N\ge2 and \mathbf X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_N, define \pi^i(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=x_i and \pi^{i,j}(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=(x_i,x_j). For \boldsymbol\mu\in\mathcal P(\mathbf X), its marginals are \mu^i:=\pi^i_\#\boldsymbol\mu and \boldsymbol\mu^{ij}:=\pi^{i,j}_\#\boldsymbol\mu. Given \mu^i\in\mathcal P(X_i), define \Gamma(\mu^1,\ldots,\mu^N):=\{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathcal P(\mathbf X):\pi^i_\#\boldsymbol\mu=\mu^i,\ i=1,\ldots,N\}. For N=2 its elements are transport plans, and \Gamma(\mu^1,\mu^2)=\{\mu^1\times\mu^2\} if either marginal is a Dirac mass. If \mu^2=\mathbf r_\#\mu^1 for a Borel map \mathbf r:X_1\to X_2, then (\mathbf i\times\mathbf r)_\#\mu^1\in\Gamma(\mu^1,\mu^2) is induced by \mathbf r. Conversely, a transport plan concentrated on a measurable graph admits this representation for a \mu^1-measurable map; when X_1,X_2 are Polish, the corresponding assertion holds with Borel graphs and Borel maps. For \sigma(x_1,x_2)=(x_2,x_1), define the inverse plan by \boldsymbol\mu^{-1}:=\sigma_\#\boldsymbol\mu.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Marginals are pushforwards under coordinate projections, and a multi-marginal coupling is a joint probability measure with prescribed marginals. A transport map induces a graph-supported plan, while graph-supported plans admit a map representation under the stated measurability conditions. Swapping coordinates defines the inverse plan.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf r:X_1\to X_2\text{ is Borel and }\mu^2=\mathbf r_\#\mu^1\text{ for the induced-plan construction}
\boldsymbol\mu\text{ is concentrated on a measurable graph for the converse representation}
X_1,X_2\text{ are Polish for the Borel-graph/Borel-map version}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma(\mu^1,\ldots,\mu^N)=\{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathcal P(\mathbf X):\pi^i_\#\boldsymbol\mu=\mu^i\ \forall i\},\quad \mu^2=\mathbf r_\#\mu^1\Rightarrow(\mathbf i\times\mathbf r)_\#\mu^1\in\Gamma(\mu^1,\mu^2),\quad \boldsymbol\mu^{-1}=\sigma_\#\boldsymbol\mu.

children.title: Pushforward Measures
children.top_down_role: Measure transport represented through measurable maps.

assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to Y\) is measurable and \(\mu\) is a measure on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pushforward \(T_\#\mu\) is the measure on \(Y\) given by \((T_\#\mu)(B)=\mu(T^{-1}(B))\).

notation.meaning: Pushforward, or image, measure of mu under T
Inverse image of a measurable set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pushforward under a measurable map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The pushforward of \(\mu\) by \(T\) is the measure \(T_\#\mu\) on \((Y,\Sigma_Y)\) defined by
\[
(T_\#\mu)(B):=\mu\bigl(T^{-1}(B)\bigr),\qquad B\in\Sigma_Y.
\]
Equivalently, for every nonnegative measurable function \(\varphi:Y\to[0,+\infty]\),
\[
\int_Y\varphi(y)\,d(T_\#\mu)(y)=\int_X\varphi(T(x))\,d\mu(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pushforward transfers a measure through a measurable map by assigning each target set the mass of its inverse image.
knowledge_statements.title: Pushforward Measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pushforward definition and integration identity match the leaf and are internally consistent, but the record has no source or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pushforward measure and its basic properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, integration identity, absolute-continuity preservation, composition, narrow continuity, and support behavior of pushforward measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X_1,X_2 be separable metric spaces, \mu\in\mathcal P(X_1), and let \mathbf r:X_1\to X_2 be Borel, or more generally \mu-measurable. Define (\mathbf r_\#\mu)(B):=\mu(\mathbf r^{-1}(B)) for B\in\mathcal B(X_2). For every bounded Borel, or \mathbf r_\#\mu-integrable Borel, function f:X_2\to\mathbb R, \int_{X_1}f(\mathbf r(x))\,d\mu(x)=\int_{X_2}f(y)\,d(\mathbf r_\#\mu)(y). If \nu\ll\mu, then \mathbf r_\#\nu\ll\mathbf r_\#\mu. For measurable \mathbf s:X_1\to X_2 and \mathbf r:X_2\to X_3, (\mathbf r\circ\mathbf s)_\#\mu=\mathbf r_\#(\mathbf s_\#\mu). If \mathbf r is continuous, then \mathbf r_\#:\mathcal P(X_1)\to\mathcal P(X_2) is narrowly continuous and \mathbf r(\operatorname{supp}\mu)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf r_\#\mu)=\overline{\mathbf r(\operatorname{supp}\mu)}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pushforward measure assigns to each Borel set the measure of its inverse image. Integration against it equals integration of the pulled-back function. Pushforwards preserve absolute continuity and composition; continuous maps also induce narrowly continuous pushforward operators, with support equal to the closure of the image of the original support.
assumptions_latex: f:X_2\to\mathbb R\text{ is bounded Borel or }\mathbf r_\#\mu\text{-integrable Borel}
\mathbf s:X_1\to X_2,\ \mathbf r:X_2\to X_3\text{ are measurable for composition}
\mathbf r\text{ is continuous for narrow continuity and the support assertions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mathbf r_\#\mu)(B)=\mu(\mathbf r^{-1}(B)),\quad \int f\circ\mathbf r\,d\mu=\int f\,d(\mathbf r_\#\mu),\quad \nu\ll\mu\Rightarrow\mathbf r_\#\nu\ll\mathbf r_\#\mu,\quad (\mathbf r\circ\mathbf s)_\#\mu=\mathbf r_\#(\mathbf s_\#\mu),\quad \mathbf r_\#\text{ is narrowly continuous if }\mathbf r\text{ is continuous},\quad \mathbf r(\operatorname{supp}\mu)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf r_\#\mu)=\overline{\mathbf r(\operatorname{supp}\mu)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Narrow convergence of pushforwards under varying maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint stability of pushforward measures when both the measures and maps vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X_1,X_2 be separable metric spaces. Let \mathbf r_n:X_1\to X_2 be Borel maps converging uniformly to \mathbf r on compact subsets of X_1, and let (\mu_n)\subset\mathcal P(X_1) be tight and converge narrowly to \mu. If \mathbf r is continuous, then (\mathbf r_n)_\#\mu_n converges narrowly to \mathbf r_\#\mu.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a tight narrowly convergent sequence of probability measures is pushed forward by Borel maps converging uniformly on compact sets to a continuous map, then the resulting pushforward measures converge narrowly to the limiting pushforward.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf r_n\to\mathbf r\text{ uniformly on compact subsets of }X_1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mathbf r_n)_\#\mu_n\rightharpoonup\mathbf r_\#\mu\quad\text{narrowly in }\mathcal P(X_2).

children.title: Map-Induced Coupling Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinction between general couplings and those representable by transport maps.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupling \(\gamma\) is map-induced if and only if its conditional measures \(\gamma_x\) are Dirac measures for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\).

notation.meaning: Coupling induced by the graph of T
Disintegration of gamma over its first marginal
Dirac probability measure at a point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between deterministic plans and general Kantorovich couplings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A coupling \(\gamma\) is induced by a measurable map \(T:X\to Y\), namely \(\gamma=(\operatorname{id}_X,T)_\#\mu\), if and only if a disintegration \(\gamma(dx,dy)=\mu(dx)\gamma_x(dy)\) satisfies \(\gamma_x=\delta_{T(x)}\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\). Consequently, any coupling whose conditional measure \(\gamma_x\) is non-Dirac on a set of positive \(\mu\)-measure is not map-induced. In particular, \(\mu\otimes\nu\) is not map-induced when \(\nu\) is non-Dirac.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupling comes from a deterministic map exactly when its conditional target distribution is almost everywhere a Dirac mass.
knowledge_statements.title: Map-Induced Coupling Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the container, and the standard-Borel hypothesis is appropriate for the disintegration characterization. An authoritative locator is required for the existence and measurable Dirac-kernel characterization used in the equivalence.

children.title: Finite-Valued Cost Functions
children.top_down_role: Transport costs taking finite values throughout their domain.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite-valued transport cost is a measurable map \(c:X\times Y\to[0,+\infty)\).

notation.meaning: Transport cost assigned to a source-target pair

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative costs finite at every source-target pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite-valued transport cost is a measurable function
\[
c:X\times Y\longrightarrow[0,+\infty).
\]
Thus \(c(x,y)<+\infty\) for every \((x,y)\in X\times Y\). For a coupling \(\gamma\in\mathcal P(X\times Y)\), its total cost is the extended integral \(\int_{X\times Y}c(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)\), which may still equal \(+\infty\) despite pointwise finiteness of \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-valued transport cost is measurable and finite at every pair, although its integral under a coupling may still be infinite.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Valued Cost Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Finite-Valued Cost Functions leaf and correctly distinguishes pointwise finiteness from integrability. No citation or specific locator supports the adopted transport-cost convention.

children.title: Extended-Valued Cost Functions
children.top_down_role: Costs encoding forbidden transport through infinite values.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An extended-valued transport cost is a measurable map \(c:X\times Y\to[0,+\infty]\), with \(+\infty\) encoding forbidden transport pairs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative costs permitting infinite values as hard constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An extended-valued transport cost is a measurable function
\[
c:X\times Y\longrightarrow[0,+\infty].
\]
Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}c:=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:c(x,y)<+\infty\}\). Assigning \(c(x,y)=+\infty\) excludes the pair \((x,y)\) from every finite-cost plan: if \(\gamma(\{c=+\infty\})>0\), then \(\int c\,d\gamma=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-valued cost may equal infinity, thereby encoding transport pairs that no finite-cost coupling can charge.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Valued Cost Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Extended-Valued Cost Functions leaf and correctly describes infinite cost as a finite-cost feasibility constraint. No source reference or locator is supplied.

children.title: Cost Integrability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes determined by integrability of the transport objective.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The planwise finite-cost condition is \(c\in L^1(\gamma)\), while feasibility of the transport problem requires some \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) with \(\int c\,d\gamma<+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Cost functional evaluated at a coupling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Planwise and problemwise integrability for nonnegative costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cost is integrable with respect to \(\gamma\) precisely when
\[
\mathcal C_c(\gamma):=\int_{X\times Y}c(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)<+\infty,
\]
equivalently \(c\in L^1(\gamma)\) for nonnegative \(c\). Define
\[
\Pi_c(\mu,\nu):=\{\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu):\mathcal C_c(\gamma)<+\infty\}.
\]
The transport problem has a finite-cost feasible plan exactly when \(\Pi_c(\mu,\nu)\neq\varnothing\), equivalently when \(\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\mathcal C_c(\gamma)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A plan is cost-integrable when its cost integral is finite; the transport problem is finite-cost feasible when at least one such coupling exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost Integrability Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the integrability-regime leaf, and the planwise and problemwise conditions are precise for nonnegative measurable costs. No source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Nonintegrable Cost Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failure modes caused by infinite or undefined transport costs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\int_X a\,d\mu=+\infty\) or \(\int_Y b\,d\nu=+\infty\), then every \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) has \(\int c\,d\gamma=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp marginal-moment obstruction for separable nonnegative costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\), the marginal identities give
\[
\int_{X\times Y}c(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)=\int_X a(x)\,d\mu(x)+\int_Y b(y)\,d\nu(y).
\]
Hence, if either marginal integral is infinite, then \(\Pi_c(\mu,\nu)=\varnothing\): no choice of dependence structure can produce a finite-cost coupling. This failure can occur even when \(a\), \(b\), and therefore \(c\), are finite-valued pointwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a separable cost, an infinite required marginal moment forces every coupling to have infinite cost, even if the cost is pointwise finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonintegrable Cost Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and separable-cost obstruction fit the leaf, but no source or locator is supplied. The displayed marginal identity is followed by derivational language and should be recast as a direct statement when the record is revised after sourcing.

children.title: Tightness of Transport Plans
children.top_down_role: Uniform concentration properties for admissible transport-plan families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is uniformly tight in \(\mathcal P(X\times Y)\).

notation.meaning: Set of couplings with fixed marginals
Compact subsets selected to capture marginal mass

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform tightness arising from fixed tight marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), choose compact sets \(K_X\subseteq X\) and \(K_Y\subseteq Y\) such that \(\mu(K_X)\geq1-\varepsilon/2\) and \(\nu(K_Y)\geq1-\varepsilon/2\). Then every \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) satisfies
\[
\gamma(K_X\times K_Y)\geq1-\varepsilon.
\]
Therefore the entire family \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is uniformly tight as a subset of \(\mathcal P(X\times Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Couplings with fixed probability marginals are uniformly tight because compact sets capturing each marginal jointly capture every coupling.
knowledge_statements.title: Tightness of Transport Plans

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform-tightness property is correct for fixed probability marginals on Polish spaces and fits the leaf. The record lacks a source locator and is written partly as a proof by instructing the reader to choose compact sets and deriving the conclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tightness of transport plans with tight marginal families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform tightness of coupling families on products of Polish spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Y\) be Polish spaces, and let \(\mathcal P\subset P(\mathcal X)\) and \(\mathcal Q\subset P(\mathcal Y)\) be tight families. Then \(\Pi(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q):=\{\pi\in P(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y):(\operatorname{pr}_{\mathcal X})_\#\pi\in\mathcal P,\ (\operatorname{pr}_{\mathcal Y})_\#\pi\in\mathcal Q\}\) is tight in \(P(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a product of Polish spaces, all transport plans whose two marginals range over tight families form a tight family.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Y\) are Polish spaces.
\(\mathcal P\subset P(\mathcal X)\) and \(\mathcal Q\subset P(\mathcal Y)\) are tight families.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)\text{ is tight in }P(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y).\)

children.title: Compactness of Feasible Couplings
children.top_down_role: Sequential compactness within sets of couplings having fixed marginals.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupling set \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is nonempty and compact for weak convergence in \(\mathcal P(X\times Y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak compactness of fixed-marginal couplings on Polish spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(\Pi(\mu,
u)\) is nonempty because \(\mu\otimes
u\in\Pi(\mu,
u)\). It is uniformly tight, and it is closed under weak convergence: if \(\gamma_n\in\Pi(\mu,
u)\) and \(\gamma_nightharpoonup\gamma\) in \(\mathcal P(X	imes Y)\), then continuity of the coordinate projections implies \((p_X)_\#\gamma=\mu\) and \((p_Y)_\#\gamma=
u\). Consequently, by weak compactness of uniformly tight families on Polish spaces, \(\Pi(\mu,
u)\) is weakly compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On Polish spaces, the set of all couplings with two fixed probability marginals is nonempty and weakly compact.

children.title: Escape-of-Mass Failures
children.top_down_role: Loss of compactness through mass migration beyond controlled regions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(\gamma_n\in\Pi(\mu_n,\nu_n)\), the family \(\{\gamma_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\) is not tight and has no weakly convergent subsequence.

notation.meaning: Dirac probability measure at the diagonal point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of compactness when prescribed marginals vary without uniform tightness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(n\in\mathbb N\), the unique coupling of \(\mu_n=\delta_n\) and \(\nu_n=\delta_n\) is \(\gamma_n=\delta_{(n,n)}\). For any compact set \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), one has \((n,n)\notin K\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), and hence \(\gamma_n(K)=0\) eventually. Thus \(\{\gamma_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\) is not tight and admits no weakly convergent subsequence. Fixed-marginal compactness therefore does not extend to arbitrarily varying, non-uniformly-tight marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dirac marginals escaping to infinity produce coupling measures that are not tight, so compactness fails when marginals vary without uniform tightness.
knowledge_statements.title: Escape-of-Mass Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample role exactly fits Escape-of-Mass Failures, and the example correctly shows loss of tightness for varying marginals. It has no citation or locator and includes proof-style derivation rather than only the counterexample statement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monge and Kantorovich formulations of static optimal transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines deterministic and relaxed static transport and records their feasibility, attainment, and value-equivalence boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be separable metric Radon spaces, \(c:X	imes Y	o[0,+\infty]\) a Borel function, and \(\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\), \(
u\in\mathcal P(Y)\). The Monge problem is \(\inf\{\int_X c(x,t(x))\,d\mu(x):t:X	o Y	ext{ measurable},\ t_\#\mu=
u\}\), and the Kantorovich problem is \(\min\{\int_{X	imes Y}c(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y):\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu,
u)\}\). A feasible Monge map need not exist, whereas \(\Gamma(\mu,
u)
eq\varnothing\) since \(\mu	imes
u\in\Gamma(\mu,
u)\). If \(c\) is lower semicontinuous, the Kantorovich minimum is attained. If \(c\) is bounded and continuous and \(\mu\) is nonatomic, the Kantorovich minimum equals the Monge infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monge transport optimizes over measurable maps pushing the source measure to the target, whereas Kantorovich transport optimizes over couplings. A Monge map may not exist, but a coupling always does. Lower semicontinuity gives attainment of the Kantorovich problem; bounded continuity of the cost and atomlessness of the source make its value equal to the Monge infimum.
assumptions_latex: X,Y\text{ are separable metric Radon spaces}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible maps and their graph-supported transport plans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A deterministic transport map from \(\mu\) to \(\nu\) is a measurable function \(T:X\to Y\) satisfying
\[
T_\#\mu=\nu.
\]
It induces the coupling \(\gamma_T:=(\operatorname{id}_X,T)_\#\mu\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\), which is concentrated on the graph of \(T\). Its transport cost is
\[

\]
The feasible deterministic class consists of all measurable maps satisfying the pushforward constraint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurable-map feasibility for the Monge problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A measurable map \(T:X\to Y\) is a feasible transport map from \(\mu\) to \(\nu\) when its pushforward equals the target measure:
\[
T_\#\mu=\nu,
\qquad
\text{equivalently }\mu(T^{-1}(B))=\nu(B)\text{ for every Borel }B\subseteq Y.
\]
The feasible Monge class is
\[
\mathcal T(\mu,\nu):=\{T:X\to Y:T\text{ is measurable and }T_\#\mu=\nu\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic transport is feasible precisely when the mass that its measurable map sends into every target Borel set equals the target measure of that set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The obstruction is non-Dirac conditional transport from a positive-mass set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The coupling \(\pi\) is induced by a deterministic transport map exactly when there is a measurable \(T:X\to Y\) such that
\[
\kappa_x=\delta_{T(x)}\quad\text{for }\mu\text{-almost every }x.
\]
Consequently, if the set of \(x\) for which \(\kappa_x\) assigns positive mass to two disjoint Borel subsets of \(Y\) has positive \(\mu\)-measure, then \(\pi\) cannot equal \((\mathrm{id},T)_\#\mu\) for any map \(T\). This is the mass-splitting obstruction to Monge representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transport plan is deterministic exactly when almost every source point has a Dirac conditional destination law; genuine conditional splitting prevents representation by a map.

knowledge_statements.title: Atomic Source Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact deterministic feasibility boundary for a countably atomic source measure with distinct atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\delta_{x_i}\), where the points \(x_i\) are pairwise distinct. A feasible deterministic transport from \(\mu\) to \(\nu\) exists if and only if there are points \(y_i\in Y\) such that
\[
\nu=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\delta_{y_i}.
\]
Thus each source atom must be transported as a whole, although the masses of multiple atoms may merge at a common destination. In particular, no purely atomic source admits a deterministic transport to a nonatomic target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A countably atomic source can reach exactly those targets obtained by sending each whole source atom to one destination, with masses allowed to merge at common destinations.

\(X\) and \(Y\) are standard Borel spaces, \(\mu=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\delta_{x_i}\), and \(\nu\in\mathcal P(Y)\).

u=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\delta_{y_i}\) for some family \((y_i)_{i\in I}\subseteq Y\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvexity of graph-supported couplings with fixed marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(T_0(x)=0\) on \([0,1/2)\) and \(T_0(x)=1\) on \([1/2,1]\), and let \(T_1=1-T_0\). Both maps satisfy \((T_j)_\#\mu=\nu\). However, for
\[
\bar\pi:=\tfrac12(\mathrm{id},T_0)_\#\mu+\tfrac12(\mathrm{id},T_1)_\#\mu,
\]
the conditional destination law at every \(x\) is \(\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\delta_1\). Hence \(\bar\pi\) is not induced by any measurable map, although its two endpoints are feasible Monge couplings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two feasible graph couplings may have a midpoint that splits every source point between destinations and therefore is not a graph coupling.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible Monge couplings are not closed under weak convergence in \(\mathcal P(X\times Y)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak nonclosure caused by increasingly fine deterministic oscillations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\geq1\), define
\[
T_n(x):=\mathbf 1_{[1/2,1)}(\{nx\}).
\]
Each \(T_n\) pushes \(\mu\) to \(\nu\), so \(\pi_n=(\mathrm{id},T_n)_\#\mu\) is a feasible Monge coupling. As \(n\to\infty\),
\[
\pi_n\rightharpoonup\mu\otimes\nu.
\]
The limiting plan has conditional destination law \(\nu\) at every source point and is therefore not induced by a map. Thus the Monge class is not weakly closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rapidly oscillating feasible maps converge weakly to an independent coupling that splits mass at every source point and lies outside the Monge class.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Limits Outside the Monge Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disintegration-kernel representation of weak limits of deterministic graph measures on Polish spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The weak limit admits a disintegration kernel \(x\mapsto\kappa_x\) satisfying
\[
\int_{X\times Y}f(x,y)\,d\pi(x,y)
=
\int_X\left(\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\kappa_x(y)\right)d\mu(x)
\]
for every bounded Borel function \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\). The limiting plan belongs to the Monge class if and only if there is a measurable map \(T:X\to Y\) such that \(\kappa_x=\delta_{T(x)}\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\). A non-Dirac conditional kernel therefore represents relaxed mass splitting outside the Monge class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak limit of graph plans is represented by a conditional destination kernel and remains deterministic exactly when that kernel is almost everywhere Dirac.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are Polish spaces, \(\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\), and \(T_n:X\to Y\) is Borel measurable for every \(n\).
The first marginal of \(\pi\) is \(\mu\), and \(\pi(dx,dy)=\mu(dx)\kappa_x(dy)\) is a disintegration over that marginal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limit \(\pi\) is represented by \(x\mapsto\kappa_x\), and \(\pi=(\mathrm{id}_X,T)_\#\mu\) for some measurable \(T\) if and only if \(\kappa_x\) is Dirac for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal static transport-plan formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The admissible transport plans are
\[
\Pi(\mu,\nu):=\{\pi\in\mathcal P(X\times Y):(p_X)_\#\pi=\mu,\ (p_Y)_\#\pi=\nu\}.
\]
The Kantorovich problem is represented by
\[
K_c(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times Y}c(x,y)\,d\pi(x,y).

Every feasible map \(T\) yields the graph plan \((\mathrm{id},T)_\#\mu\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\), while general plans may distribute the mass at one source point among several destinations.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence by Direct Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence for lower-semicontinuous, bounded-below costs on Polish spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The coupling set \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is nonempty and weakly compact, and the functional
\[
\pi\longmapsto\int_{X\times Y}c(x,y)\,d\pi(x,y)
\]
is weakly lower semicontinuous. The Kantorovich infimum is attained: there exists \(\pi^\star\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) such that
\[
\int_{X\times Y}c\,d\pi^\star
=
\min_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times Y}c\,d\pi
=
K_c(\mu,\nu).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-semicontinuous bounded-below cost on Polish spaces, every finite Kantorovich problem has an optimal transport plan.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are Polish spaces, \(\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\), and \(\nu\in\mathcal P(Y)\).
\(c:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous and bounded below.

knowledge_statements.title: Stability Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of value stability under weak convergence alone for an unbounded cost without moment control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The marginals satisfy \(\mu_n\rightharpoonup\delta_0\) and \(\nu_n\rightharpoonup\delta_0\). Because the target is \(\delta_0\), the only coupling gives
\[
K_c(\mu_n,\nu_n)=\int_{\mathbb R}|x|\,d\mu_n(x)=1
\quad\text{for every }n.

The limiting value is
\[
K_c(\delta_0,\delta_0)=0.

Thus weak marginal convergence alone does not ensure value stability for an unbounded cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete Kantorovich relaxation and coupling polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines mass-splitting couplings with prescribed marginals, their polyhedral and transpose-symmetry properties, and the resulting discrete optimal-transport linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbf a\in\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(\mathbf b\in\mathbb R_+^m\) have equal total mass. The discrete Kantorovich relaxation replaces a deterministic transport assignment by a coupling \(\mathbf P\) in
\[
\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\{\mathbf P\in\mathbb R_+^{n\times m}:\mathbf P\mathbb 1_m=\mathbf a,\ \mathbf P^{\mathsf T}\mathbb 1_n=\mathbf b\}.
\]
The set \(\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\) is a bounded convex polytope, and
\[
\mathbf P\in\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\iff \mathbf P^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbf U(\mathbf b,\mathbf a).
\]
For \(\mathbf C\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), the Kantorovich transport value is
\[
L_{\mathbf C}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\min_{\mathbf P\in\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)}\langle\mathbf C,\mathbf P\rangle
=\min_{\mathbf P\in\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)}\sum_{i,j}C_{ij}P_{ij}.
\]
This is a linear program, and its optimal coupling need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative source and target histograms having equal total mass, the Kantorovich relaxation permits mass splitting. Couplings are nonnegative matrices with the prescribed row and column sums; they form a bounded convex polytope and transpose into couplings with the marginals reversed. Minimizing transport cost over this set is a linear program whose optimizer need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\{\mathbf P\ge 0:\mathbf P\mathbb 1_m=\mathbf a,\ \mathbf P^{\mathsf T}\mathbb 1_n=\mathbf b\}\text{ is a bounded convex polytope},\quad \mathbf P\in\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\iff\mathbf P^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbf U(\mathbf b,\mathbf a),\quad L_{\mathbf C}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\min_{\mathbf P\in\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)}\langle\mathbf C,\mathbf P\rangle.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-supported Kantorovich plans generated by deterministic transport maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The plan induced by \(T\) is \(\gamma_T:=(\operatorname{Id}_X,T)_\#\mu\), characterized by \[\int_{X\times Y}f(x,y)\,d\gamma_T(x,y)=\int_X f(x,T(x))\,d\mu(x)\] for every bounded Borel function \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Narrow Convergence of Map-Induced Plans
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between convergence of maps and convergence of their graph plans under a fixed reference measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X,Y$ be separable metric spaces, $\mu\in\mathcal P(X)$, and let $\mathbf r_n,\mathbf r:X\to Y$ be Borel maps. Then $(\mathbf i\times\mathbf r_n)_\#\mu\rightharpoonup(\mathbf i\times\mathbf r)_\#\mu$ narrowly in $\mathcal P(X\times Y)$ iff $\mathbf r_n\to\mathbf r$ in $\mu$-measure. Under these equivalent conditions, for $1\le p<\infty$, one has $\mathbf r_n\to\mathbf r$ in $L^p(\mu;Y)$ iff the pushforwards $(\mathbf r_n)_\#\mu$ have uniformly integrable $p$-moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Borel maps defined on a fixed probability space, their graph plans converge narrowly to the graph plan of a limiting map exactly when the maps converge in measure. Under this convergence, convergence in Lp is equivalent to uniform integrability of the p-moments of the image measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mathbf i\times\mathbf r_n)_\#\mu\rightharpoonup(\mathbf i\times\mathbf r)_\#\mu\iff\mathbf r_n\to\mathbf r\text{ in measure};\quad \mathbf r_n\to\mathbf r\text{ in }L^p\iff\{(\mathbf r_n)_\#\mu\}\text{ has uniformly integrable }p\text{-moments under these equivalent conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criterion for Unique Solvability of the Monge Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions ensuring that the Kantorovich optimizer is unique, deterministic, and therefore yields the unique Monge solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mu)$ and $(\mathcal Y,
u)$ be Polish probability spaces. Let $a\in L^1(\mu)$ and $b\in L^1(
u)$ be real-valued upper semicontinuous functions, and let $c:\mathcal X	imes\mathcal Y	o\mathbb R$ be lower semicontinuous with $c(x,y)\ge a(x)+b(y)$ for all $(x,y)$. Suppose $C(\mu,
u)<+\infty$ and, for every $c$-convex function $\psi:\mathcal X	o\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, the set $\{x\in\mathcal X:|\partial_c\psi(x)|>1\}$ is $\mu$-negligible. Then there is a unique-in-law optimal coupling $(X,Y)$ of $(\mu,
u)$, and it is deterministic. Among all couplings, it is characterized by the existence of a $c$-convex function $\psi$ such that $Y\in\partial_c\psi(X)$ almost surely. Consequently, the Monge problem from $\mu$ to $
u$ admits a unique solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assume the stated semicontinuity, integrable lower-bound, and finite-cost conditions. If the c-subdifferential of every c-convex function contains at most one point for almost every source point, then the optimal coupling is unique in law and is induced by a transport map. It is characterized by lying almost surely in the c-subdifferential of a c-convex potential, and the Monge problem has a unique solution.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal X,\mu)\text{ and }(\mathcal Y,\nu)\text{ are Polish probability spaces}
a\in L^1(\mu),\quad b\in L^1(\nu),\quad a,b\text{ are real-valued and upper semicontinuous}
c:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\text{ is lower semicontinuous and }c(x,y)\ge a(x)+b(y)\quad\forall(x,y)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\text{ an optimal coupling in law};\ \text{it is deterministic and is characterized by }Y\in\partial_c\psi(X)\ \text{a.s. for some }c\text{-convex }\psi;\ \text{hence the Monge problem admits a unique solution.}

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Relaxation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict separation between deterministic and relaxed transport values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \[C_M:=\inf_{T_\#\mu=
u}\int_X c(x,T(x))\,d\mu(x),\qquad C_K:=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,
u)}\int_{X	imes Y}c(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y),\] with \(C_M:=+\infty\) if no admissible map exists. Every admissible map induces a coupling, so \(C_K\le C_M\). The relaxation has a positive gap precisely when \(C_K<C_M\). This includes the infinite-gap case where \(C_K<+\infty\) but no measurable map pushes \(\mu\) to \(
u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxation gap is positive exactly when the best coupling costs strictly less than the Monge infimum, including when finite-cost couplings exist but no admissible transport map does.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Polish spaces, \(\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\), and \(\nu\in\mathcal P(Y)\).
\(c:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is measurable and both displayed infima are well-defined as extended-real values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A positive relaxation gap occurs exactly when \(C_K<C_M\).

notation.meaning: Monge optimal value, equal to positive infinity when no admissible map exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Transport-Map Recovery Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure to represent any relaxed optimizer by a deterministic map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\operatorname{Opt}_K(\mu,
u)\) denote the nonempty set of Kantorovich minimizers. Transport-map recovery fails when \[\operatorname{Opt}_K(\mu,
u)\cap igl\{(\operatorname{Id}_X,T)_\#\mu:T:X	o Y	ext{ is Borel measurable and }T_\#\mu=
u igr\}=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, for every optimal coupling, its disintegration with respect to \(\mu\) is non-Dirac on a set of positive \(\mu\)-measure. This structural failure does not by itself imply a positive value gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovery fails when no optimal coupling is induced by an admissible deterministic map; equivalently, every optimal coupling splits mass on a source set of positive measure. This need not create a value gap.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are Polish spaces with \(\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\) and \(\nu\in\mathcal P(Y)\).
The Kantorovich problem over \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) has at least one optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transport-map recovery fails exactly when no Kantorovich optimizer equals \((\operatorname{Id}_X,T)_\#\mu\) for a Borel measurable map \(T\) satisfying \(T_\#\mu=\nu\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Monge Infima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite deterministic infimum approached but not realized by any map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Monge infimum is nonattained when \[C_M:=\inf_{T_\#\mu=\nu}J(T)<+\infty\qquad\text{and}\qquad J(T)>C_M\ \text{for every admissible }T.\] Equivalently, for every integer \(k\ge1\), there exists an admissible map \(T_k\) such that \(J(T_k)\le C_M+1/k\), but no admissible map realizes \(C_M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite Monge infimum is nonattained when admissible maps approach its value but no admissible map realizes it.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are measurable spaces, \(\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\), and \(\nu\in\mathcal P(Y)\).
At least one measurable map \(T:X\to Y\) satisfies \(T_\#\mu=\nu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Monge infimum is nonattained exactly when every admissible \(T\) satisfies \(J(T)>C_M\), although admissible maps approach \(C_M\).

notation.meaning: Monge objective evaluated at a transport map.
Infimum of the Monge objective over admissible maps.

children.top_down_role: Balanced discrete transport with one-to-one allocation structure.

assumptions_latex: Every source and target item must be matched exactly once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The permutation problem and its linear relaxation over the doubly stochastic polytope have the same optimal value, and an optimal permutation matrix exists.

notation.meaning: Symmetric group of permutations of the item indices.
Birkhoff polytope of doubly stochastic matrices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balanced one-to-one bipartite assignment and its exact linear-programming formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear assignment value admits the equivalent representations \[\min_{\sigma\in S_n}\sum_{i=1}^n c_{i,\sigma(i)}=\min_{X\in\mathcal B_n}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij},\] where \[\mathcal B_n:=\left\{X\in\mathbb R_+^{n\times n}:\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}=1\right\}.\] Every extreme point of \(\mathcal B_n\) is a permutation matrix; therefore the linear relaxation has an optimal permutation matrix whenever the cost entries are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-to-one assignment minimizes total pair cost. Its doubly stochastic linear relaxation is exact because the feasible polytope has permutation matrices as its extreme points.

children.title: Weighted Matching Problems
children.top_down_role: Discrete transport interpreted through weighted bipartite matching.

assumptions_latex: Vertex requirements \(b_v\) and edge capacities \(u_e\) are nonnegative integers.
Each edge has a real cost \(w_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimum-cost weighted matching is an integral feasible vector minimizing \(\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e\) under the incidence and capacity constraints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost capacitated bipartite matching with prescribed vertex multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible capacitated bipartite \(b\)-matching is a vector \(x\in\mathbb Z_+^E\) satisfying \[\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e=b_v\quad(v\in U\cup V),\qquad 0\le x_e\le u_e\quad(e\in E).\] The weighted matching problem is \[\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e:x\text{ satisfies these constraints}\right\}.\] Feasibility requires balanced total multiplicity \(\sum_{v\in U}b_v=\sum_{v\in V}b_v\), together with the capacity-compatible cut conditions imposed by \(E\) and \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted bipartite matching assigns integral edge multiplicities satisfying vertex requirements and capacities while minimizing total edge cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Matching Problems

children.title: Integral Optimizer Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where optimal discrete plans occur at integral configurations.

assumptions_latex: The constraint matrix is the node-edge incidence matrix of a finite bipartite graph, possibly augmented by identity rows for integral bounds.
The right-hand side and all finite variable bounds are integral.
The linear program is feasible and has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible polyhedron has integral vertices and possesses an integral optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality supplied by bipartite incidence and integral marginal data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[P:=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}.\] The bipartite node-edge incidence matrix \(A\) is totally unimodular, and adjoining signed identity rows preserves total unimodularity. Hence every vertex of \(P\) is integral when \(b\) and the finite components of \(u\) are integral. Consequently, for every cost vector \(w\in\mathbb R^E\), if \(\min_{x\in P}w^\top x\) is finite and attained, then at least one optimal solution belongs to \(\mathbb Z^E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bipartite assignment relaxations have integral vertices, and therefore integral optimizers, when their requirements and capacities are integral and the incidence structure is preserved.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Optimizer Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The total-unimodularity theorem and optimizer-integrality conclusion are correctly delimited and appropriately classified, but no authoritative theorem locator is provided.

assumptions_latex: Assignment variables are required to be integral in the combinatorial problem.
The linear relaxation permits nonnegative real variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonintegral marginal requirements can force fractional relaxed solutions and eliminate every integral assignment.

notation.meaning: Assignment from the single left vertex to target j.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of assignment integrality when integral right-hand-side hypotheses fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider one left vertex of supply \(1\) and two right vertices, each of demand \(1/2\). The relaxed balance equations are \[x_1+x_2=1,\qquad x_1=\tfrac12,\qquad x_2=\tfrac12,\qquad x_1,x_2\ge0.\] Their unique solution is fractional, while no solution lies in \(\mathbb Z^2\). Thus total unimodularity alone does not imply integral vertices without an integral right-hand side. More generally, additional side constraints that destroy total unimodularity can create fractional vertices even when the original marginals are integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional assignments arise when marginal data are nonintegral, or when added constraints destroy total unimodularity; then the relaxed problem may have no integral feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Assignment Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly marks failure of the integral-right-hand-side hypothesis, and the side-constraint observation is properly stated as a possibility. A specific supporting source is still required.

children.title: Histogram Transport Problems
children.top_down_role: Transport between finitely supported mass histograms.

knowledge_statements.title: Histogram Transport Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite discrete optimal transport between histograms of equal total mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The histogram transport problem is \[\min_{\pi\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times n}}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}\pi_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j=1}^n\pi_{ij}=a_i\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \sum_{i=1}^m\pi_{ij}=b_j\ (1\le j\le n),\] using the convention \(0\cdot(+\infty)=0\). A feasible matrix \(\pi\) is a discrete transport plan. If some \(c_{ij}=+\infty\), a finite-cost feasible plan must assign zero mass to those entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Histogram transport minimizes total transport cost over nonnegative matrices having the prescribed row and column sums. Infinite-cost edges must carry zero mass in every finite-cost plan.
assumptions_latex: \(a\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(b\in\mathbb R_+^n\) satisfy \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Discrete optimal transport minimizes \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}\pi_{ij}\) over nonnegative matrices with row sums \(a\) and column sums \(b\), with \(0\cdot(+\infty)=0\).

notation.meaning: Transport matrix carrying mass from source bin i to target bin j.

children.title: Transportation Polytope Geometry
children.top_down_role: Feasible-plan geometry determined by prescribed row and column masses.

knowledge_statements.title: Transportation Polytope Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full bipartite transportation polytope with strictly positive margins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\mathcal T(a,b):=\left\{\pi\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times n}:\sum_j\pi_{ij}=a_i,\ \sum_i\pi_{ij}=b_j\right\}.\] This set is a nonempty compact convex polytope; for example, \(\pi_{ij}=a_ib_j/M\) is strictly positive and feasible. Among the \(m+n\) marginal equalities, exactly one is redundant, so their rank is \(m+n-1\). Because a strictly positive feasible point exists, nonnegativity does not reduce the affine dimension, and \[\dim\mathcal T(a,b)=mn-(m+n-1)=(m-1)(n-1).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With positive equal-mass margins, feasible transport matrices form a nonempty compact convex polytope of affine dimension (m−1)(n−1).
assumptions_latex: The margins have common total mass \(M:=\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transportation polytope is nonempty, compact, convex, and has affine dimension \((m-1)(n-1)\).

notation.meaning: Transportation polytope with margins a and b.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Acyclic Support of Transportation-Polytope Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the support graph and sparsity of extreme discrete transport plans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf a\in\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(\mathbf b\in\mathbb R_+^m\) have equal total mass, and let \(\mathbf P\) be an extreme point of \(\mathbf U(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\). Form the bipartite support graph \(G(\mathbf P)\) with an edge \(\{i,j'\}\) exactly when \(P_{ij}>0\). Then \(G(\mathbf P)\) is acyclic. Consequently, \(|\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf P)|\le n+m-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bipartite support graph of an extreme transportation plan has no cycles, so the plan has at most n+m−1 positive entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(\mathbf P)\text{ is acyclic},\qquad |\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf P)|\le n+m-1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Birkhoff theorem for the uniform transportation polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the extreme points of the uniformly normalized doubly stochastic polytope and gives the resulting deterministic-transport conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\geq1\) and \(C=\{M\in\mathbb R_+^{N\times N}:\sum_{i=1}^N M_{ij}=1/N\ \forall j,\ \sum_{j=1}^N M_{ij}=1/N\ \forall i\}\). Then \(\operatorname{ext}(C)=\{M:M_{ij}=N^{-1}\delta_{i,\sigma(j)},\ \sigma\in S_N\}\). Consequently, if \(\mu=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{x_i}\) and \(\nu=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N\delta_{y_j}\), with the \(x_i\) distinct and the \(y_j\) distinct, an optimal Kantorovich plan can be chosen to be induced by a transport map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extreme points of the nonnegative matrix polytope having every row and column sum equal to 1/N are exactly the 1/N-scaled permutation matrices. Consequently, optimal transport between two uniform measures on N distinct atoms can be realized by a deterministic map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ext}(C)=\left\{M:M_{ij}=\frac1N\delta_{i,\sigma(j)},\ \sigma\in S_N\right\};\quad \mu=\frac1N\sum_i\delta_{x_i},\ \nu=\frac1N\sum_j\delta_{y_j}\Rightarrow\text{an optimal transport plan is induced by a map}.

children.title: Extreme-Point Transport Plans
children.top_down_role: Vertex structure and sparse representatives of transportation polytopes.

assumptions_latex: \(a\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\) and \(b\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) have equal total mass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The plan \(\pi\) is an extreme point of \(\mathcal T(a,b)\) if and only if its positive-support bipartite graph is acyclic.

notation.meaning: Bipartite graph whose edges are the positive entries of the transport plan.
Transportation polytope with margins a and b.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial characterization of vertices by acyclic positive support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_\pi\) have left vertices \(1,\ldots,m\), right vertices \(1,\ldots,n\), and edge \((i,j)\) exactly when \(\pi_{ij}>0\). Then \(\pi\) is an extreme point of \(\mathcal T(a,b)\) if and only if \(G_\pi\) is a forest. Consequently every extreme transport plan has at most \(m+n-1\) positive entries. A nondegenerate extreme point has exactly \(m+n-1\) positive entries, in which case its support graph is a spanning tree; degenerate extreme points have fewer positive entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transport plan is a polytope vertex exactly when its positive entries contain no bipartite cycle. Thus a vertex uses at most m+n−1 transport edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Transport Plans

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forest-support characterization and support-size consequences are correct for positive margins and fit the theorem container, but no authoritative theorem or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Polytope Degeneracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial degeneracies caused by marginal mass relations.

assumptions_latex: The marginals satisfy \(a\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{m}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{n}\), and \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(a,b)\) is nondegenerate exactly when no proper nonempty index sets \(I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(J\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfy \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\).

notation.meaning: Transportation polytope with row marginal a and column marginal b.
Index sets witnessing a balanced proper subproblem.

review_flags: Standard transportation-polytope criterion; supplied locators do not support the claim.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-marginal degeneracy criterion for classical transportation polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(a,b)=\{\pi\in\mathbb{R}_+^{m\times n}:\pi\mathbf 1=a,\ \pi^{\mathsf T}\mathbf 1=b\}\). The positive-marginal transportation polytope lies in a degenerate regime precisely when there exist proper nonempty sets \(I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(J\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\). Equivalently, nondegeneracy requires every such pair to have unequal subtotal masses. In the degenerate regime, a feasible support can split along the balanced cut \(I\times J\), and some basic feasible solutions have fewer than \(m+n-1\) positive entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-marginal transportation polytope is degenerate exactly when proper row and column subsets have equal total mass.
knowledge_statements.title: Polytope Degeneracy Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the degeneracy-regime leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no citation supports the exact iff criterion or the basic-feasible-solution claim.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semi-discrete transport and its Laguerre-cell representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the semi-discrete support regime and conditionally records the continuous-to-discrete cell representation, including the quadratic-cost specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\nu=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\delta_{y_i}\) be discrete and let \(\mu\) be arbitrary. Optimal transport between \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) is semi-discrete. If \(\mu\) has a density and the continuous-to-discrete transport is represented by an optimal map, then, up to \(\mu\)-null sets, the source is partitioned into disjoint cells \(L_i\) mapped to the atoms \(y_i\). For \(c(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert^2\), these cells are Laguerre cells, equivalently weighted Voronoi or power-diagram cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transport is semi-discrete when one measure is discrete and the other is arbitrary. When a continuous source is transported to discrete target atoms through an optimal map, the source is partitioned, up to null sets, into cells assigned to those atoms. Under squared Euclidean cost, the cells are Laguerre cells, also known as weighted Voronoi or power-diagram cells.
assumptions_latex: \mu\text{ has a density for the cell-partition representation}
\text{the transport is represented by an optimal map for the map-induced cell conclusion}
c(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert^2\text{ for the Laguerre-cell conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{L_i\}_{i=1}^n\text{ partitions the source up to }\mu\text{-null sets and maps }L_i\text{ to }y_i;\text{ for quadratic cost, the }L_i\text{ are Laguerre cells.}

children.title: Laguerre Cell Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Weighted cell partitions arising in semi-discrete transport.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cells \(L_i(w)\) cover \(X\), and their interiors are pairwise disjoint.

notation.meaning: Laguerre cell associated with site i and weight vector w.

review_flags: Standard semi-discrete transport definition; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-cost Laguerre decomposition restricted to the source domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\), define the Laguerre cell
\[
L_i(w)=\bigl\{x\in X:\lVert x-y_i\rVert^2-w_i\leq \lVert x-y_j\rVert^2-w_j\ \text{for every }j\bigr\}.
\]
Then \(X=\bigcup_{i=1}^N L_i(w)\), and the interiors of distinct cells are disjoint. A point belongs to several cells exactly when the minimum weighted squared distance is attained by several sites. Thus \(\{L_i(w)\}_{i=1}^N\) is a closed-cell decomposition, modulo its shared boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Laguerre cells assign each source point to sites minimizing weighted squared distance; they cover the domain with disjoint interiors.
knowledge_statements.title: Laguerre Cell Decompositions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. Moreover, pairwise-disjoint interiors require an appropriate full-dimensional or relative-interior setting; for arbitrary X contained in a tie hyperplane, distinct cells can have overlapping relative interiors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Laguerre Cells and the Constant-Weight Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and covering property of semi-discrete Laguerre cells, including the failure of literal disjointness at ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(c:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\), let \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\in\mathcal Y\), and let \(\mathbf g\in\mathbb R^m\). Define
\[
\mathbb L_{\mathbf g}(y_j):=\left\{x\in\mathcal X: c(x,y_j)-g_j\le c(x,y_{j'})-g_{j'}\ \text{for every }j'\ne j\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\mathcal X=\bigcup_{j=1}^m\mathbb L_{\mathbf g}(y_j).
\]
The cells are disjoint at points having a unique minimizing index; ties can place a point in multiple cells unless a tie-breaking convention is imposed. If \(\mathbf g\) is constant, these cells are the unweighted \(c\)-Voronoi cells. They coincide with the ordinary Euclidean Voronoi cells when ordering by \(c(x,y)\) is equivalent to ordering by Euclidean distance, as for Euclidean distance or squared Euclidean distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Laguerre cell contains the points for which one site's cost minus its weight is minimal. The cells cover the source space, but ties can make their closed-cell definitions overlap unless minimizers are unique or ties are broken. Constant weights recover the unweighted cost-Voronoi cells and, for Euclidean distance-type costs, the ordinary Voronoi diagram.
assumptions_latex: Literal disjointness requires unique minimizing indices or an explicit tie-breaking convention.
The ordinary Euclidean Voronoi specialization requires that comparison by \(c(x,y)\) agree with comparison by Euclidean distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal X=\bigcup_{j=1}^m\mathbb L_{\mathbf g}(y_j)\); uniqueness or tie-breaking yields a disjoint decomposition, while constant weights yield unweighted \(c\)-Voronoi cells.

children.title: Power-Diagram Representation
children.top_down_role: Euclidean weighted-diagram representation of semi-discrete transport cells.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each Laguerre cell is the intersection of \(X\) with a power-diagram cell having power weights \(w_i\).

notation.meaning: Affine score equivalent to weighted squared distance.

review_flags: Standard computational-geometry representation; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine half-space representation of quadratic Laguerre cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Expanding the quadratic terms gives
\[
\lVert x-y_i\rVert^2-w_i\leq\lVert x-y_j\rVert^2-w_j
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
2\langle x,y_i-y_j\rangle\geq \lVert y_i\rVert^2-w_i-\lVert y_j\rVert^2+w_j.
\]
Consequently,
\[
L_i(w)=X\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^N\bigl\{x:2\langle x,y_i-y_j\rangle\geq \lVert y_i\rVert^2-w_i-\lVert y_j\rVert^2+w_j\bigr\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(L_i(w)=\{x\in X:s_i(x)\geq s_j(x)\ \text{for all }j\}\), where \(s_i(x)=2\langle x,y_i\rangle-\lVert y_i\rVert^2+w_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding weighted squared distances represents every Laguerre cell as an intersection of affine half-spaces, hence as a power-diagram cell.
knowledge_statements.title: Power-Diagram Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The half-space expansion and representation content kind fit the leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Cell-Mass Geometry
children.top_down_role: Dependence of cell masses on weights and target sites.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu=\rho(x)\,dx\) on \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), and cell interfaces have zero \(\mu\)-mass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mass map obeys \(M(w+t\mathbf 1)=M(w)\), \(\sum_iM_i(w)=\mu(X)\), and \(\partial M_i/\partial w_j=-\int_{F_{ij}(w)}\rho/(2\lVert y_i-y_j\rVert)\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}\) for \(i\ne j\).

notation.meaning: Common interface between cells i and j.

review_flags: Differentiability formula requires regular interfaces and trace regularity of the density.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mass-map invariance and facet derivative in a regular Laguerre regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(M_i(w)=\mu(L_i(w))\). Then \(M(w+t\mathbf 1)=M(w)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^N M_i(w)=\mu(X)\). At a weight vector where all relevant interfaces are regular and differentiation under moving facets is valid, for \(i\ne j\),
\[
\frac{\partial M_i}{\partial w_j}(w)=-\int_{F_{ij}(w)}\frac{\rho(x)}{2\lVert y_i-y_j\rVert}\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x).
\]
The diagonal derivative satisfies \(\partial M_i/\partial w_i=-\sum_{j\ne i}\partial M_i/\partial w_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cell masses conserve total mass, ignore common weight shifts, and vary across shared facets according to weighted interface area.
knowledge_statements.title: Cell-Mass Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The invariance and conservation claims are standard, but the facet-derivative formula needs precise geometric and density regularity assumptions and an authoritative locator.

children.title: Cell-Boundary Degeneracies
children.top_down_role: Ties, empty cells, and unstable combinatorial interfaces.

assumptions_latex: \(L_i(w)\) are quadratic Laguerre cells for distinct sites in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive source mass on tie sets or nontransversal cell incidences can destroy differentiability of the cell-mass and dual-gradient maps.

notation.meaning: Tie set between sites i and j.

review_flags: Failure mechanisms are standard but need a dedicated semi-discrete transport source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary events limiting smooth cell-mass sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The regular cell-mass calculus fails at weights \(w\) when a tie set \(B_{ij}(w)\) has positive \(\mu\)-mass, when a cell is created or disappears with nonregular contact, or when several interfaces meet nontransversally on a set carrying relevant boundary measure. In particular, if \(\mu(B_{ij}(w))>0\), an arbitrarily small perturbation of \(w_i-w_j\) can reassign positive mass between cells \(i\) and \(j\). Hence \(M(w)=(\mu(L_i(w)))_i\) need not be continuous under arbitrary singular sources and need not be differentiable at such degenerate configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive mass on ties, cell birth or death, and nontransversal interfaces are boundaries of smooth Laguerre cell-mass geometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Cell-Boundary Degeneracies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind matches the leaf, but the continuity and differentiability failure mechanisms are uncited and require a source specifying the relevant singular-measure and interface hypotheses.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a probability measure on \(X\), \(\nu=\sum_{i=1}^N b_i\delta_{y_i}\), and \(c\) is measurable with finite primal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transport value equals \(\sup_{w\in\mathbb{R}^N}\left[\sum_i b_iw_i+\int_X\min_i(c(x,y_i)-w_i)\,d\mu(x)\right]\) under Kantorovich duality hypotheses.

notation.meaning: Transport couplings of the two marginals.

review_flags: Standard Kantorovich dual specialization; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-target specialization of Kantorovich duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\nu=\sum_{i=1}^N b_i\delta_{y_i}\), where \(b_i>0\) and \(\sum_i b_i=1\). Define
\[
D(w)=\sum_{i=1}^N b_iw_i+\int_X\min_{1\leq i\leq N}\bigl(c(x,y_i)-w_i\bigr)\,d\mu(x).
\]
Under hypotheses ensuring Kantorovich duality and attainment of the displayed integrals,
\[
\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times\{y_i\}}c(x,y)\,d\pi(x,y)=\sup_{w\in\mathbb{R}^N}D(w).
\]
If ties have zero \(\mu\)-mass, then \(D\) is differentiable and \(\partial D/\partial w_i=b_i-\mu(L_i(w))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a discrete target, Kantorovich duality becomes a finite-dimensional concave maximization whose gradient is target mass minus cell mass.
knowledge_statements.title: Semi-Discrete Dual Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality kind fits the topic, but no source is supplied. The primal integral domain written as X times {y_i} leaves i unbound and should instead denote X times the finite target support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Semi-Discrete Transport Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of the transport cost when the target marginal has finite support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\beta=\sum_{j=1}^m b_j\delta_{y_j}\) and
\[
\mathbf g^{\bar c}(x)=\min_{1\le j\le m}\bigl(c(x,y_j)-g_j\bigr).
\]
Under the hypotheses of the semi-discrete Kantorovich dual formulation,
\[
\mathcal L_c(\alpha,\beta)=\max_{\mathbf g\in\mathbb R^m}\mathcal E(\mathbf g),
\qquad
\mathcal E(\mathbf g):=\int_{\mathcal X}\mathbf g^{\bar c}(x)\,d\alpha(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m b_jg_j.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the target measure is supported on m points, the semi-discrete Kantorovich dual is a finite-dimensional maximization over one weight per target point. The objective is the source integral of the discrete backward cost transform plus the target-weighted sum of those weights.
assumptions_latex: The standing hypotheses of the cited semi-discrete Kantorovich dual formulation hold, including existence of the displayed integrals and maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L_c(\alpha,\beta)=\max_{\mathbf g\in\mathbb R^m}\left[\int_{\mathcal X}\mathbf g^{\bar c}(x)\,d\alpha(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m b_jg_j\right].\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete Backward Cost Transform
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-support backward cost transform used in semi-discrete transport duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(c:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\) and \(\beta=\sum_{j=1}^m b_j\delta_{y_j}\). For \(\mathbf g\in\mathbb R^m\), its discrete \(\bar c\)-transform is
\[
\mathbf g^{\bar c}(x):=\min_{1\le j\le m}\bigl(c(x,y_j)-g_j\bigr),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.
\]
This is the ordinary \(\bar c\)-transform with minimization restricted to the finite support of \(\beta\). If \(c(\cdot,y_j)\) is continuous for every \(j\), then \(\mathbf g^{\bar c}\in C(\mathcal X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finitely supported target measure, the discrete backward cost transform of a vector g is the pointwise minimum of c(x,y_j)-g_j over the target sites. It is the ordinary transform restricted to those sites and is continuous when each cost function c(·,y_j) is continuous.
assumptions_latex: For the continuity conclusion, \(c(\cdot,y_j)\in C(\mathcal X)\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbf g^{\bar c}(x)=\min_{1\le j\le m}(c(x,y_j)-g_j)\); under the stated continuity assumption, \(\mathbf g^{\bar c}\in C(\mathcal X)\).

assumptions_latex: Independent samples \(X_k\sim\mu\) are available, and \(b\) is the discrete target mass vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The averaged projected stochastic supergradient iterates provide an approximate maximizer of the semi-discrete dual objective.
review_flags: Convergence conditions and rates depend on the chosen step schedule and boundedness assumptions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected stochastic supergradient ascent for the finite-dimensional dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input sites \(y_i\), target masses \(b_i\), steps \(\eta_k>0\), and samples \(X_k\sim\mu\). Initialize \(w^0\in H=\{w\in\mathbb{R}^N:\sum_iw_i=0\}\). For \(k\geq0\), choose
\[
I_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\leq i\leq N}\bigl(c(X_k,y_i)-w_i^k\bigr),\qquad g_k=b-e_{I_k},
\]
and update \(w^{k+1}=\operatorname{proj}_H(w^k+\eta_kg_k)\). Stop after \(K\) samples and output the weighted average \(\bar w_K=(\sum_{k<K}\eta_kw^k)/(\sum_{k<K}\eta_k)\), or stop earlier when an empirical mass residual is below a prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample the source, assign each sample to its cheapest weighted site, and ascend the dual using target mass minus sampled assignment.

children.title: Atomic Source Regime
children.top_down_role: Transport problems whose source measure contains point masses.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Polish space and \(\mu\) is a finite Borel measure on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The source is purely atomic exactly when \(\mu=\sum_{k\in K}a_k\delta_{x_k}\) for an at most countable set of distinct points with \(a_k>0\).

notation.meaning: At most countable atom index set.

review_flags: Standard measure-theoretic definition; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Purely atomic finite source measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite Borel source measure \(\mu\) on a Polish space \(X\) is in the purely atomic regime when there exist an at most countable index set \(K\), distinct points \(x_k\in X\), and masses \(a_k>0\) such that
\[
\mu=\sum_{k\in K}a_k\delta_{x_k},\qquad \sum_{k\in K}a_k=\mu(X).
\]
Equivalently, every measurable set of positive \(\mu\)-mass contains a \(\mu\)-atom. Transport plans may split each mass \(a_k\), whereas a deterministic map must send the entire atom at \(x_k\) to one image point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A purely atomic source is a finite or countable weighted sum of Dirac masses; deterministic maps cannot split any source atom.
knowledge_statements.title: Atomic Source Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the atomic-source leaf, but the countable representation and stated equivalence have no cited measure-theory source.

children.title: Singular Nonatomic Source Regime
children.top_down_role: Sources singular to volume measure without atomic concentration.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is Borel and \(\mu\) is a finite Borel measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is characterized by \(\mu\perp\mathcal L^d\) and \(\mu(\{x\})=0\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: A Lebesgue-null carrier of the source.

review_flags: Standard measure decomposition terminology; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomless measures singular with respect to ambient Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite Borel source measure \(\mu\) on \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is singular nonatomic when
\[
\mu\perp\mathcal L^d
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mu(\{x\})=0\ \text{for every }x\in X.
\]
Thus there is a Borel set \(S\subset X\) with \(\mathcal L^d(S)=0\) and \(\mu(X\setminus S)=0\), but no singleton has positive mass. This regime includes measures distributed continuously on lower-dimensional sets and does not satisfy the ambient absolute-continuity hypothesis used in the standard Euclidean quadratic-map theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular nonatomic source lives on a Lebesgue-null set but assigns zero mass to every individual point.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Nonatomic Source Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly targets the singular nonatomic regime, but no inspectable source supports the terminology and characterization.

children.title: Mixed Source Regime
children.top_down_role: Sources combining atomic, singular, or absolutely continuous components.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is Borel and \(\mu\) is a finite Borel measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mixed regime has both a nonzero atomic component \(\mu_{\mathrm{at}}\) and a nonzero nonatomic component \(\mu_{\mathrm{na}}\).

notation.meaning: Purely atomic component of the source.

review_flags: Standard atomic–nonatomic decomposition; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical mixture of atomic and atomless source components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every finite Borel measure \(\mu\) admits the decomposition
\[
\mu=\mu_{\mathrm{at}}+\mu_{\mathrm{na}},
\qquad
\mu_{\mathrm{at}}=\sum_{x:\,\mu(\{x\})>0}\mu(\{x\})\delta_x,
\]
where \(\mu_{\mathrm{na}}(\{x\})=0\) for every \(x\). The source lies in the mixed regime when \(\mu_{\mathrm{at}}(X)>0\) and \(\mu_{\mathrm{na}}(X)>0\). The nonatomic component may itself have absolutely continuous and singular parts; the defining feature here is coexistence of indivisible source atoms with atomless mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed source has both positive atomic mass and positive atomless mass; its atomless part may be absolutely continuous or singular.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Source Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atomic–nonatomic decomposition fits the mixed-source leaf, but the canonical decomposition and countability implicit in the atomic sum require a cited measure-theory locator.

children.title: Deterministic Transport Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on map existence caused by singular source structure.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are measurable spaces, \(T:X\to Y\) is measurable, and \(\mu\) has an atom \(x_0\) of mass \(a>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every deterministic pushforward \(T_\#\mu\) has an atom of mass at least \(a\) at \(T(x_0)\); hence it cannot equal an atomless target.
review_flags: Elementary pushforward obstruction; supplied locators are unrelated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic obstruction to deterministic transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(x_0\) is a source atom with \(a=\mu(\{x_0\})>0\), then every measurable map \(T:X\to Y\) satisfies
\[
(T_\#\mu)(\{T(x_0)\})=\mu(T^{-1}(\{T(x_0)\}))\geq a.
\]
Therefore no deterministic map can push a measure having an atom onto an atomless target. More generally, deterministic transport cannot subdivide any source atom: each atomic mass must be assigned wholly to one target point, possibly together with other source mass. Kantorovich plans cross this boundary because they may split the mass at \(x_0\) among several destinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic map sends each source atom intact, so any atomic source cannot map to an atomless target; transport plans may split it.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Transport Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atomic pushforward obstruction is mathematically precise and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no authoritative transport or measure-theory source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone Rearrangement Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, and measure-preserving factorization of the nondecreasing rearrangement of a real-valued function on the unit interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\ge 1\) and \(h\in L^p([0,1];\mathbb R)\). Then there exists a unique nondecreasing rearrangement \(h^\#\) of \(h\). Moreover, there exists a measure-preserving map \(s:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) such that \(h=h^\#\circ s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real-valued L-p function on the unit interval, with p at least 1, has a unique nondecreasing rearrangement and is its composition with a measure-preserving self-map of the interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,h^\#\text{ a nondecreasing rearrangement of }h,\qquad \exists s:[0,1]\to[0,1]\text{ measure-preserving such that }h=h^\#\circ s.
