children.title: Atomic Quantile Jumps
children.top_down_role: Discontinuities in quantile representations caused by atoms.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R\).
\(Q_\mu\) is the generalized inverse of the right-continuous distribution function \(F_\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu(\{x\})=a>0\) exactly when \(Q_\mu=x\) on a parameter interval of length \(a\).

notation.meaning: Left limit of the distribution function.
Mass of the atom at the point.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atoms create CDF jumps and quantile plateaus, not quantile jumps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\mathbb R\),
\[
\mu(\{x\})=F_\mu(x)-F_\mu(x-).
\]
Consequently, \(x\) is an atom of mass \(a>0\) if and only if
\[
Q_\mu(u)=x\quad\text{for almost every }u\in(F_\mu(x-),F_\mu(x)],
\]
whose length is \(a\). Thus an atomic jump of \(F_\mu\) corresponds under generalized inversion to a constant quantile interval. A discontinuous jump of \(Q_\mu\), by contrast, records a gap in the support rather than an atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atom of mass a is a jump of the CDF and produces a constant quantile interval of length a; quantile jumps instead reflect support gaps.
knowledge_statements.title: Atomic Quantile Jumps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly distinguishes CDF jumps caused by atoms from quantile jumps caused by support gaps. This terminological interpretation of the immutable title requires an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Tie Intervals
children.top_down_role: Intervals or level sets permitting multiple monotone allocations.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A positive-length level interval of \(Q_\mu\) exists exactly at an atom of \(\mu\), and its length equals the atomic mass.

notation.meaning: Parameter interval on which the quantile is tied at one value.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tie intervals are level sets of a generalized quantile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R\), define \(I_x=(F_\mu(x-),F_\mu(x)]\). Then
\[
Q_\mu(u)=x\quad\text{for every }u\in I_x,
\qquad |I_x|=\mu(\{x\}).
\]
Conversely, if \(Q_\mu(u)=x\) almost everywhere on an interval \(I\subset(0,1)\) of positive length, then \(I\subseteq I_x\) up to endpoints and \(\mu(\{x\})\ge |I|>0\). Hence positive-length tie intervals occur precisely because the transported measure has atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quantile has a positive-length tie interval exactly at an atom; the maximal interval length equals that atom's mass.
knowledge_statements.title: Tie Intervals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atom–quantile-level-interval characterization is precise, and condition is a suitable content kind. No supporting source or locator is provided.

children.title: Nonunique Monotone Maps
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of deterministic monotone transports.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu,\nu\) are Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R\).
Maps are required to be Borel and nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Monotone pushforward maps are unique \(\mu\)-almost everywhere when they exist; atoms can instead prevent existence, while pointwise representatives remain nonunique on \(\mu\)-null sets.

notation.meaning: Pushforward of the source measure by a map.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes representative nonuniqueness from failure of map existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If nondecreasing maps \(S,T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(S_\#\mu=T_\#\mu=\nu\), then \(S=T\) \(\mu\)-almost everywhere. They may nevertheless differ on \(\mu\)-null sets, so pointwise representatives are nonunique. More substantially, if \(x\) is a source atom of mass \(a>0\), every deterministic map sends its entire mass to the single atom \(T(x)\); therefore \(T_\#\mu=\nu\) is impossible whenever no target atom can receive that indivisible mass consistently. In such cases the monotone quantile coupling generally splits the atom and is not induced by a map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Existing monotone pushforward maps are unique almost everywhere. Apparent nonuniqueness is null-set freedom; source atoms can instead force splitting and destroy map existence.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Monotone Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between null-set representative freedom and failure of deterministic-map existence is plausible and fits a failure boundary, but the phrase about a target atom receiving mass 'consistently' is not a precise compatibility condition. The immutable title also makes the intended notion of nonuniqueness ambiguous. A source is needed to settle the intended formulation.

children.title: Unique-Map Recovery Regimes
children.top_down_role: Source-target configurations that remove atomic or tie-driven ambiguity.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu,\nu\) are Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=Q_\nu\circ F_\mu\) pushes \(\mu\) to \(\nu\) and is the unique nondecreasing pushforward map \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomless-source recovery of the deterministic monotone rearrangement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(\mu\) is atomless, \(F_\mu\) is continuous and \((F_\mu)_\#\mu\) is the uniform probability measure on \((0,1)\). Hence the map
\[
T(x)=Q_\nu(F_\mu(x))
\]
is Borel, nondecreasing, and satisfies \(T_\#\mu=\nu\). If \(S:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is any other nondecreasing Borel map with \(S_\#\mu=\nu\), then \(S=T\) \(\mu\)-almost everywhere. For costs \(c(x,y)=h(x-y)\) with \(h\) convex, the induced coupling \((\mathrm{id},T)_\#\mu\) is optimal whenever its cost is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With an atomless source, composing its CDF with the target quantile gives the unique almost-everywhere monotone transport map.
knowledge_statements.title: Unique-Map Recovery Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atomless-source monotone rearrangement theorem and its convex displacement-cost qualification are standard and appropriately placed, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Metric-Cost Transport
children.top_down_role: Static transport problems using an underlying metric as cost.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum transport cost for \(c=d\) is \(W_1(\mu,\nu)\).

notation.meaning: Couplings of the two probability measures.
Probability measures with finite first moment.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static optimal transport with the ambient metric as cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Metric-cost transport is the Kantorovich problem with \(c(x,y)=d(x,y)\):
\[
\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\pi(x,y).
\]
The finite-first-moment assumptions make this value finite, and lower semicontinuity of \(d\) ensures that the infimum is attained. Its value is, by definition, \(W_1(\mu,\nu)\). Unlike strictly convex displacement costs, the metric cost is only linear along distance-minimizing directions and may admit several optimal couplings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric-cost transport minimizes expected distance over all couplings. For finite-first-moment measures, its attained value is the one-Wasserstein distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Cost Transport

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and attainment statement are correct for finite-first-moment measures on a Polish metric space, and definition fits the terminal container. No supporting transport reference is supplied.

children.title: One-Wasserstein Geometry
children.top_down_role: Metric geometry associated with first-order transport cost.

assumptions_latex: A base point \(x_0\in X\) is fixed, and measures lie in \(\mathcal P_1(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_1\) is a metric on \(\mathcal P_1(X)\) and metrizes weak convergence together with convergence of first moments.

notation.meaning: Probability measures having finite first moment.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric and convergence structure induced by expected distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(W_1:\mathcal P_1(X)\times\mathcal P_1(X)\to[0,\infty)\) is a metric. In particular, it is symmetric, obeys the triangle inequality, and \(W_1(\mu,\nu)=0\) holds exactly when \(\mu=\nu\). Moreover,
\[
W_1(\mu_n,\mu)\to0
\]
if and only if \(\mu_n\rightharpoonup\mu\) and
\[
\int_X d(x,x_0)\,d\mu_n(x)\to\int_X d(x,x_0)\,d\mu(x).
\]
The characterization is independent of the chosen base point \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-Wasserstein distance is a genuine metric, and its convergence is exactly weak convergence plus convergence of first moments.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Wasserstein Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric and convergence characterization is standard and matches the container, but it lacks an authoritative citation with a section, theorem, or page locator.

children.title: Lipschitz Dual Potentials
children.top_down_role: Dual-potential geometry characteristic of metric transport costs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_1(\mu,\nu)=\sup_{\operatorname{Lip}(f)\le1}\int_X f\,d(\mu-\nu)\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz seminorm of a real-valued function.
Signed difference of the two measures.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality for metric cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The metric-cost transport value admits the dual representation
\[
W_1(\mu,\nu)=\sup\left\{\int_X f\,d\mu-\int_X f\,d\nu: f:X\to\mathbb R,\ \operatorname{Lip}(f)\le1\right\}.
\]
Adding a constant to \(f\) does not change the objective, so one may impose \(f(x_0)=0\) at any fixed \(x_0\in X\). If an optimal coupling \(\pi\) and an optimal potential \(f\) exist, complementary slackness gives \(f(x)-f(y)=d(x,y)\) for \(\pi\)-almost every \((x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-Wasserstein distance equals the largest expectation difference over all real-valued 1-Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Dual Potentials

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Kantorovich–Rubinstein formula and conditional complementary-slackness statement are internally consistent with the stated sign convention. No inspectable source with a precise locator is supplied.

children.title: Nondifferentiable Cost Boundary
children.top_down_role: Map-structure limitations caused by nonsmooth metric costs.

assumptions_latex: The cost is \(c(x,y)=\|x-y\|\) on a normed vector space.
Differentiability is considered with respect to either transport variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metric cost is nondifferentiable on the diagonal and lacks the strict convexity needed for standard smooth quadratic-cost map arguments.

notation.meaning: Diagonal where source and target positions coincide.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothness boundary separating metric and quadratic costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(c(x,y)=\|x-y\|\), the cost is generally nondifferentiable when \(x=y\). In Euclidean space,
\[
\partial_x c(x,y)=\left\{\frac{x-y}{\|x-y\|}\right\}\quad\text{if }x\ne y,
\qquad
\partial_x c(x,x)=\{v:\|v\|\le1\}.
\]
Furthermore, displacement homogeneity makes \(c\) non-strictly convex along rays. Therefore arguments relying on a single-valued smooth cost gradient or strict convexity—such as direct quadratic-cost recovery of a unique transport map—can fail, even though Kantorovich duality and optimal couplings remain available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance cost is nonsmooth on the diagonal and non-strictly convex along rays, so smooth quadratic-cost arguments for unique maps do not directly apply.
knowledge_statements.title: Nondifferentiable Cost Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Euclidean subdifferential formula and the identified smoothness and strict-convexity boundary are appropriate for a failure-boundary record. An authoritative source with a precise locator is missing.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Transport Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean Brenier theorem for absolutely continuous source measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists a convex lower-semicontinuous function \(\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) whose gradient \(T=\nabla\varphi\) is defined \(\mu\)-almost everywhere and satisfies \(T_\#\mu=\nu\). The coupling
\[
\pi=(\mathrm{id},T)_\#\mu
\]
is the unique minimizer in \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) of
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d}\tfrac12\|x-y\|^2\,d\pi(x,y).
\]
Consequently, the optimal quadratic transport is induced by a map \(T\) that is unique \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For quadratic Euclidean cost and an absolutely continuous source, the unique optimal coupling is induced by the almost-everywhere unique gradient map of a convex function.
assumptions_latex: The source measure \(\mu\) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(c(x,y)=\tfrac12\|x-y\|^2\), the unique optimal plan is \((\mathrm{id},\nabla\varphi)_\#\mu\) for a convex \(\varphi\), and \(\nabla\varphi\) is unique \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.

notation.meaning: Identity map on the source space.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) are open and \(c\in C^1(X\times Y)\).
For every \(x\in X\), the map \(y\mapsto\nabla_xc(x,y)\) is injective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At differentiability points of an active dual potential, the twist condition determines the paired target uniquely.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical source-side twist condition for smooth costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cost \(c\) satisfies the source twist condition when
\[
y_1\ne y_2\implies \nabla_xc(x,y_1)\ne\nabla_xc(x,y_2)
\]
for every fixed \(x\in X\). If dual potentials satisfy \(\phi(x)+\psi(y)\le c(x,y)\), equality holds at \((x,y)\), and \(\phi\) is differentiable at \(x\), then
\[
\nabla\phi(x)=\nabla_xc(x,y).
\]
By twist, this equation has at most one solution \(y\). Thus an optimal plan concentrated on the equality set is induced by a map wherever the source potential is differentiable, subject to the usual existence hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth cost is twisted when its source gradient identifies the target uniquely; then differentiable dual potentials determine a transport map.
knowledge_statements.title: General Twisted Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The source twist condition, dual sign convention, and local uniqueness conclusion are consistent. The condition content kind fits, but the map-level consequence and its usual auxiliary hypotheses require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimizing \(I_c\) penalizes mass concentrated near the diagonal \(\Delta=\{(x,x):x\in X\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-marginal radial repulsion with a singular collision penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the repulsive transport cost \(c:X\times X\to[0,+\infty]\) by
\[
c(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
h(d(x,y)),&x\ne y,\\+\infty,&x=y.
\end{cases}
\]
For probability measures \(\mu,\nu\), its transport problem minimizes \(I_c(\gamma)=\int c\,d\gamma\) over \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\). Because \(h\) is nonincreasing, pairs at larger separation have no greater cost; because \(h(r)\to+\infty\) as \(r\downarrow0\), collisions and near-collisions are penalized. In particular, every finite-cost coupling satisfies \(\gamma(\Delta)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A repulsive cost decreases with separation and diverges at collisions, so every finite-cost coupling avoids the diagonal.

u)\ \gamma(F)=0}}\int c_0\,d\gamma,\] with \(\inf\varnothing:=+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strassen coupling theorem at tolerance \(\varepsilon\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dual characterization of the minimum probability that a coupling exceeds a prescribed metric tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,d)\) be a Polish metric space, let \(\mu,\nu\in\mathcal P(X)\), and let \(\varepsilon\ge 0\). For \(A\subseteq X\), set \(A^{\varepsilon}:=\{y\in X:d(y,A)\le\varepsilon\}\), where \(d(y,A):=\inf_{z\in A}d(y,z)\). Then

\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\pi\bigl(\{(x,y):d(x,y)>\varepsilon\}\bigr)=\sup_{A\subseteq X,\ A\text{ closed}}\bigl\{\mu(A)-\nu(A^{\varepsilon})\bigr\}.
\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal cost transforms for the dual constraint \(f(x)+g(y)\le c(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), its cost transform on \(Y\) is
\[
f^c(y):=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(c(x,y)-f(x)\bigr).
\]
For \(g:Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), define analogously
\[
g^c(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}\bigl(c(x,y)-g(y)\bigr).
\]
Whenever these expressions are defined, \(f(x)+f^c(y)\le c(x,y)\) and \(g^c(x)+g(y)\le c(x,y)\). Moreover, \(f_1\le f_2\) implies \(f_1^c\ge f_2^c\), and the analogous order reversal holds for functions on \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost transform takes the infimum of cost minus potential over the opposite space; it produces a dual-feasible partner and reverses order.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Points where an extended-valued cost transform ceases to be a finite dual potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the finite transform domain by
\[
D_c(f):=\left\{y\in Y:-\infty<\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(c(x,y)-f(x)\bigr)<+\infty\right\}.
\]
If \(c(x,y)=+\infty\) for every \(x\in X\), then \(f^c(y)=+\infty\). If there exists a sequence \((x_n)\) with \(c(x_n,y)-f(x_n)\to-\infty\), then \(f^c(y)=-\infty\). Therefore the transform is a finite-valued dual potential on a prescribed set \(D\subseteq Y\) only if \(D\subseteq D_c(f)\); outside this boundary the ordinary finite-potential calculus fails.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-domain boundary characterization is precise and its failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common scalar gauges for probability-marginal Kantorovich potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a dual pair \((\phi,\psi)\), a normalization chooses \(a\in\mathbb R\) and replaces the pair by \((\widehat\phi,\widehat\psi)=(\phi+a,\psi-a)\). Mean normalization imposes
\[
\int_X\widehat\phi\,d\mu=0,
\quad\text{so that}\quad
 a=-\int_X\phi\,d\mu.
\]
If a base point \(x_0\in X\) satisfies \(\phi(x_0)\in\mathbb R\), point normalization imposes \(\widehat\phi(x_0)=0\) and uses \(a=-\phi(x_0)\). If \(\sup_X\phi\in\mathbb R\), supremum normalization imposes \(\sup_X\widehat\phi=0\) and uses \(a=-\sup_X\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mean, point, or supremum condition fixes the additive constant whenever the corresponding integral, point value, or supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Potential Normalization Choices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three conditional normalization choices are correctly stated and the condition kind fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Additive Gauge Orbits

assumptions_latex: Gauge shifts are restricted to constants preserving defined extended-real sums.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The orbit \(\{(\phi+a,\psi-a):a\in\mathbb R\}\) consists of equivalent dual-feasible representatives.

notation.meaning: Gauge orbit of a dual pair

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic symmetry of the Kantorovich dual constraint
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-parameter additive symmetry of two-potential Kantorovich duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(a\in\mathbb R\), define
\[
T_a(\phi,\psi):=(\phi+a,\psi-a).
\]
Then \(T_0\) is the identity, \(T_a\circ T_b=T_{a+b}\), and
\[
(\phi(x)+a)+(\psi(y)-a)=\phi(x)+\psi(y)
\]
for all \((x,y)\) where the sums are defined. Consequently, dual feasibility is constant along
\[
\mathcal O(\phi,\psi):=
\{T_a(\phi,\psi):a\in\mathbb R\}.
\]
If both potentials take at least one finite value, the action is free: \(T_a(\phi,\psi)=(\phi,\psi)\) implies \(a=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a constant to one dual potential and subtracting it from the other preserves their sum and hence dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Additive Gauge Orbits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive action and feasibility invariance are mathematically consistent and fit the property leaf, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Noncompact-Space Duality Regime
children.top_down_role: Duality on spaces lacking ambient compactness.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Polish spaces with probability measures \(\mu,\nu\).
\(c:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and bounded below.
After fixing one additive constant, the feasible normalized potential class is sequentially compact in \(L^1(\mu)\times L^1(\nu)\), and both integral functionals are upper semicontinuous on it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite dual value is attained by an integrable feasible pair.
review_flags: This abstract compactness regime needs a transport-specific source and comparison with standard moment hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract compactness criterion isolating what replaces compact ambient spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_0\) be the set of integrable pairs \((\varphi,\psi)\) satisfying \(\varphi(x)+\psi(y)\le c(x,y)\), with one additive normalization imposed. If \(D_c:=\sup_{(varphi,\psi)\in\mathcal F_0}J(\varphi,\psi)<\infty\), choose a maximizing sequence in \(\mathcal F_0\). Sequential compactness gives a subsequence converging to \((\varphi^ast,\psi^ast)\in\mathcal F_0\), while upper semicontinuity gives \(J(\varphi^ast,\psi^ast)\ge D_c\). Hence \(J(\varphi^ast,\psi^ast)=D_c\), so the dual optimum is attained despite noncompactness of \(X\) and \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On noncompact spaces, normalized dual potentials still attain a finite supremum when feasibility is closed and the normalized potential class is sequentially compact with upper-semicontinuous objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact-Space Duality Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this abstract noncompact attainment criterion or connects it to the named transport regime. The topology underlying sequential compactness, convergence, feasibility closure, and upper semicontinuity must be stated consistently. Several formulas omit backslashes in \(\varphi\), \(\psi\), and \(\mu\), and the statement is written as a proof argument.

u)}\int c\,d\pi\) is finite. Tightness of \(\Pi(\mu,

children.title: Coercive Recovery Regimes
children.top_down_role: Additional control restoring compactness or attainment.

assumptions_latex: \(D_c<infty\) and \((\varphi_n,\psi_n)\) is a feasible maximizing sequence.

Constants are chosen so that \(\int
otin\varphi_n\,d\mu=0\).
The normalized sequence is uniformly integrable in \(L^1(\mu)\times L^1(\nu)\), and feasibility is closed under its weak subsequential limits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A weak cluster point is a dual maximizer.
review_flags: A source connecting coercive transport estimates to this compactness criterion is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coercive estimates recover attainment by preventing loss of compactness of normalized potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Uniform integrability gives a subsequence, not relabeled, with \(\varphi_n\rightharpoonup\varphi^\ast\) in \(L^1(mu)\) and \(\psi_n\rightharpoonup\psi^\ast\) in \(L^1(\nu)\). Closedness preserves \(\varphi^ast(x)+\psi^ast(y)\le c(x,y)\). Since integration against the constant function \(1\) is weakly continuous, \[J(\varphi^\ast,\psi^\ast)=\lim_nJ(\varphi_n,\psi_n)=D_c.\] Thus any coercive estimate implying the stated uniform integrability and closedness recovers a dual optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coercive bounds recover dual attainment when they make normalized maximizing potentials uniformly integrable and preserve feasibility under weak limits.

children.title: Dual Nonattainment
children.top_down_role: Finite dual values lacking optimizing potential pairs.

assumptions_latex: The feasible dual class \(\mathcal F\) is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Kantorovich dual problem is nonattained in \(\mathcal F\) when \(D_c\in\mathbb R\) but there is no \((varphi^ast,psi^ast)\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \(J(varphi^ast,psi^ast)=D_c\). Equivalently, every feasible pair obeys \(J(varphi,psi)<D_c\), although for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some feasible pair satisfies \(J(varphi,psi)>D_c-varepsilon\). intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected definition kind fits the leaf, and the mathematical distinction between nonattainment and a duality gap is appropriate. children.title: Potential Integrability Failures
children.top_down_role: Dual candidates outside the required integrability classes.

assumptions_latex: Dual objectives are required to be finite Lebesgue integrals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair is inadmissible whenever either potential lacks an integrable positive or negative part needed to define a finite objective.
review_flags: A source specifying admissibility conventions for extended-valued potentials is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between pointwise dual feasibility and a well-defined finite dual objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Pointwise feasibility alone does not make a pair admissible. A finite dual objective requires \(varphi
otin L^1(mu)\) and \(psi\in L^1(\nu)\), equivalently finite integrals of their positive and negative parts. If, for example, \(\intvarphi^+\,dmu=\intvarphi^-\,dmu=+infty\), then \(\intvarphi\,dmu\) is undefined; if \(\intvarphi^-\,dmu=+infty\), its contribution is \(-infty\). Such feasible potentials cannot certify a finite dual value under the finite-integral convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise feasible potential pair fails admissibility when its integrals are undefined or nonfinite, so it cannot realize a finite dual objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Potential Integrability Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source specifies the adopted admissibility convention for extended-valued potentials. The statement incorrectly says that a finite objective requires \(\varphi\notin L^1(\mu)\), contradicting the assumptions and plain statement; it should require integrability under the stated finite-integral convention. Numerous commands and symbols, including infinity, direct sums, measures, and integrals, are malformed.

children.title: Unbounded Maximizing Sequences
children.top_down_role: Maximizing potential sequences lacking controlled representatives.

assumptions_latex: \(mathcal F_0\) is a normalized feasible dual class in a normed space \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every maximizing sequence is unbounded in \(E\), no dual maximizer exists in \(\mathcal F_0\).
review_flags: A transport-specific source relating norm blow-up to potential nonattainment is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm blow-up after removal of the additive-constant symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A maximizing sequence is unbounded when \(J(z_n)\to D_c\) and \(\sup_n\|z_n\|_E=+infty\). If every maximizing sequence has this property, then no maximizer \(z^ast\in\mathcal F_0\) exists: otherwise the constant sequence \(z_n=z^ast\) would be bounded and maximizing. Normalization is essential because the transformation \((varphi,psi)\mapsto(varphi+a,psi-a)\) can create spurious unboundedness without changing feasibility or objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every normalized maximizing sequence blows up in the chosen potential norm, dual attainment is impossible; normalization removes irrelevant constant drift.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Maximizing Sequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the constant-sequence argument is mathematically sound after normalization. However, the assumption says \(z_n\notin\mathcal F_0\), contradicting the claim that \((z_n)\) is a feasible maximizing sequence. No transport-specific source is supplied, and several instances of \(\mathcal F_0\), \(\varphi\), \(\psi\), infinity, and star notation are malformed.

children.title: Finite-Value Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Transition from meaningful dual values to divergent or indeterminate objectives.

assumptions_latex: The primal value \(P_c\) and dual value \(D_c\) are defined in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-value duality requires \(-infty<D_c=P_c<+infty\); failure occurs when finiteness or equality is lost.

notation.meaning: Primal–dual gap when both values are finite

review_flags: A source distinguishing extended-value pathologies from dual nonattainment is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating finite strong duality from infinite values or a positive duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-value regime is \(-infty<D_c=P_c<+infty\). Its boundary is crossed if \(P_c=+infty\), if \(D_c=-infty\), if either objective is undefined under the adopted integration convention, or if both values are finite but \(D_c<P_c\). Only in the last case is the finite primal–dual gap \(G:=P_c-D_c\) strictly positive. These failures concern value formation or equality and therefore differ from nonattainment with \(D_c=P_c\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-value duality fails when a value is infinite or undefined, or when finite primal and dual values have a positive gap; this differs from nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Value Failure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the stated classification of finite-value failures. The finite regime is correctly characterized by real equality, but the enumerated boundary is not exhaustive for arbitrary extended-real values: it mentions only \(P_c=+\infty\) and \(D_c=-\infty\), while the assumptions do not rule out other nonfinite or undefined cases. The admissible cost and integration conventions must be fixed before the classification is reliable.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupling and potentials are respectively primal and dual optimal, with zero duality gap.
review_flags: A standard optimal-transport source for the contact-set optimality criterion is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(pi(Gamma_{varphi,psi})=1\), \[\int c\,dpi=\int(varphiopluspsi)\,dpi=\intvarphi\,dmu+\intpsi\,d\nu.\] Weak duality places every feasible dual value below every feasible primal value. notation.meaning: Primal objective minus feasible dual objective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive Kantorovich duality certificate, including approximate optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the primal-dual gap by
\[
G(\pi,\varphi,\psi):=\int_{X\times Y}c\,d\pi-\int_X\varphi\,d\mu-\int_Y\psi\,d\nu.
\]
Weak duality gives \(G(\pi,\varphi,\psi)\ge0\). If \(G(\pi,\varphi,\psi)\le\varepsilon\) for some \(\varepsilon\ge0\), then
\[
\int c\,d\pi\le \inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int c\,d\gamma+\varepsilon.
\]
Thus the feasible triple is an externally checkable \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate. For \(\varepsilon=0\), both \(\pi\) and \((\varphi,\psi)\) attain their respective primal and dual values whenever those values are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible coupling and dual pair certify approximate optimality when their objective gap is at most the stated tolerance; zero gap certifies exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Gap Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role and gap argument fit the leaf, but source_refs is empty. An authoritative locator is required for the precise measurable extended-cost setting and the attainment wording.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are sets, and \(c:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a cost for which the displayed sums are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma\) is cyclically monotone exactly when no finite cyclic reassignment of its selected targets lowers total cost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-cycle definition for a general transport cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(\Gamma\subset X\times Y\) is \(c\)-cyclically monotone if, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every selection \((x_i,y_i)\in\Gamma\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), one has
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(x_i,y_i)\le 
\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(x_{i+1},y_i),
\qquad x_{n+1}:=x_1.
\]
Equivalently, among the two assignments appearing in this inequality, retaining each selected pair costs no more than cyclically shifting the selected source coordinates. A coupling is concentrated on a \(c\)-cyclically monotone support if some such \(\Gamma\) has full coupling measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support is cyclically monotone when every finite collection of its pairs costs no more than any cyclic reassignment of their source coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: c-Cyclically Monotone Sets and Transport Plans
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines cyclical monotonicity for arbitrary extended-real costs and its extension to transport plans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\) be sets and \(c:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). children.title: Rockafellar Potential Construction
children.top_down_role: Potential representation associated with cyclically monotone sets.

assumptions_latex: \(c:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is finite-valued and \(\Gamma\subset X\times Y\) is nonempty and \(c\)-cyclically monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed \(\varphi\) satisfies \(\Gamma\subset\partial^c\varphi\), provided the infimum is finite on the relevant domain.

notation.meaning: Cost transform of the constructed potential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chain-infimum construction with the additive cost-transform convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(\varphi(x_0)=0\) and, for \(x\in X\), define
\[
\varphi(x):=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=0}^{n}\bigl[c(x_{i+1},y_i)-c(x_i,y_i)\bigr]: n\ge0,\ (x_i,y_i)\in\Gamma,\ x_{n+1}=x\right\}.
\]
The infimum ranges over all finite chains beginning at the fixed pair \((x_0,y_0)\). Cyclical monotonicity prevents negative closed-chain inconsistencies. Wherever \(\varphi\) is finite, define \(\varphi^c(y):=\inf_{z\in X}\{c(z,y)-\varphi(z)\}\). Then every \((x,y)\in\Gamma\) satisfies \(\varphi(x)+\varphi^c(y)=c(x,y)\), so \(\Gamma\subset\partial^c\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take an infimum of accumulated cost increments over finite support chains. Cyclical monotonicity makes the resulting potential contact the cost on the support.
knowledge_statements.title: Rockafellar Potential Construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic construction fits the leaf, but the exact chain formula, finiteness conditions, and conclusion that every support pair lies in the cost subdifferential require an authoritative theorem-level locator.

children.title: Cost-Potential Representation
children.top_down_role: Support geometry encoded through transport-cost potentials.

assumptions_latex: \(c:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\varphi:X\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) are such that the cost transform is well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every pair in \(\partial^c\varphi\) lies in the equality set of a dual-feasible cost-potential representation.

notation.meaning: Cost transform of the source potential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive cost-transform and contact-set representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\varphi^c(y):=\inf_{x\in X}\{c(x,y)-\varphi(x)\}.
\]
Then \(\varphi(x)+\varphi^c(y)\le c(x,y)\) for every \((x,y)\in X\times Y\). The associated cost subdifferential is
\[
\partial^c\varphi:=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:\varphi(x)+\varphi^c(y)=c(x,y)\}.
\]
Thus a set \(\Gamma\) has a cost-potential representation when \(\Gamma\subset
\partial^c\varphi\) for some proper potential \(\varphi\). More generally, dual-feasible functions \((\varphi,\psi)\) represent \(\Gamma\) when \(\varphi(x)+\psi(y)\le c(x,y)\) everywhere and equality holds throughout \(\Gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A potential and its cost transform lie below the cost everywhere; their equality set represents the associated cost subdifferential and any support it contains.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Potential Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind matches the leaf and the formulas are coherent, but source_refs is empty. A source must specify the properness and extended-value conventions under which the transform and contact equalities are well-defined.

children.title: Representation Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where monotone-support and potential descriptions coincide.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are compact metric spaces, and \(c:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma\) is \(c\)-cyclically monotone if and only if it is contained in the contact set of a proper cost potential.

notation.meaning: Contact set of a cost potential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact, continuous, finite-cost regime avoiding integrability and extended-value pathologies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated compactness and continuity assumptions, the following are equivalent:
\[
\Gamma\text{ is }c\text{-cyclically monotone};
\]
\[
\text{there exists a finite-valued }c\text{-concave potential }\varphi\text{ with }
\Gamma\subset\partial^c\varphi.
\]
Equivalently, there exist finite-valued functions \(\varphi:X\to\mathbb R\) and \(\psi:Y\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(\varphi(x)+\psi(y)\le c(x,y)\) everywhere and \(\varphi(x)+\psi(y)=c(x,y)\) for every \((x,y)\in\Gamma\). The implication from representation to cyclical monotonicity follows by summing the contact equalities and the global feasibility inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuous finite costs on compact metric spaces, cyclical monotonicity is equivalent to containment in the contact set of a cost potential.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Equivalence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the equivalence-regime leaf, but the asserted equivalence, finite-valued c-concave potential, and equivalent finite-valued feasible pair need a precise authoritative locator.

children.title: Nonrepresentable Support Boundary
children.top_down_role: Support configurations lacking the required global potential representation.

assumptions_latex: Representing potentials are required to be real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(\Gamma\) satisfies the extended-order cycle inequalities, no real-valued feasible potential pair can represent it by equality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued cost boundary for real-valued potential representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every finite cycle selected from the singleton \(\Gamma\), both sides of the cyclical inequality equal \(+\infty\); hence the inequality holds in the extended order. Suppose real-valued functions \(\varphi:X\to\mathbb R\) and \(\psi:Y\to\mathbb R\) represented \(\Gamma\) through contact. They would have to satisfy
\[
\varphi(0)+\psi(0)=c(0,0)=+
\infty,
\]
which is impossible because the left side is finite. Thus cyclical monotonicity alone does not guarantee a real-valued cost-potential representation when the cost may be infinite on the proposed support. Finite-cost or compatible extended-potential hypotheses are therefore essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinite cost on a cyclically monotone singleton cannot equal the sum of two real-valued potentials, so real-valued representation fails without finite-cost assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonrepresentable Support Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate and the singleton calculation is self-contained, but treating +infinity <= +infinity as an admissible cyclical-monotonicity test depends on a convention that requires a cited locator.

children.title: Necessity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conditions forced by optimal transport support structure.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Polish spaces and \(c:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and bounded below.
\(\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) minimizes \(\int c\,d\gamma\) and has finite objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a Borel \(c\)-cyclically monotone set \(\Gamma\) such that \(\pi(\Gamma)=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of cyclical monotonicity for finite-cost optimal transport plans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\pi\) is an optimal coupling, then there exists a Borel set \(\Gamma\subset X\times Y\) with \(\pi(\Gamma)=1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\) and every \((x_i,y_i)\in\Gamma\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(x_i,y_i)
\le
\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(x_{i+1},y_i),
\qquad x_{n+1}:=x_1.
\]
Consequently, failure of a finite-cycle inequality on every full-measure representative of the support rules out optimality. This is a necessity statement: its conclusion alone does not assert sufficiency outside regimes where a suitable cost-potential representation and integrability are available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-cost optimal coupling for a continuous cost is concentrated on a cyclically monotone Borel set.
knowledge_statements.title: Necessity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the necessity-regime leaf, but no source supports the exact Polish-space, continuous bounded-below hypotheses or the existence of a Borel full-measure cyclically monotone set.

children.title: Sufficiency Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conditions strong enough to certify transport optimality.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are measurable spaces, \(\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\), and \(\int c\,d\pi\) is finite.
There are \(\varphi\in L^1(\mu)\) and \(\psi\in L^1(\nu)\) with \(\varphi+\psi\le c\) everywhere and equality \(\pi\)-almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupling \(\pi\) minimizes \(\int c\,d\gamma\) over all \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficiency through an integrable contact potential pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every competitor \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\), dual feasibility and the marginal constraints give
\[
\int c\,d\gamma
\ge
\int_X\varphi\,d\mu+
\int_Y\psi\,d\nu.
\]
Because contact holds \(\pi\)-almost surely,
\[
\int c\,d\pi
=
\int_X\varphi\,d\mu+
\int_Y\psi\,d\nu.
\]
Therefore \(\int c\,d\pi\le\int c\,d\gamma\) for every feasible competitor \(\gamma\), and \(\pi\) is optimal. In particular, concentration on a cyclically monotone set is sufficient whenever that set admits such an integrable cost-potential representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupling is optimal when an integrable dual-feasible potential pair contacts the cost almost surely on that coupling.
knowledge_statements.title: Sufficiency Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sufficiency theorem and content kind fit the leaf, but c is not explicitly introduced with a domain or measurability condition, and no source locator supports the stated general measurable-space regime.

children.title: Full Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where support conditions and optimality characterize one another.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are compact metric spaces, \(c:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, and \(\mu,\nu\) are Borel probability measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimality, concentration on a \(c\)-cyclically monotone set, and almost-sure cost-potential contact are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact continuous-cost equivalence of optimality, monotonicity, and dual contact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated assumptions, the following assertions are equivalent:
\[
\text{(i) }\pi\text{ minimizes }\int c\,d\gamma\text{ over }\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu);
\]
\[
\text{(ii) }\pi(\Gamma)=1\text{ for some }c\text{-cyclically monotone Borel set }\Gamma;
\]
\[
\text{(iii) there are continuous }\varphi,
\psi\text{ with }\varphi(x)+\psi(y)\le c(x,y)
\text{ everywhere and equality }\pi\text{-almost surely.}
\]
Compactness and continuity make the cost bounded and the potentials integrable, eliminating the extended-value and integrability qualifications that separate necessity from sufficiency in more general settings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuous costs on compact metric spaces, optimality, cyclically monotone concentration, and almost-sure contact with feasible potentials are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Full Equivalence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the full-equivalence leaf, but the three-way equivalence and the existence of continuous finite-valued contact potentials require an exact authoritative theorem or section locator.

children.title: Equivalence Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cost or regularity regimes where one implication breaks down.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pairwise monotonicity does not imply cyclical monotonicity or transport optimality; the first obstruction may occur on a three-cycle.

notation.meaning: Uniform coupling on the directed three-cycle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of equivalence when only two-cycle inequalities are checked.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The diagonal support satisfies every two-cycle inequality because, for distinct \(i,j\),
\[
c(i,i)+c(j,j)=0=c(i,j)+c(j,i).
\]
Nevertheless, its directed three-cycle inequality fails:
\[
c(1,1)+c(2,2)+c(3,3)=0>-3=c(1,2)+c(2,3)+c(3,1).
\]
Accordingly, \(\int c\,d\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}=0\), whereas \(\int c\,d\pi_{\mathrm{cyc}}=-1\). Thus the locally pairwise-monotone diagonal coupling is not optimal. Replacing full cyclical monotonicity by two-cycle monotonicity therefore destroys the optimality equivalence, even on finite spaces with a finite cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a three-point transport problem, every two-cycle test can pass while a three-cycle lowers cost, so pairwise monotonicity does not certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalence Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is correct and the finite calculation is consistent, but the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale as evidence for the nontrivial boundary claim.

children.title: Local Monotonicity Conditions
children.top_down_role: Pairwise or neighborhood-level monotonicity of transport supports.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are sets, \(c:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\), and \(\Gamma\subset X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local two-cycle monotonicity is precisely the displayed pairwise inequality, but it need not control cycles of length at least three.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise, or two-cycle, form of cost monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(\Gamma\) satisfies the local two-cycle monotonicity condition if every \((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\in\Gamma\) obeys
\[
c(x_1,y_1)+c(x_2,y_2)
\le
c(x_1,y_2)+c(x_2,y_1).
\]
This predicate says that swapping the two selected target coordinates cannot lower their total cost. It is exactly the \(n=2\) instance of \(c\)-cyclical monotonicity. Unless additional structure on \(c\) converts pairwise comparisons into all finite-cycle comparisons, it imposes no inequality for cycles containing three or more distinct pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local two-cycle monotonicity requires that swapping the targets of any two support pairs cannot reduce their combined cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Monotonicity Conditions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf and the displayed inequality is the two-cycle instance, but no source with a specific locator supports the terminology and the stated local-to-global limitation.

children.title: Globally Nonoptimal Supports
children.top_down_role: Supports satisfying local tests while failing global optimality.

assumptions_latex: The cost satisfies \(c(i,i)=0\), forward-cycle costs \(-1\), and reverse-cycle costs \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diagonal support is locally two-cycle monotone but supports a coupling that is globally nonoptimal.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite three-cycle counterexample separating local monotonicity from global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Specify
\[
c(1,2)=c(2,3)=c(3,1)=-1,
\qquad
c(2,1)=c(3,2)=c(1,3)=1.
\]
Every pair of points in \(\Gamma\) passes the two-cycle condition because the two cross-costs sum to zero, equal to the corresponding diagonal-cost sum. Yet the coupling
\[
\widetilde\pi:=\frac13\bigl(\delta_{(1,2)}+
\delta_{(2,3)}+
\delta_{(3,1)}\bigr)
\]
has the same uniform marginals and satisfies \(\int c\,d\widetilde\pi=-1<0=
\int c\,d\pi_{\Gamma}\). Hence a locally monotone support can carry a globally nonoptimal transport plan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagonal coupling on three points passes every pairwise swap test but loses to a cyclic reassignment, making its locally monotone support globally nonoptimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Globally Nonoptimal Supports

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind precisely fits the globally nonoptimal-support leaf, and its arithmetic is consistent. Nevertheless, source_refs is empty and no explicit standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Cycle-Level Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Longer transport cycles that expose failures invisible to local comparisons.

assumptions_latex: The quadratic cost is \(c(x,y)=\tfrac12\lVert x-y\rVert^2\) on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A single positive cycle defect excludes optimality of every transport plan whose support contains the cycle.

notation.meaning: Finite cycle of support pairs, with the convention \(x_{m+1}=x_1\).
Cost decrease obtained by cyclically reassigning destinations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-cycle obstruction for quadratic-cost optimal transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For pairs \((x_i,y_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), define
\[
\Delta:=\sum_{i=1}^m c(x_i,y_i)-\sum_{i=1}^m c(x_i,y_{i+1}),\qquad y_{m+1}:=y_1.
\]
A support is cyclically monotone only if \(\Delta\le 0\) for every finite cycle. Hence, if some cycle has \(\Delta>0\), cyclic reassignment strictly lowers its total cost, and no optimal transport plan can have all \((x_i,y_i)\) in its support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite cycle whose cyclic reassignment lowers total cost is an explicit obstruction to optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Level Obstructions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-cycle obstruction is mathematically consistent with quadratic-cost cyclical monotonicity and fits the failure-boundary container, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports the optimal-support conclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Brenier Map Existence Under the Small-Set Nullity Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence portion only; the extract does not independently state uniqueness or optimality. The gradient is understood μ-almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu\) and \(
u\) be probability measures on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose that \(\mu\) gives no mass to small sets. Then there exists a convex function \(\varphi\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(
abla\varphi\) is defined \(\mu\)-almost everywhere and \[(
abla\varphi)_\#\mu=
u.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the source probability measure gives no mass to small sets, the target measure is its pushforward by the almost-everywhere-defined gradient of a convex function.
assumptions_latex: \mu\text{ gives no mass to small sets}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ convex }\varphi\text{ on }\mathbb{R}^n\text{ such that }(\nabla\varphi)_\#\mu=\nu

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Refined Brenier Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and almost-everywhere uniqueness of a convex-gradient transport map under the source measure's small-set nullity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu\) and \(
u\) be probability measures on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose that \(\mu\) gives no mass to small sets. Then there exists a measurable map \(T\) such that \(T_{\#}\mu=
u\) and \(T=
abla\varphi\) for some convex function \(\varphi\). Any two maps satisfying these properties coincide \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For probability measures on Euclidean space, if the source measure gives no mass to small sets, there exists a measurable transport map to the target that is the gradient of a convex function, and every two such maps agree almost everywhere with respect to the source measure.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) gives no mass to small sets
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\,T=\nabla\varphi\text{ with }\varphi\text{ convex and }T_{\#}\mu=\nu\), and any two such maps coincide \(\mu\text{-a.e.}\)

source_evidence.locator: Geometry of Optimal Transportation / 2.3. Alternative arguments / Theorem 2.32

source_refs.locator: Geometry of Optimal Transportation / 2.3. Alternative arguments / Theorem 2.32

knowledge_statements.title: Refined Brenier Theorem

source_witnesses.locator: Geometry of Optimal Transportation / 2.3. Alternative arguments / Theorem 2.32

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic optimal transport is induced \(\mu\)-almost everywhere by the gradient of a convex function.

notation.meaning: Pushforward of a measure by a map.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean quadratic-cost form of Brenier's representation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), differentiable \(\mu\)-almost everywhere, such that
\[
T(x)=\nabla\varphi(x)\quad\text{for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\)},
\qquad T_\#\mu=\nu.
\]
Moreover, the coupling \((\operatorname{id},T)_\#\mu\) minimizes \(\int c\,d\gamma\) over \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\). The gradient \(\nabla\varphi\) is determined uniquely \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With an absolutely continuous source, quadratic optimal transport is represented almost everywhere by the gradient of a convex potential.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Gradient Map Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and hypotheses match the Euclidean quadratic-cost Brenier theorem and the leaf container, but the record supplies no source or theorem locator for existence, plan optimality, and almost-everywhere uniqueness.

children.title: Transport-Map Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Regimes admitting a single optimal deterministic transport.

assumptions_latex: Both induced couplings minimize quadratic transport cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One has \(T_1=T_2\) \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness is modulo equality on a \(\mu\)-null set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose
\[
(T_i)_\#\mu=\nu,
\qquad
(\operatorname{id},T_i)_\#\mu\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}
\int\tfrac12\lVert x-y\rVert^2\,d\gamma(x,y),
\quad i=1,2.
\]
Then Brenier's quadratic-cost uniqueness conclusion gives
\[
T_1(x)=T_2(x)\quad\text{for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\)}.
\]
Thus the optimal transport map is unique as an element of \(L^0(\mu;\mathbb R^d)\), although its pointwise values on a \(\mu\)-null set remain arbitrary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an absolutely continuous source, any two quadratic-cost optimal transport maps agree almost everywhere with respect to the source.
knowledge_statements.title: Transport-Map Uniqueness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem correctly states uniqueness of optimal transport maps modulo a source-null set under absolute continuity, and its content kind fits the container. An authoritative theorem locator is absent.

children.title: Optimal-Plan Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Regimes admitting a single optimal coupling.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Kantorovich minimizer is unique and equals \((\operatorname{id},\nabla\varphi)_\#\mu\).

notation.meaning: Set of couplings having marginals \(\mu\) and \(\nu\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness in the full Kantorovich class, not merely among maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The minimization problem
\[
\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}
\int_{\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d}\tfrac12\lVert x-y\rVert^2\,d\gamma(x,y)
\]
has exactly one minimizer. More precisely, for a convex Brenier potential \(\varphi\) satisfying \((\nabla\varphi)_\#\mu=\nu\),
\[
\gamma^\star=(\operatorname{id},\nabla\varphi)_\#\mu,
\]
and every optimal \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) equals \(\gamma^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute continuity of the source makes the entire quadratic-cost optimal coupling unique and concentrated on the Brenier map's graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Plan Uniqueness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim distinguishes uniqueness in the full Kantorovich class and is mathematically standard under the stated quadratic-cost assumptions, but no source with a specific locator supports the stronger plan-uniqueness conclusion.

children.title: Divergent Uniqueness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where map uniqueness and plan uniqueness do not coincide.

assumptions_latex: The source and target are finite atomic probability measures on \(\mathbb R^2\).
The cost is squared Euclidean distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniqueness among feasible transport maps does not imply uniqueness among transport plans.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation of map uniqueness from plan uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
\mu=\tfrac35\delta_{(-1,0)}+\tfrac25\delta_{(1,0)},
\qquad
\nu=\tfrac35\delta_{(0,-1)}+\tfrac25\delta_{(0,1)}.
\]
Mass constraints permit exactly one deterministic transport map, sending the atoms of masses \(\tfrac35\) and \(\tfrac25\) to the correspondingly weighted target atoms. Nevertheless, every coupling in \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is optimal because every source-target squared distance equals \(2\). Since \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) contains nondeterministic couplings, the optimal map is unique while the optimal plan is not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atomic problem can have one feasible map but many optimal plans, showing that the two uniqueness notions can diverge.
knowledge_statements.title: Divergent Uniqueness Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atomic example is internally correct: exactly one deterministic map is feasible, all couplings have the same cost, and nondeterministic couplings exist. It fits the counterexample role, but it has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Multiplicity from Source Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Nonuniqueness driven by singular or insufficiently regular source data.

assumptions_latex: The source and target are equally weighted two-atom measures on \(\mathbb R^2\).
The cost is squared Euclidean distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Source degeneracy can permit multiple distinct optimal transport maps.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic example demonstrating failure of Brenier-type uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
\mu=\tfrac12\delta_{(-1,0)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(1,0)},
\qquad
\nu=\tfrac12\delta_{(0,-1)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(0,1)}.
\]
Both bijections between the two source atoms and the two target atoms define transport maps \(T_+\) and \(T_-\) satisfying \((T_+)_\#\mu=(T_-)_\#\mu=\nu\). Every source-target squared distance equals \(2\), so both induced plans have the same minimal cost. Hence \(T_+\ne T_-\) on a set of full \(\mu\)-measure, and optimal-map uniqueness fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two equally weighted source atoms can be matched optimally in two different ways when all cross-distances are equal.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity from Source Degeneracy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equal-weight atomic construction correctly yields two distinct optimal maps and fits the multiplicity container, but the record provides no source or specific locator.

children.title: Singular Source Measures
children.top_down_role: Source measures outside the regular-density regime of Brenier-type map results.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The measure \(\mu\) is singular exactly when it is concentrated on a Lebesgue-null Borel set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-theoretic singularity relevant to the boundary of Brenier's hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The source measure \(\mu\) is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure, written \(\mu\perp\mathcal L^d\), if there exists a Borel set \(S\subset\mathbb R^d\) such that
\[
\mathcal L^d(S)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mu(\mathbb R^d\setminus S)=0.
\]
Atomic measures and measures concentrated on lower-dimensional submanifolds are singular. Singularity removes the absolute-continuity hypothesis used in the standard Brenier theorem, but it alone does not assert nonexistence or nonuniqueness of an optimal map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular source is concentrated on a Lebesgue-null set; singularity removes Brenier's standard hypothesis but does not alone determine map existence.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Source Measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of singularity is correct and appropriately notes that singularity alone does not imply map failure. The definition and examples nevertheless lack a cited measure-theory source with a specific locator.

children.title: Optimal-Map Nonexistence
children.top_down_role: Optimal transport problems having no deterministic optimizer.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No measurable transport map sends \(\mu\) to \(\nu\), although a Kantorovich coupling exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal atomic example of Monge infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every measurable map \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\),
\[
T_\#\delta_0=\delta_{T(0)},
\]
which is a Dirac measure and therefore cannot equal \(\nu=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_1\). Thus the Monge feasible set \(\{T:T_\#\mu=\nu\}\) is empty, so an optimal transport map does not exist for any cost. In contrast, \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single source atom cannot be mapped deterministically onto two target atoms, so the Monge problem is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Map Nonexistence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Dirac-source example correctly proves Monge infeasibility while allowing a Kantorovich coupling, and the counterexample kind fits the leaf. No supporting source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Plan-Only Optimal Transport
children.top_down_role: Optimal couplings that cannot be represented by source maps.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique optimal transport exists only as a nondeterministic plan.

notation.meaning: Set of couplings with prescribed marginals.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kantorovich solvability despite Monge infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The prescribed marginals determine the sole coupling
\[
\gamma=\tfrac12\delta_{(0,-1)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(0,1)}\in\Pi(\mu,\nu).
\]
Consequently \(\gamma\) is automatically the unique quadratic-cost minimizer, with cost
\[
\int c\,d\gamma=\tfrac12.
\]
Its conditional target distribution above \(x=0\) is not a Dirac measure, so \(\gamma\) cannot equal \((\operatorname{id},T)_\#\mu\) for any measurable map \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The atom-splitting example has a unique optimal coupling, but that coupling is not induced by any transport map.
knowledge_statements.title: Plan-Only Optimal Transport

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The marginals determine the stated unique coupling, its quadratic cost is correctly computed as one half, and it is not map-induced. The plan-only example lacks a cited source and inspectable locator.

children.title: Atomic Splitting Failures
children.top_down_role: Map failure caused by target demands requiring division of source atoms.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are probability measures on measurable spaces.
\(x_0\) is an atom of \(\mu\) with mass \(a>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A deterministic map cannot split the mass \(a\) carried by the source atom \(x_0\).

notation.meaning: Pushforward measure induced by a map.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary mass-allocation condition for deterministic transport from atomic sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every measurable map \(T\), the entire mass at \(x_0\) is sent to the single point \(T(x_0)\); specifically,
\[
(T_\#\mu)(\{T(x_0)\})\ge \mu(\{x_0\})=a.
\]
Therefore, if the target requires the mass \(a\) to be divided among distinct locations and no allocation of whole source atoms realizes its atomic masses, no map \(T\) can satisfy \(T_\#\mu=\nu\). Kantorovich plans avoid this obstruction by allowing a non-Dirac conditional distribution above \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic map sends each source atom wholly to one point; targets requiring that atom's mass to split admit no such map.
knowledge_statements.title: Atomic Splitting Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The no-splitting property of deterministic pushforwards is correct and fits a failure-boundary container. The broader whole-atom allocation criterion requires an authoritative source and precise locator, neither of which is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Brenier polar factorization theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, and metric-projection characterization for nondegenerate square-integrable maps; “small set” retains the source-defined meaning not supplied in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be bounded with positive Lebesgue measure, and let h\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^n) satisfy |h^{-1}(N)|=0 for every small set N\subset\mathbb R^n. Then there exist a unique rearrangement \nabla\psi of h among the L^2 gradients of convex functions and a unique measure-preserving map s\in S(\Omega) such that h=\nabla\psi\circ s. Moreover, s is the unique L^2 projection of h onto S(\Omega).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square-integrable map satisfying the stated nondegeneracy condition factors uniquely as a convex gradient composed with a measure-preserving map. The measure-preserving factor is also its unique L2 projection onto the measure-preserving maps.
assumptions_latex: |h^{-1}(N)|=0\text{ for every small set }N\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ in the source-defined sense}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,\nabla\psi\text{ rearranging }h\text{ among }L^2\text{ gradients of convex functions},\quad\exists!\,s\in S(\Omega):h=\nabla\psi\circ s,\quad s=\operatorname*{argmin}_{r\in S(\Omega)}\|h-r\|_{L^2}\text{ uniquely}.

source_evidence.locator: Brenier's Polar Factorization Theorem / 3.1. Rearrangements and polar factorization / Theorem 3.8

source_refs.locator: Brenier's Polar Factorization Theorem / 3.1. Rearrangements and polar factorization / Theorem 3.8

source_witnesses.locator: Brenier's Polar Factorization Theorem / 3.1. Rearrangements and polar factorization / Theorem 3.8

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) has finite positive Lebesgue measure.
\(u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)\) admits a polar factorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The factor \(s\) preserves normalized Lebesgue measure and carries points to their monotone-rearrangement coordinates.

notation.meaning: Convex potential in the polar factorization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factor identity within Euclidean polar factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Writing \(m:=\mathcal L^d\mathbin{|}_\Omega/\mathcal L^d(\Omega)\), a polar factorization of \(u\) has the form
\[
u=\nabla\varphi\circ s\quad m\text{-almost everywhere},
\]
where \(\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex and \(s:\Omega\to\Omega\) satisfies
\[
s_\#m=m.
\]
Equivalently, \(m(s^{-1}(A))=m(A)\) for every Borel set \(A\subset\Omega\). Thus \(s\) rearranges the source domain without changing its probability distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a polar factorization, the inner factor rearranges the source domain while preserving normalized Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Measure-Preserving Factor

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed factor is measure preserving if the assumed polar factorization exists, and representation is an appropriate content kind. However, the exact existence regime for a map-valued polar factorization is hidden in the assumption that one is admitted, and no source or theorem locator identifies the required hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Factorization with a Measure-Preserving Factor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, almost-everywhere uniqueness, and variational characterization of the measure-preserving factor in polar factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(\mathcal L_\Omega\) be rescaled Lebesgue measure on \(\Omega\), and let \(\xi:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfy \(\xi_\#\mathcal L_\Omega\ll\mathcal L^d\). Then there exist a convex function \(u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) and a map \(s:\Omega\to\Omega\) such that \(s_\#\mathcal L_\Omega=\mathcal L_\Omega\) and \(\xi=(\nabla u)\circ s\). Both \(s\) and \(\nabla u\) are uniquely defined almost everywhere, and \(s\) solves \[\max\left\{\int_\Omega \xi(x)\cdot r(x)\,dx: r_\#\mathcal L_\Omega=\mathcal L_\Omega\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the pushforward of rescaled Lebesgue measure by a vector map ξ is absolutely continuous, then ξ factors as the gradient of a convex function composed with a measure-preserving self-map of Ω. The map s and the gradient map ∇u are unique almost everywhere, and s maximizes correlation with ξ among measure-preserving self-maps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,u\text{ convex},\ \exists\,s:\Omega\to\Omega:\ s_\#\mathcal L_\Omega=\mathcal L_\Omega,\ \xi=(\nabla u)\circ s;\quad s\text{ and }\nabla u\text{ are unique a.e., and }s\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{r_\#\mathcal L_\Omega=\mathcal L_\Omega}\int_\Omega\xi(x)\cdot r(x)\,dx.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Measure-preserving map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by invariance of the underlying measure under pushforward.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (W,\lambda) be a measure space. A measurable map s:W\to W is measure-preserving if s_\#\lambda=\lambda; equivalently, \lambda(s^{-1}(A))=\lambda(A) for every measurable set A\subseteq W.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measurable self-map is measure-preserving when its pushforward leaves the measure unchanged, equivalently when every measurable set and its inverse image have equal measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_\#\lambda=\lambda\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda(s^{-1}(A))=\lambda(A)\ \text{for every measurable }A\subseteq W.
