assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) has finite positive Lebesgue measure.
\(u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)\) admits a polar factorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The outer factor is the convex-gradient transport from normalized Lebesgue measure to \(u_\#m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-gradient outer factor in Euclidean polar factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m:=\mathcal L^d\mathbin{|}_\Omega/\mathcal L^d(\Omega)\) and \(\eta:=u_\#m\). The monotone rearrangement of \(u\) is the map
\[
T=\nabla\varphi,
\qquad
T_\#m=\eta,
\]
where \(\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex. For a measure-preserving map \(s:\Omega\to\Omega\), the polar factorization is
\[
u=T\circ s\quad m\text{-almost everywhere}.
\]
Under the hypotheses ensuring Brenier uniqueness, \(T\) is uniquely determined \(m\)-almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The outer polar factor is the convex-gradient map transporting the source-domain measure to the value distribution of the original map.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone-Rearrangement Factor

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex-gradient outer factor is the appropriate representation for this leaf, but the existence and uniqueness conditions for the stated map-valued polar factorization are not specified independently of the assumption that a factorization exists. No authoritative source or theorem locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aleksandrov Monge–Ampère Equation for a Convex Target
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absence of singular Hessian mass under convex target support and positive target density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \mu=f\,dx and 
u=g\,dy be absolutely continuous probability measures on \mathbb R^n, with respective supports X and Y. Let \varphi be convex and satisfy 
abla\varphi\#\mu=
u. If Y is convex and g>0 almost everywhere on Y, then the Hessian measure \det_H D^2\varphi has no singular part on X. In particular, \varphi solves the Monge--Amp\`ere equation in the Aleksandrov sense on X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a convex-gradient transport has convex target support and target density positive almost everywhere, the potential's Hessian measure has no singular part on the source support, and the Monge–Ampère equation holds there in the Aleksandrov sense.
assumptions_latex: \mu=f\,dx\text{ and }\nu=g\,dy\text{ are probability measures on }\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\det_H D^2\varphi)_{sing}\!\restriction_X=0,\qquad \varphi\text{ solves the Monge--Amp\`ere equation on }X\text{ in the Aleksandrov sense.}

source_evidence.locator: The Monge-Ampère Equation / 4.2. Regularity / Theorem 4.10

source_refs.locator: The Monge-Ampère Equation / 4.2. Regularity / Theorem 4.10

knowledge_statements.title: Aleksandrov Monge–Ampère Equation for a Convex Target

source_witnesses.locator: The Monge-Ampère Equation / 4.2. Regularity / Theorem 4.10

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical quadratic-cost route for smooth positive densities and a convex gradient map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega,\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d\) be domains, let \(f\) and \(g\) be positive densities, and let \(u\in C^2(\Omega)\) be convex with \(T=\nabla u\) mapping \(\Omega\) into \(\Lambda\). If \(T_\#(f\,dx)=g\,dy\) and \(T\) is injective almost everywhere, the change-of-variables formula gives
\[
f(x)=g(\nabla u(x))\det D^2u(x)
\]
for almost every \(x\in\Omega\). Thus the transport equation is
\[
\det D^2u(x)=\frac{f(x)}{g(\nabla u(x))},
\]
together with the second boundary condition \(\nabla u(\Omega)=\Lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth convex gradient transport, change of variables converts mass preservation into a Monge–Ampère equation with the target-image boundary condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Jacobian-Equation Route

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the Jacobian-equation route, but no citation supports the area/change-of-variables hypotheses or the asserted target-image equality. Almost-everywhere injectivity and mapping into Λ do not by themselves transparently justify every stated conclusion.

children.title: Alexandrov Solution Route
children.top_down_role: Measure-geometric treatment of Monge–Ampère transport potentials.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) solves \(\det D^2u=\mu\) in the Alexandrov sense exactly when \(M_u=\mu\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-valued Monge–Ampère formulation for finite convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every Borel set \(E\subset\Omega\), define the Alexandrov Monge–Ampère measure of \(u\) by
\[
M_u(E)=|\partial u(E)|.
\]
Given a nonnegative Borel measure \(\mu\) on \(\Omega\), the convex function \(u\) is an Alexandrov solution of \(\det D^2u=\mu\) when
\[
M_u(E)=\mu(E)
\]
for every Borel set \(E\subset\Omega\). If \(u\in C^2(\Omega)\), then \(M_u=(\det D^2u)\,dx\), so this definition extends the classical equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function is an Alexandrov solution when the volume of every subgradient image equals the prescribed Monge–Ampère measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Alexandrov Solution Route

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and formulation are standard for the Alexandrov route, but no inspectable source supports the measure definition or its agreement with the classical determinant.

children.title: Weak Monge–Ampère Solution Route
children.top_down_role: Distributional or generalized solution perspectives for transport equations.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\Omega\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb S^d\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and degenerate elliptic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) is a viscosity solution when it is both a viscosity subsolution and supersolution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Viscosity route for the degenerate elliptic Monge–Ampère operator on convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(u\) is a viscosity subsolution of
\[
F(x,u,Du,D^2u)=0
\]
if, whenever \(u-\phi\) has a local maximum at \(x_0\), one has \(F(x_0,u(x_0),D\phi(x_0),D^2\phi(x_0))\leq0\). It is a viscosity supersolution if, whenever \(u-\phi\) has a local minimum at \(x_0\), the reverse inequality holds. It is a viscosity solution when both conditions hold, with convexity enforcing the elliptic branch of the Monge–Ampère equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The viscosity route tests the Monge–Ampère equation against smooth functions touching a convex candidate from above or below.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Monge–Ampère Solution Route

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition gives a generic viscosity framework, but the convention for degenerate ellipticity and the precise convex Monge–Ampère operator are not specified sufficiently to verify the inequality directions or supersolution notion.

children.title: Solution-Notion Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Regimes where generalized Monge–Ampère solution concepts agree.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is open and \(f\in C(\Omega)\) is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_u=f\,dx\) if and only if \(u\) solves \(\det D^2u=f\) in the convex viscosity sense.

notation.meaning: Alexandrov Monge–Ampère measure of the convex function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of Alexandrov and convex viscosity notions for continuous nonnegative density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated assumptions, the following are equivalent:
\[
M_u=f\,dx,
\]
and \(u\) is a viscosity solution of
\[
\det D^2u=f
\]
on the convex elliptic branch. In particular, if \(u\in C^2(\Omega)\), both weak notions agree with the pointwise classical equation. Boundary conditions and additive normalization are separate requirements and must be imposed identically when comparing global boundary-value problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex continuous functions and continuous nonnegative density, Alexandrov and convex-viscosity Monge–Ampère solutions coincide; smooth solutions recover the classical equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Notion Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A theorem is the correct role for this compatibility leaf, but the exact hypotheses under which Alexandrov and convex-viscosity solutions coincide require an authoritative theorem-level citation.

children.title: Weak-Solution Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity arising from insufficiently restrictive generalized solution classes.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is a nonempty open convex set.
No boundary data or additive normalization is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equation \(M_u=0\) has infinitely many distinct convex Alexandrov solutions.

notation.meaning: affine convex function with slope and intercept

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete nonuniqueness caused by omitting boundary data and normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(a\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(b\in\mathbb R\), the affine function
\[
u_{a,b}(x)=a\cdot x+b
\]
is convex and satisfies \(\partial u_{a,b}(E)\subset\{a\}\) for every Borel set \(E\subset\Omega\). Hence \(M_{u_{a,b}}(E)=0\) and therefore
\[
M_{u_{a,b}}=0.
\]
Distinct choices of \(a\) or \(b\) give distinct weak solutions. Thus the weak Monge–Ampère equation alone does not ensure uniqueness; appropriate boundary conditions and, where relevant, additive normalization are indispensable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without boundary data or normalization, every affine convex function solves the zero Monge–Ampère equation, giving immediate weak-solution nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Solution Nonuniqueness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine family is a mathematically appropriate counterexample for weak-solution nonuniqueness, but the record contains no source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Twist Condition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cost geometries supporting pointwise identification of target locations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The twist condition holds precisely when \(y\mapsto D_xc(x,y)\) is injective for every fixed \(x\).

notation.meaning: gradient of the cost in its source variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Source-side twist convention; a symmetric target-side condition may also be imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cost \(c\) satisfies the source twist condition on \(X\times Y\) if, for every \(x\in X\),
\[
D_xc(x,y_1)=D_xc(x,y_2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_1=y_2
\]
for all \(y_1,y_2\in Y\). Equivalently, the relation
\[
p=-D_xc(x,y)
\]
determines at most one \(y\) for each admissible pair \((x,p)\). On the range of \(-D_xc(x,\cdot)\), this permits the single-valued definition \(y=\operatorname{cExp}_x(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twist means the source gradient of the cost distinguishes target points, allowing a source covector to determine at most one destination.
knowledge_statements.title: Twist Condition Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition and source-side sign convention are internally consistent and fit the leaf, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Twist Condition for a Transport Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global pointwise injectivity of the source-cost gradient as a function of the target. The informal mixed-Hessian criterion is not asserted as a global equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\). A cost \(c:\Omega\times\Omega\to\mathbb R\) satisfies the twist condition if it is differentiable with respect to \(x\) at every point and, for every \(x_0\in\Omega\), the map
\[
y\longmapsto\nabla_xc(x_0,y)
\]
is injective. This is also called the Spence--Mirrlees condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transport cost satisfies the twist condition when, at every fixed source point, distinct target points produce distinct source-variable gradients of the cost. It is also known as the Spence–Mirrlees condition.
assumptions_latex: c\text{ is differentiable with respect to }x\text{ at every point}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x_0\in\Omega,\quad y\mapsto\nabla_xc(x_0,y)\text{ is injective}

source_evidence.locator: Primal and dual problems / 1.3. The case \( c\left( {x, y}\right) = h\left( {x - y}\right) \) for \( h \) strictly convex, and the existence of an optimal T / Definition 1.16

source_refs.locator: Primal and dual problems / 1.3. The case \( c\left( {x, y}\right) = h\left( {x - y}\right) \) for \( h \) strictly convex, and the existence of an optimal T / Definition 1.16

knowledge_statements.title: Twist Condition for a Transport Cost

source_witnesses.locator: Primal and dual problems / 1.3. The case \( c\left( {x, y}\right) = h\left( {x - y}\right) \) for \( h \) strictly convex, and the existence of an optimal T / Definition 1.16

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Twist-Based Sufficient Condition for Optimality of a Transport Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General-cost optimality of a map recovered pointwise from a differentiable c-concave potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be compact, let \(c\in C^1(\Omega	imes\Omega)\) satisfy the twist condition, and let \(\mu\in\mathcal P(\Omega)\) satisfy \(\mu(\partial\Omega)=0\). Suppose \(\varphi\in c	ext{-}\operatorname{conc}(\Omega)\) is differentiable \(\mu\)-a.e. and a map \(T\) satisfies \(
abla_xc(x,T(x))=
abla\varphi(x)\) for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\). Then \(T\) is optimal for the cost \(c\) between \(\mu\) and \(
u=T_\#\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact domain, a continuously differentiable twisted cost and a c-concave potential whose gradient identifies a map T certify that T optimally transports μ to its pushforward, provided the potential is μ-almost everywhere differentiable and μ gives no mass to the boundary.
assumptions_latex: c\in C^1(\Omega\times\Omega)\text{ satisfies the twist condition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is optimal for cost }c\text{ between }\mu\text{ and }T_\#\mu.

source_evidence.locator: Primal and dual problems / 1.6.4. Sufficient conditions for optimality and stability / Theorem 1.47

source_refs.locator: Primal and dual problems / 1.6.4. Sufficient conditions for optimality and stability / Theorem 1.47

knowledge_statements.title: Twist-Based Sufficient Condition for Optimality of a Transport Map

source_witnesses.locator: Primal and dual problems / 1.6.4. Sufficient conditions for optimality and stability / Theorem 1.47

children.title: Cost Nondegeneracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Mixed cost geometry supporting local invertibility.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cost nondegeneracy holds exactly when \(\det D^2_{xy}c(x,y)\neq0\) throughout the stated regime.

notation.meaning: mixed source-target Hessian of the cost
differential with respect to the target variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local nondegeneracy condition for equal-dimensional Euclidean source and target domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cost is nondegenerate at \((x,y)\in X\times Y\) when the linear map
\[
D_y[-D_xc(x,y)]=-D^2_{xy}c(x,y):\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d
\]
is invertible, equivalently when
\[
\det D^2_{xy}c(x,y)\neq0.
\]
It is nondegenerate on a regime \(U\subset X\times Y\) when this condition holds at every point of \(U\). The inverse function theorem then makes \(y\mapsto-D_xc(x,y)\) a local diffeomorphism near each point of \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost is nondegenerate where its mixed Hessian is invertible; there the cost-gradient coordinates are locally diffeomorphic.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost Nondegeneracy Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equal-dimensional Euclidean nondegeneracy condition is appropriately classified, but its definition and local-diffeomorphism consequence lack cited support.

children.title: Transport-Map Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of deterministic transport from dual-potential data.

assumptions_latex: \(c\in C^1(X\times Y)\) satisfies the source twist condition.
\(u:X\to\mathbb R\) is a Kantorovich potential differentiable \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.
An optimal coupling is concentrated on \(u(x)+v(y)=c(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The destination is recovered by \(T(x)=\operatorname{cExp}_x(-Du(x))\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Map recovery from differentiability and source twist under the dual convention \(u+v\leq c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At every differentiability point \(x\) of \(u\), equality
\[
u(x)+v(y)=c(x,y)
\]
on the support of an optimal coupling implies
\[
Du(x)=D_xc(x,y).
\]
The source twist condition makes this equation admit at most one \(y\). With the convention \(-D_xc(x,\operatorname{cExp}_x(p))=p\), the unique destination is
\[
T(x)=\operatorname{cExp}_x(-Du(x)).
\]
Consequently, if \(u\) is differentiable \(\mu\)-almost everywhere, every optimal coupling satisfying these hypotheses is induced \(\mu\)-almost everywhere by the recovered map \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiating dual equality and applying twist recovers the unique destination as the cost exponential of the negative potential gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Transport-Map Recovery

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recovery formula is sign-consistent with the stated dual convention, but X and Y are not explicitly introduced and the conclusion that every optimal coupling is map-induced needs a source confirming all measure-theoretic hypotheses.

children.title: Map-Recovery Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity or degeneracy preventing deterministic reconstruction.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimality does not select a unique coupling or permit destination recovery from a dual gradient.

notation.meaning: set of couplings of the marginals

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure when twist is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the constant cost, \(D_xc(x,y)=0\) for every \((x,y)\), so the twist condition fails maximally. Moreover,
\[
\int_{X\times Y}c(x,y)\,d\pi(x,y)=0
\]
for every \(\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\). Hence every coupling is optimal, including the product coupling \(\mu\otimes\nu\) and couplings induced by distinct measure-preserving maps. The dual gradient contains no target information, so no unique transport map can be recovered from optimality and the potential alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For constant cost, all couplings are optimal and the cost gradient is target-independent, so potential-based map recovery completely fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Map-Recovery Failure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-cost example correctly targets the map-recovery failure boundary, but no citation supports the coupling and measurable-map assertions.

children.title: Cost-Exponential Coordinates
children.top_down_role: Coordinate representation induced by the transport cost.

assumptions_latex: For fixed \(x\), the map \(y\mapsto-D_xc(x,y)\) is injective on a set \(Y_x\subset Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cExp}_x\) is the inverse of \(y\mapsto-D_xc(x,y)\) on its image.

notation.meaning: cost-exponential map based at the source point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Source cost-exponential convention using the negative source gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the admissible covector set
\[
P_x=\{-D_xc(x,y):y\in Y_x\}.
\]
The cost-exponential map based at \(x\) is the inverse coordinate map
\[
\operatorname{cExp}_x:P_x\to Y_x,
\qquad -D_xc\bigl(x,\operatorname{cExp}_x(p)\bigr)=p.
\]
Injectivity makes this definition single-valued. If \(c\in C^2\) and \(D^2_{xy}c\) is invertible, then \(\operatorname{cExp}_x\) is locally smooth by the inverse function theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cost-exponential coordinates invert the negative source cost-gradient, converting an admissible source covector into its unique target point.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Exponential Coordinates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits cost-exponential coordinates and is internally sign-consistent, but X and Y are not separately introduced and no source fixes this convention or supports the smoothness assertion.

children.title: Cut-Locus Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric loci where cost-exponential representations lose regularity or uniqueness.

assumptions_latex: A source point \(x\in X\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outside \(\operatorname{Cut}_c(x)\), the chosen cost-exponential branch is single-valued and regular on its coordinate domain.

notation.meaning: cost cut locus relative to the source point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational cost cut locus defined through failure of global regular cost-exponential coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Relative to a selected maximal regular branch, the cost cut locus \(\operatorname{Cut}_c(x)\subset Y\) consists of target points \(y\) at which the coordinate relation
\[
p=-D_xc(x,y)
\]
fails to admit a locally single-valued regular inverse continuing that branch. Failure may arise from collision with another target having the same covector, singularity of the mixed derivative, or loss of continuation at the coordinate-domain boundary. Thus \(Y\setminus\operatorname{Cut}_c(x)\) is the region covered by the selected regular cost-exponential coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cost cut locus marks targets where a chosen cost-exponential coordinate branch ceases to be uniquely and regularly invertible.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Locus Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Cost cut-locus conventions vary substantially. The selected maximal regular branch and its continuation boundary are not formally defined, so an authoritative framework-specific source is necessary before the statement can be assessed.

children.title: Injectivity Domains
children.top_down_role: Regions supporting single-valued cost-exponential inversion.

assumptions_latex: A source point \(x\in X\) and an open set \(U_x\subset Y\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_x\) is a regular injectivity domain exactly when the cost-gradient coordinate is one-to-one and nonsingular there.

notation.meaning: target-side injectivity domain based at the source point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular target injectivity domains for a fixed source point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(U_x\) is a regular injectivity domain for the cost exponential if the map
\[
y\longmapsto-D_xc(x,y)
\]
is injective on \(U_x\) and
\[
\det D^2_{xy}c(x,y)\neq0
\]
for every \(y\in U_x\). Writing \(P_x=-D_xc(x,U_x)\), the inverse function theorem and injectivity yield a single-valued local diffeomorphism
\[
\operatorname{cExp}_x:P_x\to U_x.
\]
A maximal injectivity domain is one not properly contained in another open set with these properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An injectivity domain is an open target region where the cost-gradient coordinates are one-to-one and nonsingular, so their cost-exponential inverse is regular.
knowledge_statements.title: Injectivity Domains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition is coherent for a regular injectivity domain and fits the leaf, but the terminology, global inverse claim, and maximality convention lack an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Cost-Exponential Degeneracies
children.top_down_role: Branching, singularity, or multivalued behavior near geometric obstructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Exponential Degeneracies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential degeneracy of cost-exponential coordinates, distinguished from global noninjectivity and the cost cut locus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be smooth manifolds of the same finite dimension and let \(c\in C^2(X\times Y)\). For fixed \(x\in X\), define \(F_x:Y\to T_x^*X\) by \(F_x(y)=-D_xc(x,y)\). A pair \((x,y)\in X\times Y\) is a cost-exponential degeneracy when the derivative \(D_yF_x(y)=-D^2_{xy}c(x,y)\) is singular. Equivalently, in local coordinates, \[\det D^2_{xy}c(x,y)=0.\] At such a pair, the inverse-function theorem does not provide a locally unique smooth inverse \(y=\operatorname{cExp}_x(p)\). This differential degeneracy is distinct from failure of global injectivity at points where \(D^2_{xy}c(x,y)\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost-exponential degeneracy is a point where the mixed cost Hessian is singular, so the cost-covector map is not a local smooth coordinate system there.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are smooth finite-dimensional manifolds with \(\dim X=\dim Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At a cost-exponential degeneracy, \(D_yF_x(y)\) is singular and the inverse-function theorem does not yield a local smooth cost-exponential coordinate map.

notation.meaning: The cost-covector map \(y\mapsto-D_xc(x,y)\) at the base point x
A local smooth inverse of the cost-covector map when it exists

assumptions_latex: \(c\in C^4(X\times Y)\) satisfies twist and \(D^2_{xy}c\) is nonsingular.
The vectors \(\xi\in T_xX\) and \(\eta\in T_x^*X\) satisfy \(\eta(\xi)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The signs \(\operatorname{MTW}_c\geq 0\), \(\operatorname{MTW}_c>0\) on nonzero orthogonal pairs, and sign failure define the weak, strong, and negative regimes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak, strong, and sign-violating MTW regimes under a fixed cross-curvature sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix the convention
\[
\operatorname{MTW}_c(x,p)(\xi,\eta)=-\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\bigg|_{t=0}D^2_{xx}c\bigl(x,\operatorname{cExp}_x(p+t\eta)\bigr)[\xi,\xi].
\]
The weak regime \(A3w\) requires \(\operatorname{MTW}_c(x,p)(\xi,\eta)\geq 0\) whenever \(\eta(\xi)=0\). The strong regime \(A3s\) requires strict positivity for every such pair with \(\xi\neq0\) and \(\eta\neq0\). A negative cross-curvature regime occurs when an admissible orthogonal pair satisfies \(\operatorname{MTW}_c(x,p)(\xi,\eta)<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MTW regimes classify a cost by whether its cross-curvature is nonnegative, strictly positive, or negative on orthogonal direction pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Curvature Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local topic fit, but the MTW sign convention and the precise strong-condition formulation are convention-sensitive. No citation is supplied to verify them.

children.title: Interior Regularity
children.top_down_role: Regularity away from domain boundaries and singular sets.

assumptions_latex: \(c\in C^{4,\alpha}\) is twisted, nondegenerate, and satisfies a strong MTW condition on the relevant domains.
The source and target domains are locally uniformly \(c\)-convex, and their densities lie in \(C^\alpha\) with positive local upper and lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transport potential belongs to \(C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}\), and its induced optimal map belongs to \(C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}\).

notation.meaning: Optimal map induced by the cost exponential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative strong-MTW interior Schauder regularity statement, away from source and target boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u\) be a \(c\)-convex potential transporting \(f(x)\,dx\) to \(g(y)\,dy\), and set
\[
T_u(x)=\operatorname{cExp}_x(Du(x)).
\]
Under the stated structural, convexity, and density hypotheses, every compact set \(K\) contained in the source interior and mapped a positive distance from the target boundary admits a constant \(C_K\) such that
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{C^{2,\alpha}(K)}+\lVert T_u\rVert_{C^{1,\alpha}(K)}\leq C_K.
\]
Consequently, \(u\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}\) and \(T_u\in C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}\) on the corresponding interior transport locus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong MTW geometry, local cost-convexity, and positive Hölder densities yield interior Hölder regularity of the potential Hessian and transport derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior Regularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is appropriately a theorem, but the stated structural and domain hypotheses are not sufficiently tied to a specific interior regularity theorem. The convention in \(T_u=\operatorname{cExp}_x(Du)\) also requires verification.

children.title: Boundary Regularity
children.top_down_role: Regularity behavior near source or target domain boundaries.

assumptions_latex: The hypotheses of the selected global second-boundary-value regularity theorem hold for \(c\), the densities, and the closures of both domains.
The domain boundaries are sufficiently smooth and uniformly \(c\)-convex and \(c^*\)-convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transport potential and optimal map retain their prescribed regularity up to the source boundary.

notation.meaning: Optimal transport map induced by u

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Up-to-boundary regularity for the generated Jacobian equation with the second boundary condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u\) solve the optimal-transport second boundary value problem
\[
(T_u)_\#(f\,dx)=g\,dy,
\qquad T_u(\Omega)=\Omega^*.
\]
Assume a boundary regularity theorem whose structural hypotheses include twist, nondegeneracy, the required MTW condition, positive regular densities, and uniform cost-convexity of both boundaries. Then its a priori estimates extend from compact interior subsets to \(\overline\Omega\). In the standard Hölder formulation this yields
\[
u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega),
\qquad T_u\in C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega).
\]
Thus boundary regularity requires geometric boundary hypotheses not supplied by an interior estimate alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Up-to-boundary estimates require smooth, uniformly cost-convex source and target boundaries in addition to the interior MTW and density hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Regularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement assumes an unspecified boundary regularity theorem rather than listing a checkable hypothesis package. A precise cited theorem is needed to determine the boundary smoothness, MTW, density, convexity, and obliqueness requirements.

children.title: Global Regularity
children.top_down_role: Whole-domain regularity under compatible geometric and measure data.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global regularity obtained by combining uniform interior estimates, boundary estimates, and global transport geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\) and \(\Omega^*\) be bounded domains, and let \(u\) be the normalized \(c\)-convex potential transporting \(f(x)\,dx\) on \(\Omega\) to \(g(y)\,dy\) on \(\Omega^*\). Assume uniform structural, cross-curvature, domain-convexity, boundary, and density hypotheses sufficient for the selected global second-boundary-value regularity theorem. Then \[u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega),\qquad T_u\in C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega).\] If that theorem additionally guarantees global injectivity and a regular inverse, then \(T_u\) is a regular bijection from \(\overline\Omega\) onto \(\overline{\Omega^*}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the complete hypotheses of an applicable global second-boundary-value theorem, the potential and transport map are regular on the closed source domain; global bijectivity requires the theorem's additional injectivity and inverse-regularity assumptions.
assumptions_latex: The structural, cross-curvature, domain-convexity, boundary, and density hypotheses of a selected global regularity theorem hold uniformly.
The source and target densities are positive, have equal total mass, and have the regularity required by that theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected theorem yields \(u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)\) and \(T_u\in C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)\), with global regular bijectivity only when separately guaranteed by its hypotheses.

notation.meaning: Optimal transport map induced by u

children.title: Local-to-Global Regularity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Obstructions preventing interior estimates from extending globally.

assumptions_latex: An interior regularity theorem applies to a \(c\)-convex transport potential \(u\).
No boundary cost-convexity, obliqueness, or boundary smoothness assumption is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interior regularity alone does not imply regularity on the closed source domain or continuity of the transport map at its boundary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary separating compact-interior estimates from estimates on the closure of the transport domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Estimates of the form
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{C^{2,\alpha}(K)}\leq C_K,
\qquad K\Subset\Omega,
\]
permit \(C_K\) to diverge as \(\operatorname{dist}(K,\partial\Omega)\downarrow0\). Hence they do not imply \(u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)\) or \(T_u\in C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)\). Passing from local to global regularity requires independent control of the second boundary condition, including suitable source and target cost-convexity and boundary obliqueness. Removing those hypotheses leaves boundary singularity or loss of continuity compatible with complete interior regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact-interior estimates do not control boundary behavior; global regularity additionally needs cost-convex boundary geometry and obliqueness estimates.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-to-Global Regularity Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between compact-interior and boundary estimates is correct, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The stronger assertion that boundary singularity or discontinuity remains compatible requires a cited theorem or counterexample.

children.title: Negative Cross-Curvature Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cost geometries hostile to regular transport maps.

assumptions_latex: \(c\in C^4(X\times Y)\) is twisted and nondegenerate near \((x_0,y_0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The weak MTW condition fails locally, placing the cost in a regime where universal continuity of optimal maps cannot hold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise violation of weak MTW cross-curvature and its regularity consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A negative cross-curvature regime is present if there exist \((x_0,y_0)\), nonzero \(\xi_0\in T_{x_0}X\), and nonzero \(\eta_0\in T_{x_0}^*X\) with \(\eta_0(\xi_0)=0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{MTW}_c(x_0,p_0)(\xi_0,\eta_0)<0,
\qquad p_0=-D_xc(x_0,y_0).
\]
This is precisely a local failure of \(A3w\) under the fixed sign convention. For costs satisfying the usual smoothness, twist, and nondegeneracy assumptions, such failure obstructs a universal regularity theory guaranteeing continuity for optimal maps between all smooth positive data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative MTW value on an orthogonal direction pair violates weak cross-curvature and obstructs universal continuity of optimal transport.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative Cross-Curvature Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise sign violation correctly describes failure of A3w under the declared convention, but its universal-continuity consequence is a nontrivial necessity result requiring an authoritative source and precise scope.

children.title: Discontinuous Transport Maps
children.top_down_role: Loss of continuity caused by unfavorable cost geometry.

assumptions_latex: A smooth twisted, nondegenerate cost violates the weak MTW condition at an interior point.
The source and target domains contain sufficiently small neighborhoods used in the local construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist smooth strictly positive source and target densities whose unique optimal transport map is discontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loeper-type necessity of weak MTW for universal continuity of optimal maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(c\) satisfies the standard local smoothness, twist, and nondegeneracy assumptions but fails \(A3w\) at an interior point. Then one can choose smooth probability densities \(f>0\) and \(g>0\), supported in sufficiently small source and target domains, such that the optimal map \(T\) transporting
\[
\mu=f(x)\,dx
\quad\text{to}\quad
\nu=g(y)\,dy
\]
is not continuous. Thus twist, nondegeneracy, smooth data, and positivity of both densities do not by themselves guarantee continuity; nonnegative MTW cross-curvature is necessary for a continuity theorem uniform over all such data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When weak MTW fails, some smooth positive source and target densities have an optimal map that is nevertheless discontinuous.
knowledge_statements.title: Discontinuous Transport Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the leaf, but the existence of smooth positive data producing a discontinuous optimal map is a delicate necessity theorem. Its domain, support, regularity, and uniqueness hypotheses need a specific theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist a smooth compact Riemannian surface $S$ and smooth positive probability densities $f$ and $g$ on $S$ such that the optimal transport from $\mu(dx)=f(x)\,\operatorname{vol}(dx)$ to $\nu(dy)=g(y)\,\operatorname{vol}(dy)$ for $c(x,y)=d_S(x,y)^2$ is discontinuous.

$f$ and $g$ are smooth positive probability densities on $S$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The optimal transport from }f\,\operatorname{vol}\text{ to }g\,\operatorname{vol}\text{ is discontinuous.}

children.title: Potential Regularity Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Failure of expected smoothness for transport potentials.

assumptions_latex: The cost is smooth, twisted, and nondegenerate but violates \(A3w\).
The transport data are chosen as in a local discontinuity construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A corresponding \(c\)-convex Kantorovich potential fails to be differentiable at some interior point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of differentiability of transport potentials when weak MTW geometry fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For data realizing the discontinuity mechanism associated with failure of \(A3w\), there is an interior point \(x_0\) at which the contact set is not single-valued:
\[
\#\partial^c u(x_0)>1.
\]
Under twist, differentiability of \(u\) at \(x_0\) would force \(\partial^c u(x_0)\) to contain at most the single point \(\operatorname{cExp}_{x_0}(Du(x_0))\). Hence \(u\) is not differentiable at \(x_0\). In particular, smooth positive densities cannot prevent loss of \(C^1\) regularity when the cost geometry admits the MTW sign-violation construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of weak MTW can produce a multivalued cost-subdifferential, forcing an optimal transport potential to lose interior differentiability.
knowledge_statements.title: Potential Regularity Breakdown

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The twist-based implication from differentiability to a singleton cost-subdifferential is plausible, but the claim that the A3w counterexample necessarily supplies a multivalued contact set at an interior point must be verified from the underlying construction.

children.title: Geometric Instability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Transition from stable regularity to geometry-driven singular behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(c\in C^4\) satisfies twist and nondegeneracy on the transport region.
Continuity is required for optimal maps associated with every pair of smooth strictly positive densities on sufficiently small admissible domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Universal continuity requires \(A3w\); a negative orthogonal MTW direction lies beyond the geometric stability boundary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak MTW as the necessary geometric threshold for data-uniform continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The geometric stability boundary for data-uniform continuity is the inequality
\[
\operatorname{MTW}_c(x,p)(\xi,\eta)\geq0
\quad\text{whenever}\quad
\eta(\xi)=0.
\]
If this \(A3w\) condition fails at an admissible interior point, smooth positive densities can be selected for which the optimal map is discontinuous. Conversely, satisfying this inequality removes that particular local geometric obstruction, although continuity may still require cost-convex domains, density bounds, and avoidance of cut-locus degeneracies. Thus \(A3w\) is a necessary geometric threshold, not by itself a complete global regularity hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak MTW is the geometric threshold for universal continuity: violating it creates unstable data, while satisfying it does not replace other hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Instability Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the geometric threshold leaf, and the statement appropriately avoids claiming sufficiency. The asserted necessity for continuity over all smooth positive data still requires a precisely located authoritative result.

children.title: Transport Singular Sets
children.top_down_role: Exceptional loci where transport maps or potentials lose regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(u\) is a \(c\)-convex potential on an open source domain \(\Omega\).
The optimal map is represented almost everywhere by \(T_u(x)=\operatorname{cExp}_x(Du(x))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transport singular set is the complement of the largest open locus on which the potential and induced map have the selected regularity.

notation.meaning: Regular transport locus at regularity level C^{k,alpha}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity-indexed singular set for a transport potential and its induced map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(k\in\mathbb N\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Define the regular transport locus by
\[
\mathcal R_{k,\alpha}=
\bigl\{x\in\Omega:\text{some open }U\ni x\text{ has }u\in C^{k+1,\alpha}(U)
\text{ and }T_u\in C^{k,\alpha}(U)\bigr\}.
\]
The transport singular set at this regularity level is
\[
\Sigma_{k,\alpha}=
\Omega\setminus\mathcal R_{k,\alpha}.
\]
It contains points where the potential lacks the stated local smoothness, where its cost-subdifferential is multivalued, or where the induced map cannot be represented locally with the prescribed regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a chosen Hölder level, the transport singular set consists exactly of source points lacking any neighborhood with regular potential and map.
knowledge_statements.title: Transport Singular Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and fits the leaf, but it is a chosen regularity-indexed convention rather than an identified standard definition. The final containment claim also needs qualification or a source, especially where the induced map may fail for reasons not equivalent to the selected Hölder regularity.

children.title: Regular Transport Locus
children.top_down_role: Complementary regions retaining the expected transport regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Transport Locus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological and local regularity properties of the regular transport locus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(k\in\mathbb N\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). For a \(c\)-convex transport potential \(u\) on an open domain \(\Omega\), define \[\mathcal R_{k,\alpha}=\bigcup\bigl\{U\subset\Omega: U\text{ is open},\ u\in C^{k+1,\alpha}(U),\text{ and }T_u\in C^{k,\alpha}(U)\bigr\}.\] Then \(\mathcal R_{k,\alpha}\) is open. Moreover, every point of \(\mathcal R_{k,\alpha}\) has a neighborhood on which \(u\) and \(T_u\) possess the prescribed classical Hölder regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular transport locus is the union of all open neighborhoods where the potential and transport map have the selected Hölder regularity; consequently, it is open.
assumptions_latex: \(u\) is a \(c\)-convex transport potential on an open domain \(\Omega\).
The induced transport map \(T_u\) is defined on each open set entering the union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The locus \(\mathcal R_{k,\alpha}\) is open, and \(u\in C^{k+1,\alpha}\) and \(T_u\in C^{k,\alpha}\) locally on that locus.

notation.meaning: Regular transport locus at the selected Hölder level
Optimal transport map induced by u

children.title: Partial Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regularity conclusions valid outside controlled exceptional sets.

assumptions_latex: The source and target are domains in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and an optimal transport map \(T\) exists for a specified cost and pair of measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decomposition \(\Omega=R_{\alpha}(T)\cup S_{\alpha}(T)\) identifies the locus of local \(C^{1,\alpha}\) regularity and its singular complement.

notation.meaning: local regular locus of the transport map
singular complement of the regular locus

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: partial regularity is conventionally expressed by an open regular locus and a quantitatively small singular complement
exact cost, density, and singular-set size hypotheses require a transport-regularity source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a regularity regime without asserting a particular singular-set estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<\alpha\leq 1\). The \(C^{1,\alpha}\) regular locus of \(T:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is \[R_{\alpha}(T):=\bigl\{x\in\Omega:\text{there exists an open neighborhood }U\ni x\text{ such that }T|_U\in C^{1,\alpha}(U;\mathbb{R}^n)\bigr\}.\] Its singular locus is \(S_{\alpha}(T):=\Omega\setminus R_{\alpha}(T)\). A partial-regularity regime consists of hypotheses on the cost, domains, and densities under which \(R_{\alpha}(T)\) is open and \(S_{\alpha}(T)\) is negligible in a stated sense, such as zero Lebesgue measure or a prescribed Hausdorff-dimension bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial regularity means the transport map is locally Hölder differentiable on an open regular set, while the complementary singular set satisfies a specified smallness estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial Regularity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of the local regular and singular loci is coherent and fits the terminal container, but the claimed partial-regularity regime is intentionally generic and has no citation establishing the relevant cost, density, domain, or singular-set smallness hypotheses. A transport-regularity source with a theorem or section locator is required.

children.title: Singular-Set Stratification
children.top_down_role: Geometric organization of exceptional loci by dimension or defect type.

assumptions_latex: A map \(T:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is given on an open set \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The failure sets \(S^{(k)}(T)\) form a nested stratification by local Hölder-regularity threshold.

notation.meaning: failure set for local C^{1,alpha_k} regularity

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: failure sets for increasingly strong local regularity thresholds are nested
source_needed_to_confirm_that_threshold stratification is the intended transport singular-set stratification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines only a threshold-based stratification; geometric, blow-up, dimensional, or rectifiability strata require separate sourced assertions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each threshold \(\alpha_k\), define \[S^{(k)}(T):=\bigl\{x\in\Omega:T\text{ is not }C^{1,\alpha_k}\text{ on any open neighborhood of }x\bigr\}.\] Since local \(C^{1,\alpha_{k+1}}\) regularity implies local \(C^{1,\alpha_k}\) regularity whenever \(\alpha_k<\alpha_{k+1}\), the failure sets satisfy \[S^{(0)}(T)\subseteq S^{(1)}(T)\subseteq\cdots.\] Any Hausdorff-dimension, rectifiability, or blow-up characterization of these sets is an additional assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The failure sets for successively stronger local Hölder differentiability thresholds form a nested stratification; geometric or dimensional properties require additional assertions.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Set Stratification

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Wasserstein Distance of Order p
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition on all probability measures, where the value may be infinite without finite-moment assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(\mathcal X,d)$ be a Polish metric space and let $p\in[1,\infty)$. For $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$, define
\[
W_p(\mu,\nu):=\left(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{\mathcal X\times\mathcal X}d(x,y)^p\,d\pi(x,y)\right)^{1/p}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
W_p(\mu,\nu)=\inf\left\{\bigl(\mathbb E[d(X,Y)^p]\bigr)^{1/p}:\operatorname{law}(X)=\mu,\ \operatorname{law}(Y)=\nu\right\}.
\]

children.title: Narrow Convergence Topology
children.top_down_role: Weak convergence behavior of probability measures.

assumptions_latex: Let \(X\) be a metric space and \((\mu_n)\subseteq\mathcal P(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Narrow convergence is convergence against every bounded continuous real-valued function on \(X\).

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence \((\mu_n)\) converges narrowly to \(\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\), written \(\mu_n\rightharpoonup\mu\), if and only if \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_X f\,d\mu_n=\int_X f\,d\mu\qquad\text{for every }f\in C_b(X).\] The narrow topology on \(\mathcal P(X)\) is the coarsest topology making every map \(\mu\mapsto\int_X f\,d\mu\), with \(f\in C_b(X)\), continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Probability measures converge narrowly when their integrals against every bounded continuous test function converge.

children.title: Moment Control Regimes
children.top_down_role: Uniform or convergent moment conditions relevant to Wasserstein topology.

assumptions_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, choose \(x_0\in X\), fix \(p\in[1,\infty)\), and let \((\mu_n)\subseteq\mathcal P_p(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform vanishing of the tail \(p\)-moments is the moment-control condition, and it is strictly stronger than uniform boundedness of the total \(p\)-moments.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform tail integrability is the standard moment-control condition for Wasserstein convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States uniform \(p\)-moment tail control relative to a base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R>0\), define \[M_{p,R}(\mu_n):=\int_{\{x\in X:d(x,x_0)>R\}}d(x,x_0)^p\,d\mu_n(x).\] The sequence has uniformly integrable \(p\)-moments if \[\lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_{n\geq1}M_{p,R}(\mu_n)=0.\] This condition is independent of the chosen base point and is stronger than \[\sup_{n\geq1}\int_X d(x,x_0)^p\,d\mu_n(x)<\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform p-moment control means that the p-th moment in distant tails vanishes uniformly over the sequence; this is stronger than a uniform bound on total p-th moments.
knowledge_statements.title: Moment Control Regimes

children.title: Wasserstein Convergence Characterization
children.top_down_role: Relationship between narrow convergence, moment behavior, and metric convergence.

assumptions_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a Polish metric space, let \(p\in[1,\infty)\), and let \(\mu_n,mu\in\mathcal P_p(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convergence in \(W_p\) is equivalent to narrow convergence together with convergence of the \(p\)-th moments, and equivalently to narrow convergence together with uniform integrability of those moments.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical characterization of convergence in finite-order Wasserstein spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization for finite \(p\) on a Polish metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any fixed \(x_0\in X\), the following are equivalent: \[(i)\quad W_p(\mu_n,\mu)\longrightarrow0;\] \[(ii)\quad \mu_n\rightharpoonup\mu\quad\text{and}\quad\int_X d(x,x_0)^p\,d\mu_n(x)\longrightarrow\int_X d(x,x_0)^p\,d\mu(x).\] These conditions are also equivalent to narrow convergence together with uniform integrability of the \(p\)-moments. The choice of \(x_0\) does not affect the characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Polish metric space, Wasserstein-p convergence is equivalent to narrow convergence plus convergence of p-th moments, and also to narrow convergence plus uniform integrability of those moments.
knowledge_statements.title: Wasserstein Convergence Characterization

children.title: Moment-Escape Failures
children.top_down_role: Narrowly convergent sequences lacking convergence in Wasserstein distance.

assumptions_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R\) with its Euclidean distance and fix \(p\in[1,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Narrow convergence and uniformly bounded \(p\)-moments do not imply \(W_p\)-convergence without uniform moment-tail control.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete escaping-mass counterexample on the real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq1\), let \[\mu_n:=\left(1-\frac1n\right)\delta_0+\frac1n\delta_{n^{1/p}}.\] Then \[\mu_n\rightharpoonup\delta_0,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}|x|^p\,d\mu_n(x)=1,\qquad W_p(\mu_n,\delta_0)^p=1.\] Thus \(W_p(\mu_n,\delta_0)\not\to0\). The family has uniformly bounded \(p\)-moments but does not have uniformly integrable \(p\)-moment tails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mass of size 1/n placed at distance n^(1/p) disappears narrowly but retains unit p-cost, so bounded p-th moments do not suffice for Wasserstein-p convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Escape Failures

children.title: Wasserstein Completeness
children.top_down_role: Cauchy-sequence closure properties of Wasserstein spaces.

assumptions_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(p\in[1,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The space \((\mathcal P_p(X),W_p)\) is complete if and only if \((X,d)\) is complete.

notation.meaning: finite p-moment probability measures on X

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical completeness equivalence for finite-order Wasserstein spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness equivalence for a metric space and its finite-order Wasserstein space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in[1,\infty)\), the metric space \((\mathcal P_p(X),W_p)\) is complete if and only if \((X,d)\) is complete. In particular, if \((X,d)\) is complete and \((\mu_n)\subseteq\mathcal P_p(X)\) is \(W_p\)-Cauchy, then there exists \(\mu\in\mathcal P_p(X)\) such that \[W_p(\mu_n,\mu)\longrightarrow0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite p, the p-Wasserstein space is complete exactly when the underlying metric space is complete.
knowledge_statements.title: Wasserstein Completeness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Wasserstein Cauchy Sequences Are Tight
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tightness of Cauchy sequences as an intermediate property in Wasserstein completeness theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a Polish space, let \(p\ge 1\), and let \((\mu_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) be Cauchy in \((\mathcal P_p(\mathcal X),W_p)\). Then the family \(\{\mu_k:k\in\mathbb N\}\) is tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Cauchy sequence in a p-Wasserstein space over a Polish space forms a tight family of probability measures.
assumptions_latex: \((\mu_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) is Cauchy in \((\mathcal P_p(\mathcal X),W_p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\mu_k:k\in\mathbb N\}\text{ is tight}.\)

assumptions_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(p\in[1,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The space \((\mathcal P_p(X),W_p)\) is separable if and only if \((X,d)\) is separable.

notation.meaning: a countable dense subset of X
finitely supported probability measures on D with rational weights
finite p-moment probability measures on X

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical separability equivalence for finite-order Wasserstein spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separability equivalence and a canonical countable dense family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in[1,\infty)\), the metric space \((\mathcal P_p(X),W_p)\) is separable if and only if \((X,d)\) is separable. If \(D\subseteq X\) is countable and dense, then the family \(\mathcal A(D)\) of finitely supported probability measures on \(D\) with rational weights is countable and dense in \((\mathcal P_p(X),W_p)\).

children.title: Polish Wasserstein Spaces
children.top_down_role: Joint complete-separable structure inherited from the underlying space.

assumptions_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(p\in[1,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The space \((\mathcal P_p(X),W_p)\) is Polish if and only if \((X,d)\) is Polish.

notation.meaning: finite p-moment probability measures on X

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Polishness follows from the completeness and separability equivalences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(p\in[1,\infty)\), \[(X,d)\text{ is Polish}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\mathcal P_p(X),W_p)\text{ is Polish}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polish Inheritance and Finite-Support Density of Wasserstein Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness, separability, and finite-support approximation in finite-p-moment Wasserstein spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be a complete separable metric space and let \(p\in[1,\infty)\). Then \((\mathcal P_p(\mathcal X),W_p)\) is a complete separable metric space. Moreover, for every \(\mu\in\mathcal P_p(\mathcal X)\), there exists a sequence \((\mu_n)\) of finitely supported probability measures such that \(W_p(\mu_n,\mu)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The p-Wasserstein space over a Polish space is itself Polish, and finitely supported probability measures are dense in it under the p-Wasserstein metric.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal X,d)\) is a complete separable metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mathcal P_p(\mathcal X),W_p)\text{ is complete and separable, and finitely supported probability measures are }W_p\text{-dense in }\mathcal P_p(\mathcal X).

children.title: Inheritance Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Underlying-space defects preventing completeness or separability.

assumptions_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and fix \(p\in[1,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Incompleteness or nonseparability of \(X\) obstructs the corresponding property, and therefore Polishness, for \((\mathcal P_p(X),W_p)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the isometric Dirac embedding transfers metric obstructions from the base space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp inheritance obstructions induced by the Dirac isometric embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Dirac map \(\iota:X\to\mathcal P_p(X)\), defined by \(\iota(x)=\delta_x\), satisfies \[W_p(\delta_x,\delta_y)=d(x,y)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in X.\] Consequently, if \(X\) is incomplete, then \((\mathcal P_p(X),W_p)\) is incomplete; if \(X\) is nonseparable, then \((\mathcal P_p(X),W_p)\) is nonseparable. Either failure prevents the Wasserstein space from being Polish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because the Dirac embedding preserves base distances, incompleteness and nonseparability of the base remain obstructions to completeness, separability, and Polishness of its Wasserstein space.
knowledge_statements.title: Inheritance Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Narrow compactness does not imply relative compactness in \(W_p\) without uniform \(p\)-moment integrability.

notation.meaning: Probability measure placing mass one at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete narrow-convergence counterexample showing escape of the Wasserstein moment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq1\), define \(\mu_n=(1-n^{-p})\delta_0+n^{-p}\delta_n\). Then \(\mu_n\) converges narrowly to \(\delta_0\), and its \(p\)-th moments are uniformly bounded. Nevertheless, \(W_p(\mu_n,\delta_0)^p=\int_{\mathbb R}|x|^p\,d\mu_n(x)=1\). Hence no subsequence converges to \(\delta_0\) in \(W_p\); since every narrowly convergent subsequence has narrow limit \(\delta_0\), the family is not relatively compact in \((\mathcal P_p(\mathbb R),W_p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vanishing amount of mass sent increasingly far away preserves narrow convergence but prevents Wasserstein convergence because its moment contribution does not vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Moment Compactness

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Linear mixing of endpoint measures is generally not their constant-speed Wasserstein geodesic.

notation.meaning: Linear mixture of the endpoint measures
Displacement geodesic between the endpoint Dirac measures

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts affine mixing with displacement interpolation for \(p>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu_0=\delta_0\) and \(\mu_1=\delta_1\). Their constant-speed \(W_p\)-geodesic is \(\mu_t=\delta_t\), whereas their linear mixture is \(m_t=(1-t)\delta_0+t\delta_1\). For \(0<t<1\), these measures differ, and \(W_p(\mu_0,m_t)=t^{1/p}\), while a constant-speed geodesic must satisfy \(W_p(\mu_0,\mu_t)=tW_p(\mu_0,\mu_1)=t\). Thus the vector-space superposition operation does not generate Wasserstein geodesics except in degenerate cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even between two Dirac masses, affine mixing differs from displacement interpolation and fails the constant-speed identity when p is greater than one.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Linear Superposition

children.title: Branching Geodesic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geodesics sharing an initial segment before separating.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Branching in the base metric space produces branching among Dirac-valued Wasserstein geodesics.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Base-space branching lifted through the isometric Dirac embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose two constant-speed geodesics \(\gamma^1,\gamma^2:[0,1]\to X\) satisfy \(\gamma_t^1=\gamma_t^2\) for every \(t\in[0,\tau]\), for some \(0<\tau<1\), but \(\gamma_s^1\neq\gamma_s^2\) for some \(s>\tau\). Then \(\mu_t^i=\delta_{\gamma_t^i}\) are constant-speed geodesics in \((\mathcal P_p(X),W_p)\). They coincide on \([0,\tau]\) and subsequently separate. Consequently, every branching regime of \(X\) induces a branching regime in its Wasserstein space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two base-space geodesics that share an initial segment and then split lift to Wasserstein geodesics with exactly the same branching behavior.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching Geodesic Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The isometric Dirac embedding supports the stated lifting of branching, and the property fits the leaf, but an authoritative source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Nonunique Geodesic Families
children.top_down_role: Multiple displacement interpolations joining the same endpoint measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Geodesic Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness expressed through optimal dynamical transport plans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\boldsymbol\eta^1\) and \(\boldsymbol\eta^2\) be optimal probability measures on the constant-speed geodesics of \(X\), with \((e_0,e_1)_\#\boldsymbol\eta^i\) coupling the same measures \(\mu_0,\mu_1\). For each \(i\), the curve \(\mu_t^i=(e_t)_\#\boldsymbol\eta^i\) is a constant-speed \(W_p\)-geodesic from \(\mu_0\) to \(\mu_1\). If \((e_t)_\#\boldsymbol\eta^1\neq(e_t)_\#\boldsymbol\eta^2\) for some \(t\in(0,1)\), the endpoints admit at least two distinct Wasserstein geodesics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimal dynamical plans produce endpoint-sharing Wasserstein geodesics; different intermediate marginals certify that the geodesic family is nonunique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distinct optimal dynamical plans with different time marginals yield distinct Wasserstein geodesics between the same endpoints.

notation.meaning: Evaluation at time t on the geodesic path space

children.title: Optimal-Coupling Multiplicity
children.top_down_role: Geodesic multiplicity induced by multiple optimal endpoint couplings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimal-coupling multiplicity means that the optimal transport set contains at least two distinct couplings.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicity of static optimal plans for fixed endpoint measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\Pi_p^{\mathrm{opt}}(\mu_0,\mu_1)=\left\{\pi\in\Pi(\mu_0,\mu_1):\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)^p\,d\pi(x,y)=W_p(\mu_0,\mu_1)^p\right\}\). The endpoint pair \((\mu_0,\mu_1)\) has optimal-coupling multiplicity when \(\Pi_p^{\mathrm{opt}}(\mu_0,\mu_1)\) is not a singleton. Distinct elements need not generate distinct marginal curves if the base space has multiple geodesics or different dynamical lifts collapse to identical time marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimal-coupling multiplicity occurs when a fixed pair of endpoint measures has more than one transport plan minimizing the p-th power distance cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Coupling Multiplicity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is an appropriate definition of optimal-coupling multiplicity, with consistent notation and qualifications, but it lacks a specific authoritative citation.

children.title: Unique-to-Branching Boundary
children.top_down_role: Source, target, or ambient conditions separating unique geodesics from branching behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique-to-Branching Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient uniqueness criterion and the mechanisms by which it can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\Pi_p^{\mathrm{opt}}(\mu_0,\mu_1)=\{\pi\}\) and that for \(\pi\)-almost every \((x,y)\) there is a unique constant-speed geodesic \(\gamma^{x,y}\) joining \(x\) to \(y\). Then the unique Wasserstein geodesic is \(\mu_t=((x,y)\mapsto\gamma_t^{x,y})_\#\pi\). The uniqueness argument can fail through either multiple optimal couplings or multiple geodesic lifts on a set of positive \(\pi\)-measure; either failure permits nonuniqueness but alone need not force distinct time marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unique optimal coupling supported on endpoint pairs with unique base geodesics yields a unique Wasserstein geodesic; coupling or lift multiplicity marks the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniqueness of both the optimal coupling and its geodesic lift guarantees uniqueness of the Wasserstein geodesic; failure opens, but does not ensure, branching.

The Kantorovich–Rubinstein representation is \[W_1(\mu,
u)=\sup_{f\in\operatorname{Lip}_1(X)}\left\{\int_X f\,d\mu-\int_X f\,d
uight\}.\] Because \(\mu\) and \(
u\) have finite first moments, every normalized \(1\)-Lipschitz function is integrable against both measures. Adding a constant to \(f\) leaves the displayed difference unchanged, so the supremum may equivalently be restricted by fixing \(f(x_0)=0\) at any chosen \(x_0\in X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L_{x_0}=\{f:X\to\mathbb R:|f(x)-f(y)|\leq d(x,y)\text{ for all }x,y,\ f(x_0)=0\}\). Then there exists \(f^\ast\in\mathcal L_{x_0}\) such that \[W_1(\mu,\nu)=\int_X f^\ast\,d\mu-\int_X f^\ast\,d\nu.\] Thus the normalized dual supremum is a maximum. The finite-first-moment assumption supplies integrable domination through \(|f(x)|\leq d(x,x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Polish space, finite first moments ensure that the normalized W1 dual supremum is achieved by a 1-Lipschitz potential.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Potential Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Base-point normalization removes the additive-constant ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any real-valued \(1\)-Lipschitz function \(f\), set \(\widetilde f(x)=f(x)-f(x_0)\). Then \(\widetilde f\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz, \(\widetilde f(x_0)=0\), and \[\int_X\widetilde f\,d\mu-\int_X\widetilde f\,d\nu=\int_X f\,d\mu-\int_X f\,d\nu.\] Moreover, \(|\widetilde f(x)|\leq d(x,x_0)\). Hence normalization preserves the Kantorovich–Rubinstein objective while providing a common pointwise growth bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting a potential's value at a fixed base point preserves its Lipschitz constant and dual objective while imposing a useful linear growth bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every dual potential has a unique constant shift vanishing at the base point, without changing its objective value.

notation.meaning: Normalized version of a potential f

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite dual attainment when first-moment integrability is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R>0\), the function \(f_R(x)=-\min\{|x|,R\}\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz and satisfies \(f_R(0)=0\). Its dual value is \[\int_{\mathbb R} f_R\,d\mu-\int_{\mathbb R} f_R\,d\nu=\int_{\mathbb R}\min\{|x|,R\}\,d\nu(x),\] which tends to \(+\infty\) as \(R\to\infty\). Therefore the normalized dual problem has no finite-valued maximizer, and the usual real-valued attainment theorem cannot extend beyond the finite-first-moment regime without modifying its formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a probability measure has infinite first moment, normalized Lipschitz dual values can diverge, so the usual finite W1 maximizer does not exist.
assumptions_latex: \(\nu\) is a probability measure on \(\mathbb R\) satisfying \(\int_{\mathbb R}|x|\,d\nu(x)=+\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outside \(\mathcal P_1(X)\), the finite-valued normalized dual-attainment statement can fail because its supremum may be infinite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and Kantorovich–Beckmann equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The measures μ and ν and the Kantorovich problem (KP) are those fixed in the surrounding setup. The divergence constraint is weak and includes homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is a compact convex domain. Then the Beckmann problem
\[
\min\left\{|\mathbf w|(\Omega):\mathbf w\in\mathcal M^d_{\mathrm{div}}(\Omega),\ \nabla\cdot\mathbf w=\mu-\nu\right\},
\]
where
\[
-\int_\Omega\nabla\phi\cdot d\mathbf w=\int_\Omega\phi\,d(\mu-\nu)\qquad\forall\phi\in C^1(\overline\Omega),
\]
admits a solution. Its minimum equals the minimum of the corresponding Kantorovich problem, and a Beckmann minimizer can be constructed from a Kantorovich minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact convex domain, the weak-divergence Beckmann flux problem admits a minimizer. Its optimal value equals that of the corresponding Kantorovich problem, and a Beckmann minimizer can be constructed from a Kantorovich minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\text{ is a compact convex domain}
\mu,\nu\text{ and (KP) are the data fixed in the surrounding setup}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}(\mathrm{BP})\neq\varnothing,\qquad \min(\mathrm{BP})=\min(\mathrm{KP}),\qquad \text{a BP minimizer can be constructed from a KP minimizer}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every bounded Borel function \(g\) and every compactly supported continuous vector field \(\Phi\), define \[\int g\,d\sigma=\int_{\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d}\int_0^1 g((1-t)x+ty)\,|y-x|\,dt\,d\pi(x,y),\] \[\int\Phi\cdot dv=\int_{\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d}\int_0^1\Phi((1-t)x+ty)\cdot(y-x)\,dt\,d\pi(x,y).\] Then \(\operatorname{div}v=\mu-\nu\), \(|v|\leq\sigma\), and \(\sigma(\mathbb R^d)=W_1(\mu,\nu)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dacorogna–Moser realization of a divergence-constrained flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a deterministic transport plan realizing a sufficiently regular divergence-constrained vector field without directional cancellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mathbf w:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d\) is Lipschitz, \(\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf n=0\) on \(\partial\Omega\), and \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf w=f_0-f_1\), where \(f_0,f_1\) are Lipschitz probability densities bounded below by positive constants. Define \(f_t=(1-t)f_0+tf_1\) and \(\mathbf v_t=\mathbf w/f_t\), and solve \(y_x'(t)=\mathbf v_t(y_x(t))\), \(y_x(0)=x\). Let \(Y(x)=y_x(\cdot)\) and \(Q=Y_\#(f_0\,dx)\). Then \((e_t)_\#Q=f_t\,dx\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\). Consequently, \(x\mapsto y_x(1)\) transports \(f_0\,dx\) to \(f_1\,dx\), and \(\mathbf w_Q=\mathbf w\,dx\) and \(i_Q=|\mathbf w|\,dx=|\mathbf w_Q|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interpolate linearly between the two strictly positive densities and divide the prescribed vector field by that interpolation. The resulting nonautonomous flow transports the first density to the second. Its path measure realizes the original flow exactly, and its traffic intensity equals the flow magnitude, so no directional cancellation occurs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (e_t)_\#Q=f_t\,dx,\qquad (y_{(\cdot)}(1))_\#(f_0\,dx)=f_1\,dx,\qquad \mathbf w_Q=\mathbf w\,dx,\qquad i_Q=|\mathbf w|\,dx=|\mathbf w_Q|.

children.title: Density–Flux Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between transport densities and minimizing fluxes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The compatible transport density is \(\sigma=|w|\), with polar direction of unit norm \(\sigma\)-almost everywhere.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: polar decomposition of vector measures underlying Beckmann transport density
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility in the exact transport-density representation, rather than the relaxed domination condition \(|w|\leq\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The density-flux pair \((\sigma,w)\) is compatible when \(w\ll\sigma\) and its Radon--Nikodym field \(v=dw/d\sigma\) satisfies \(|v(x)|=1\) for \(\sigma\)-almost every \(x\). Equivalently, the polar decomposition is
\[
w=v\sigma,
\qquad |v|=1\ \sigma\text{-almost everywhere},
\qquad \sigma=|w|.
\]
Consequently, the Beckmann cost obeys \(|w|(\Omega)=\sigma(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transport density and flux are compatible when the density is exactly the flux's total variation and the flux has a unit polar direction almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Density–Flux Compatibility

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[
W_{1,G}(a,b)=\min_{\pi\in\Pi(a,b)}\sum_{u,v\in V}d_G(u,v)\pi_{uv},
\]
where \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum total edge length among paths joining \(u\) to \(v\), and \(\Pi(a,b)\) consists of nonnegative arrays satisfying \(\sum_v\pi_{uv}=a_u\) and \(\sum_u\pi_{uv}=b_v\).

Let \mathcal X=\llbracket 1,n\rrbracket be the vertex set of a graph with oriented edge index set \mathcal E. For \mathbf f\in\mathbb R^n, the discrete gradient \nabla:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{\mathcal E} is defined by
\[

\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential and Minimum-Cost-Flow Formulations of Graph One-Wasserstein Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent edge-Lipschitz potential and nonnegative-flow formulations on a finite connected weighted graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \mathbf a,\mathbf b\in\mathbb R_+^n have equal total mass, and let \mathcal E be the oriented-arc representation of a finite connected undirected graph with nonnegative edge lengths \mathbf w_{i,j}. With the shortest-path ground metric,
\[
\mathrm W_1(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\max_{\mathbf f\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf f_i(\mathbf a_i-\mathbf b_i):\ |(\nabla\mathbf f)_{i,j}|\leq \mathbf w_{i,j}\ \forall(i,j)\in\mathcal E\right\},
\]
and
\[
\mathrm W_1(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\min_{\mathbf s\in\mathbb R_+^{\mathcal E}}\left\{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal E}\mathbf w_{i,j}\mathbf s_{i,j}:\ \operatorname{div}(\mathbf s)=\mathbf a-\mathbf b\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For equal-mass vertex measures on a connected weighted graph, the one-Wasserstein distance equals both the maximum pairing with an edge-Lipschitz vertex potential and the minimum cost of a nonnegative edge flow having the prescribed divergence.
assumptions_latex: \text{the weighted undirected graph is finite and connected}
\mathcal E\text{ uses oriented arcs and is closed under reversal}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Displacement interpolations are Wasserstein geodesics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamical representation, existence, and compactness of geodesics in $P_p(\mathcal X)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\mathcal X,d)$ be a complete, separable, locally compact length space and let $p>1$. Given $\mu_0,\mu_1\in P_p(\mathcal X)$ and a continuous curve $(\mu_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ valued in $P(\mathcal X)$, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_t=\operatorname{law}(\gamma_t)$ for a random minimizing constant-speed geodesic $\gamma$ such that $(\gamma_0,\gamma_1)$ is an optimal coupling; (ii) $(\mu_t)$ is a geodesic in $(P_p(\mathcal X),W_p)$. At least one such curve exists for every endpoint pair. If $\mathcal K_0,\mathcal K_1\subset P_p(\mathcal X)$ are compact subsets of $P(\mathcal X)$, then the families of such geodesic curves and of dynamical optimal plans with endpoint marginals in $\mathcal K_0$ and $\mathcal K_1$ are compact and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous curve of probability measures is a Wasserstein geodesic exactly when its marginals arise from optimally coupled random constant-speed minimizing geodesics in the base space. Such curves exist, and compact endpoint families produce nonempty compact families of geodesics and dynamical plans.
assumptions_latex: $(\mathcal X,d)$ is complete, separable, locally compact, and a length space.
$(\mu_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ is continuous and valued in $P(\mathcal X)$.
For compactness, $\mathcal K_0,\mathcal K_1\subset P_p(\mathcal X)$ are compact subsets of $P(\mathcal X)$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mu_t)\text{ has the dynamical optimal-geodesic representation}\iff(\mu_t)\text{ is a }W_p\text{-geodesic};\quad\text{the stated existence, compactness, and nonemptiness hold.}
