knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique optimal subplans along a constant-speed Wasserstein geodesic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior-time uniqueness, transport induction, and endpoint-plan factorization along a constant-speed geodesic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a separable Hilbert space, let \(p>1\), and let \((\mu_t)_{t\in[0,1]}\) be a constant-speed geodesic in \(\mathcal P_p(X)\). For every \(t\in(0,1)\), \(\Gamma_o(\mu_t,\mu_1)\) and \(\Gamma_o(\mu_0,\mu_t)\) contain unique plans \(\boldsymbol\mu^{t1}\) and \(\boldsymbol\mu^{0t}\), respectively, and each is induced by a transport. Moreover,
\[
\boldsymbol\mu:=\boldsymbol\mu^{t1}\circ\boldsymbol\mu^{0t}\in\Gamma_o(\mu_0,\mu_1),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\mu^{0t}=(\pi_t^{1,1\to2})_\#\boldsymbol\mu,
\quad
\boldsymbol\mu^{t1}=(\pi_t^{1\to2,2})_\#\boldsymbol\mu.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every interior time of a constant-speed Wasserstein geodesic, the optimal plans for its two adjacent subsegments are unique and transport-induced. Their composition is an optimal endpoint plan, and the subplans are recovered by the stated interpolation pushforwards.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a separable Hilbert space}
(\mu_t)_{t\in[0,1]}\text{ is a constant-speed geodesic in }\mathcal P_p(X)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma_o(\mu_0,\mu_t)=\{\boldsymbol\mu^{0t}\},\quad \Gamma_o(\mu_t,\mu_1)=\{\boldsymbol\mu^{t1}\},\quad \boldsymbol\mu^{0t},\boldsymbol\mu^{t1}\text{ are transport-induced},\quad \boldsymbol\mu^{t1}\circ\boldsymbol\mu^{0t}\in\Gamma_o(\mu_0,\mu_1)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Every p-Wasserstein geodesic is plan induced for p greater than one
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse representation of constant-speed geodesics by optimal displacement interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\mu_t)_{t\in[0,1]}\) be a constant-speed geodesic in \(\mathbb W_p(\Omega)\) from \(\mu\) to \(\nu\), with \(p>1\). Then there exists a plan \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\), optimal for \(c(x,y)=|x-y|^p\), such that
\[
\mu_t=(\pi_t)_\#\gamma\qquad\text{for every }t\in[0,1],
\]
where \(\pi_t(x,y)=(1-t)x+ty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When p is greater than one, every constant-speed p-Wasserstein geodesic is generated by displacement interpolation along an optimal endpoint transport plan.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Velocity representation of a plan-induced Wasserstein geodesic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity-equation and metric-speed representation in the inherited strictly convex displacement setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p>1\), let \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) be optimal for \(c(x,z)=|x-z|^p\), and set \(\mu_t=(\pi_t)_\#\gamma\), where \(\pi_t(x,z)=(1-t)x+tz\). Let \(X_t,Z_t\) be the endpoint-recovery maps. For every \(t\in(0,1)\), the field \(\mathbf v_t=Z_t-X_t\) is well defined on \(\operatorname{spt}(\mu_t)\) and satisfies
\[
\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\!\cdot(\mu_t\mathbf v_t)=0,
\qquad
\|\mathbf v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}=|\mu'|(t)=W_p(\mu,\nu).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a displacement geodesic generated by an optimal p-power transport plan with p greater than one, subtracting the recovered initial point from the recovered final point gives a velocity field satisfying the continuity equation. Its L-p norm equals both the metric speed and the endpoint Wasserstein distance.
assumptions_latex: X_t,Z_t\text{ are the well-defined endpoint-recovery maps}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf v_t=Z_t-X_t,\qquad \partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\cdot(\mu_t\mathbf v_t)=0,\qquad \|\mathbf v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}=|\mu'|(t)=W_p(\mu,\nu)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal-plan characterization of constant-speed Wasserstein geodesics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between constant-speed Wasserstein geodesics and displacement interpolations generated by optimal endpoint plans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a separable Hilbert space, let \(p>1\), and let \(\mu^1,\mu^2\in\mathcal P_p(X)\). If \(\boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma_o(\mu^1,\mu^2)\), then the curve \(\mu_t:=\boldsymbol\mu_t^{1\to2}\), \(t\in[0,1]\), is a constant-speed geodesic joining \(\mu^1\) to \(\mu^2\). Conversely, every constant-speed geodesic joining these measures has this representation for some \(\boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma_o(\mu^1,\mu^2)\), and such an endpoint plan can be constructed through any interior measure \(\mu_t\), \(0<t<1\), using the preceding subplan factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every optimal endpoint transport plan generates a constant-speed displacement geodesic, and every constant-speed Wasserstein geodesic arises from such an optimal plan. The endpoint plan can be constructed through any interior point using the optimal subplans.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a separable Hilbert space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma_o(\mu^1,\mu^2)\Rightarrow (\boldsymbol\mu_t^{1\to2})_{t\in[0,1]}\text{ is a constant-speed geodesic},\quad\text{and every such geodesic has this representation for some }\boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma_o(\mu^1,\mu^2)

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Geodesics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized quadratic-Wasserstein geodesics with a prescribed common base measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p^i:(\mathbb R^d)^3\to\mathbb R^d\) denote the \(i\)-th coordinate projection and let \(p^{i,j}=(p^i,p^j)\). A generalized geodesic from \(\mu_0\) to \(\mu_1\) with base \(\nu\) is a curve
\[
\mu_t=((1-t)p^1+tp^2)_\#\boldsymbol\alpha,
\qquad t\in[0,1],
\]
where
\[
(p^{0,1})_\#\boldsymbol\alpha\in\Pi_{\mathrm{opt}}(\nu,\mu_0)
\quad\text{and}\quad
(p^{0,2})_\#\boldsymbol\alpha\in\Pi_{\mathrm{opt}}(\nu,\mu_1).
\]
The induced coupling of the two endpoint coordinates need not be optimal between \(\mu_0\) and \(\mu_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized geodesic jointly couples optimal transports from one base measure to both endpoints and then interpolates the two endpoint coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(\boldsymbol\alpha\in\mathcal P((\mathbb R^d)^3)\) has the stated optimal base-endpoint marginals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_t=((1-t)p^1+tp^2)_\#\boldsymbol\alpha\) is a generalized geodesic from \(\mu_0\) to \(\mu_1\) with base \(\nu\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard generalized geodesic with a common Wasserstein base

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized Geodesic with a Base Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a Wasserstein generalized geodesic induced by a triple coupling with optimal base-to-endpoint marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu^1,\mu^2,\mu^3\in\mathcal P_2(X)\). A generalized geodesic joining \(\mu^2\) to \(\mu^3\) with base \(\mu^1\) is a curve
\[
\mu_t^{2\to3}=(\pi_t^{2\to3})_\#\boldsymbol\mu,\qquad t\in[0,1],
\]
where \(\pi_t^{2\to3}(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(1-t)x_2+tx_3\), \(\boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma(\mu^1,\mu^2,\mu^3)\), \(\pi^{1,2}_\#\boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma_o(\mu^1,\mu^2)\), and \(\pi^{1,3}_\#\boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma_o(\mu^1,\mu^3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized geodesic between two measures, based at a third measure, is obtained by interpolating the endpoint coordinates of a triple coupling whose two base-to-endpoint marginals are optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_t^{2\to3}=(\pi_t^{2\to3})_\#\boldsymbol\mu,\quad t\in[0,1],\text{ is a generalized geodesic from }\mu^2\text{ to }\mu^3\text{ with base }\mu^1.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a generalized geodesic by interpolating quadratic-cost optimal transport maps from a common absolutely continuous base measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an absolutely continuous probability measure \(\rho\in\mathcal P(\Omega)\). Every source atom is at squared distance \(2\) from every target atom, so both bijective matchings define optimal plans. Their interpolations at \(t=\tfrac12\) are respectively
\[
\tfrac12\delta_{(-1/2,-1/2)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(1/2,1/2)}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\tfrac12\delta_{(-1/2,1/2)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(1/2,-1/2)}.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mollified approximation of continuity-equation curves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spatial regularization of time-continuous probability-measure solutions having finite p-integrable velocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let p\geq 1 and let (\mu_t)_{t\in[0,T]} be a time-continuous solution of \partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\!\cdot(v_t\mu_t)=0 such that \int_0^T\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}|v_t(x)|^p\,d\mu_t(x)\,dt<\infty. For strictly positive smooth spatial mollifiers \rho_\varepsilon, define \mu_t^\varepsilon=\mu_t*\rho_\varepsilon, E_t^\varepsilon=(v_t\mu_t)*\rho_\varepsilon, and v_t^\varepsilon=E_t^\varepsilon/\mu_t^\varepsilon. Then \mu_t^\varepsilon is a continuous solution of the continuity equation with velocity v_t^\varepsilon, the fields v_t^\varepsilon satisfy the local regularity assumptions (8.1.8), and \int_{\mathbb R^d}|v_t^\varepsilon|^p\,d\mu_t^\varepsilon\leq\int_{\mathbb R^d}|v_t|^p\,d\mu_t for every t\in(0,T). Moreover, as \varepsilon\downarrow0, E_t^\varepsilon\rightharpoonup v_t\mu_t narrowly and \|v_t^\varepsilon\|_{L^p(\mu_t^\varepsilon;\mathbb R^d)}\to\|v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t;\mathbb R^d)} for every t\in(0,T).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convolving a continuity-equation solution and its momentum produces a regular solution without increasing its pointwise p-energy. As the smoothing vanishes, the momentum converges narrowly and the velocity norms converge to their original values.
assumptions_latex: \rho_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\text{ is a strictly positive spatial mollifier}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mu_t^\varepsilon,v_t^\varepsilon)\text{ solves the continuity equation},\quad \int|v_t^\varepsilon|^p\,d\mu_t^\varepsilon\leq\int|v_t|^p\,d\mu_t,\quad E_t^\varepsilon\rightharpoonup v_t\mu_t,\quad \|v_t^\varepsilon\|_{L^p(\mu_t^\varepsilon)}\to\|v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent Vector of an Absolutely Continuous Wasserstein Curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves the proposition's characterization using conditions (8.3.6) and (8.3.7), whose definitions are not included in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu_t:I\to\mathcal P_p(X)\) be absolutely continuous and let \(v_t\in L^p(\mu_t;X)\) satisfy condition \((8.3.7)\). Then \(v_t\) also satisfies condition \((8.3.6)\) if and only if
\[
v_t=\Pi(v_t)\in\operatorname{Tan}_{\mu_t}\mathcal P_p(X)
\quad\text{for }\mathcal L^1\text{-a.e. }t\in I.
\]
Conditions \((8.3.6)\) and \((8.3.7)\) determine \(v_t\) uniquely for \(\mathcal L^1\)-almost every \(t\in I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an absolutely continuous Wasserstein curve, a field satisfying condition (8.3.7) also satisfies condition (8.3.6) exactly when it equals its tangent projection almost everywhere. Together the two conditions determine the field uniquely almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v_t\text{ satisfies }(8.3.6)\iff v_t=\Pi(v_t)\in\operatorname{Tan}_{\mu_t}\mathcal P_p(X)\quad\mathcal L^1\text{-a.e.; conditions }(8.3.6)\text{ and }(8.3.7)\text{ determine }v_t\text{ uniquely a.e.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-Everywhere Differentiability of Wasserstein Distance Along Curves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiates the pth power of the distance from an absolutely continuous Wasserstein curve to a fixed measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu_t:I\to\mathcal P_p(X)\) be absolutely continuous, let \(\sigma\in\mathcal P_p(X)\), and let \(v_t\in\operatorname{Tan}_{\mu_t}\mathcal P_p(X)\) be its tangent vector field characterized by Proposition 8.4.5. Then, for \(\mathcal L^1\)-a.e. \(t\in I\),
\[
\frac{d}{dt}W_p^p(\mu_t,\sigma)
=\int_{X^2}p|x_1-x_2|^{p-2}\langle x_1-x_2,v_t(x_1)\rangle\,d\gamma(x_1,x_2)
\]
for every \(\gamma\in\Gamma_o(\mu_t,\sigma)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For almost every time, the pth power of the Wasserstein distance from the curve to a fixed measure is differentiable, and the displayed formula holds for every optimal coupling.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Chain rule along absolutely continuous Wasserstein curves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-subdifferential chain rule at qualifying times, with absolute continuity and an almost-everywhere conclusion under additional convexity and integrability assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:\mathcal P_2(X)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be regular and satisfy \((10.1.1a,b)\), and let \(t\mapsto\mu_t\in D(\phi)\) be absolutely continuous with tangent velocity \(\mathbf v_t\). Define \(\Lambda\subset(a,b)\) as the set of times \(t\) such that \(|\partial\phi|(\mu_t)<+\infty\), \(\phi\circ\mu\) is approximately differentiable at \(t\), and condition \((8.4.6)\) holds. Then, for every \(t\in\Lambda\) and every \(\boldsymbol\xi_t\in\partial\phi(\mu_t)\), \[\frac{\widetilde d}{dt}\phi(\mu_t)=\int_X\langle\boldsymbol\xi_t(x),\mathbf v_t(x)\rangle\,d\mu_t(x).\] Moreover, if \(\phi\) is \(\lambda\)-convex and \(\int_a^b|\partial\phi|(\mu_t)|\mu'|(t)\,dt<+\infty\), then \(t\mapsto\phi(\mu_t)\) is absolutely continuous and \((a,b)\setminus\Lambda\) is \(\mathcal L^1\)-negligible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each qualifying time, the approximate derivative of the energy along an absolutely continuous Wasserstein curve equals the pairing of any strong subgradient with the tangent velocity. Under lambda-convexity and slope-speed integrability, the energy is absolutely continuous and the nonqualifying times form a null set.

t\in\Lambda\Longrightarrow |\partial\phi|(\mu_t)<+\infty,\ \phi\circ\mu\text{ is approximately differentiable at }t,\text{ and }(8.4.6)\text{ holds}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Superposition representation with a pathwise p-action bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Optimal-Transport Representation Along Wasserstein Curves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives optimal-plan, pushforward, and regular-source optimal-map representations of the tangent velocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu_t:I\to\mathcal P_p(X)\) be absolutely continuous and let \(v_t\in\operatorname{Tan}_{\mu_t}\mathcal P_p(X)\) be the tangent vector characterized by Proposition 8.4.5. For \(\mathcal L^1\)-a.e. \(t\in I\), every selection \(\boldsymbol\mu_h\in\Gamma_o(\mu_t,\mu_{t+h})\) satisfies, as \(h\to0\),
\[
\left(\pi^1,\frac{\pi^2-\pi^1}{h}\right)_{\#}\boldsymbol\mu_h
\longrightarrow(\mathbf i\times v_t)_{\#}\mu_t
\quad\text{in }\mathcal P_p(X\times X),
\]
and
\[
\frac{W_p\!\left(\mu_{t+h},(\mathbf i+h v_t)_{\#}\mu_t\right)}{|h|}\longrightarrow0.
\]
In particular, for almost every such \(t\) with \(\mu_t\in\mathcal P_p^r(X)\), the unique optimal transport map satisfies
\[
\frac{\mathbf t_{\mu_t}^{\mu_{t+h}}-\mathbf i}{h}\longrightarrow v_t
\quad\text{in }L^p(\mu_t;X).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At almost every time, every selection of nearby optimal plans recovers the tangent velocity after rescaling, and identity plus h times the velocity gives a first-order pushforward approximation. When the source measure is in the stated regular class, the rescaled unique optimal maps converge to the velocity in Lp.
assumptions_latex: v_t\in\operatorname{Tan}_{\mu_t}\mathcal P_p(X)\text{ is characterized by Proposition 8.4.5}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\pi^1,h^{-1}(\pi^2-\pi^1)\right)_{\#}\boldsymbol\mu_h\to(\mathbf i\times v_t)_{\#}\mu_t,\quad W_p\!\left(\mu_{t+h},(\mathbf i+h v_t)_{\#}\mu_t\right)=o(|h|);\quad \mu_t\in\mathcal P_p^r(X)\Rightarrow h^{-1}(\mathbf t_{\mu_t}^{\mu_{t+h}}-\mathbf i)\to v_t

children.title: Metric Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Infinitesimal metric variation along absolutely continuous Wasserstein curves.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General metric definition and almost-everywhere characterization for absolutely continuous curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At any \(t\in(a,b)\) for which the limit exists, the metric derivative of \(\mu\) is
\[
|\dot\mu_t|=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{d(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)}{|h|}.
\]
For every absolutely continuous metric-space curve, this limit exists for almost every \(t\). Moreover, \(|\dot\mu|\in L^1(a,b)\), and it is minimal almost everywhere among all \(g\in L^1(a,b)\) satisfying
\[
d(\mu_s,\mu_t)\leq\int_s^t g(r)\,dr
\quad\text{for every }a<s<t<b.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric derivative is the almost-everywhere limit of distance traveled divided by elapsed time and is the least integrable upper speed of an absolutely continuous curve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\dot\mu_t|\) exists for almost every \(t\) and is minimal almost everywhere among integrable upper speeds.

Thus every admissible velocity field supplies an upper bound on the metric speed.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Speed Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical minimal tangent-velocity theorem for absolutely continuous curves in Euclidean quadratic-Wasserstein space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists a Borel velocity field \(v^{\min}\) satisfying
\[
\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\cdot(v_t^{\min}\mu_t)=0
\]
distributionally, with \(v_t^{\min}\in\operatorname{Tan}_{\mu_t}\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\) for almost every \(t\), such that
\[
\|v_t^{\min}\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}=|\dot\mu_t|
\quad\text{for almost every }t.
\]
For every other admissible Borel velocity field \(v\) solving the same continuity equation,
\[
|\dot\mu_t|\leq\|v_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}
\quad\text{for almost every }t.
\]
The tangent velocity \(v_t^{\min}\) is unique in \(L^2(\mu_t;\mathbb R^d)\) for almost every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolutely continuous quadratic-Wasserstein curve has an almost-everywhere unique tangent velocity whose quadratic norm equals the metric derivative, while every other admissible velocity has at least that norm.
assumptions_latex: \((\mu_t)_{t\in(a,b)}\) is absolutely continuous in \((\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d),W_2)\).
Admissible velocities are Borel spacetime fields with integrable \(L^2(\mu_t)\)-norm that solve the continuity equation distributionally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is an almost-everywhere unique tangent velocity \(v_t^{\min}\) with \(\|v_t^{\min}\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}=|\dot\mu_t|\), and every admissible velocity has no smaller norm almost everywhere.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity-Equation Characterization of Absolutely Continuous Wasserstein Curves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-way correspondence between absolutely continuous Wasserstein curves and time-integrable Eulerian velocity fields, with both metric-speed inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $p>1$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact. If $(\mu_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ is absolutely continuous in $\mathbb W_p(\Omega)$, then for almost every $t$ there exists $\mathbf v_t\in L^p(\mu_t;\mathbb R^d)$ such that
\[
\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\cdot(\mathbf v_t\mu_t)=0
\]
in the weak sense and
\[
\|\mathbf v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}\le |\mu'|(t)
\quad\text{for a.e. }t.
\]
Conversely, suppose $\mu_t\in\mathcal P_p(\Omega)$ and $\mathbf v_t\in L^p(\mu_t;\mathbb R^d)$ solve the weak continuity equation and satisfy
\[
\int_0^1\|\mathbf v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}\,dt<\infty.
\]
Then $(\mu_t)_t$ is absolutely continuous in $\mathbb W_p(\Omega)$ and
\[
|\mu'|(t)\le\|\mathbf v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}
\quad\text{for a.e. }t.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For p greater than one on a compact Euclidean domain, an absolutely continuous Wasserstein curve admits a weak continuity-equation velocity field whose Lp norm does not exceed its metric speed. Conversely, a weak continuity-equation solution with time-integrable Lp velocity norm is an absolutely continuous Wasserstein curve, with metric speed bounded by that norm almost everywhere.
assumptions_latex: Forward direction: $(\mu_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ is absolutely continuous in $\mathbb W_p(\Omega)$.
Converse direction: $\mu_t\in\mathcal P_p(\Omega)$, $\mathbf v_t\in L^p(\mu_t;\mathbb R^d)$, the continuity equation holds weakly, and $\int_0^1\|\mathbf v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}dt<\infty$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&(\mu_t)_t\in\operatorname{AC}(\mathbb W_p(\Omega))\Rightarrow\exists(\mathbf v_t)_t:\ \partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\cdot(\mathbf v_t\mu_t)=0,\ \|\mathbf v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}\le|\mu'|(t)\ \text{a.e.};\\&\left[\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\cdot(\mathbf v_t\mu_t)=0,\ \int_0^1\|\mathbf v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}dt<\infty\right]\Rightarrow(\mu_t)_t\in\operatorname{AC}(\mathbb W_p(\Omega)),\ |\mu'|(t)\le\|\mathbf v_t\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}\ \text{a.e.}\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Wasserstein Barycenters and Their Coupling LP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational definition and joint-coupling formulation for barycenters of finitely many weighted histograms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b_s\in\Delta_{n_s}\), \(\lambda\in\Delta_S\), and \(C_s\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n_s}\). A finite Wasserstein barycenter is a minimizer of
\[
\min_{a\in\Delta_n}\sum_{s=1}^S\lambda_s L_{C_s}(a,b_s).
\]
Equivalently, this problem is the linear program
\[
\min_{\substack{a\in\Delta_n,\;P_s\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n\times n_s}}}
\left\{\sum_{s=1}^S\lambda_s\langle P_s,C_s\rangle:\;P_s\mathbf 1_{n_s}=a,\;P_s^\top\mathbf 1_n=b_s\ \text{for every }s\right\}.
\]
When \(n_s=n\) and \(C_s=D^p\) for every \(s\), the variational objective becomes \(\sum_s\lambda_sW_p^p(a,b_s)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A barycenter of finitely many weighted histograms minimizes their weighted optimal-transport costs. Introducing a nonnegative coupling between the barycenter and each input yields an equivalent linear program in which all couplings share the barycenter marginal. On a common grid with a p-power distance cost, the objective is the weighted sum of pth-power Wasserstein distances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{a\in\Delta_n}\sum_{s=1}^S\lambda_sL_{C_s}(a,b_s)=\min_{\substack{a\in\Delta_n,\;P_s\ge 0\\P_s\mathbf1_{n_s}=a,\;P_s^\top\mathbf1_n=b_s\ \forall s}}\sum_{s=1}^S\lambda_s\langle P_s,C_s\rangle.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic Benamou-Brenier action in density-momentum and measure formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the quadratic perspective integrand by \[\Phi(r,w)=\begin{cases}|w|^2/r,&r>0,\\0,&(r,w)=(0,0),\\+\infty,&r=0\text{ and }w\ne0.\end{cases}\] For densities relative to a reference measure, the dynamic action is \(\mathcal A(\rho,m)=\int\Phi(\rho,m)\). Intrinsically for measures, \(\mathcal A(\rho,m)=\int|v|^2\,d\rho\) when \(m=v\rho\) for some \(v\in L^2(\rho;\mathbb R^d)\), and \(\mathcal A(\rho,m)=+\infty\) otherwise. Minimizing this action subject to the continuity equation and endpoint constraints gives the squared quadratic dynamic transport cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrangian Action on a Polish Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an axiomatic path-space action, its endpoint costs, its partition representation, and endpoint-constrained minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (\mathcal X,d) be a Polish space and let t_i,t_f\in\mathbb R. A Lagrangian action consists of lower-semicontinuous functionals \mathcal A^{s,t} on C([s,t];\mathcal X), for t_i\le s<t\le t_f, and cost functions c^{s,t} on \mathcal X\times\mathcal X such that: (i) the action is additive across consecutive time intervals; (ii) c^{s,t}(x,y)=\inf\{\mathcal A^{s,t}(\gamma):\gamma\in C([s,t];\mathcal X),\ \gamma_s=x,\ \gamma_t=y\}; and (iii) for every \gamma\in C([t_i,t_f];\mathcal X), \mathcal A^{t_i,t_f}(\gamma)=\sup_{N\in\mathbb N}\sup_{t_i=t_0\le\cdots\le t_N=t_f}\sum_{j=1}^{N}c^{t_{j-1},t_j}(\gamma_{t_{j-1}},\gamma_{t_j}). A curve is action-minimizing if it minimizes \mathcal A^{t_i,t_f} among curves with the same endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lagrangian action is a lower-semicontinuous, time-additive family of path functionals. Its endpoint costs are obtained by minimizing over connecting curves, and its full action equals the supremum of accumulated costs over finite time partitions. An action-minimizing curve minimizes the action among curves with its endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mathcal A^{s,t},c^{s,t})\text{ is a Lagrangian action precisely when conditions (i)--(iii) hold.}

children.title: Endpoint Regimes
children.top_down_role: Fixed, relaxed, or partially prescribed temporal marginals in dynamic transport.

assumptions_latex: \((\rho,m)\) satisfies the distributional continuity equation on \([0,1]\times\Omega\).
The temporal traces \(\rho_{0}\) and \(\rho_{1}\) exist as finite measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The endpoint regime is imposed by \(\rho_0=\mu_0\) and \(\rho_1=\mu_1\), equivalently through the endpoint terms in the weak identity.
review_flags: No supplied locator supports endpoint traces for measure-valued continuity equations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard initial and terminal trace constraints in dynamic optimal transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The hard endpoint regime prescribes the temporal traces \(\rho_0=\mu_0\) and \(\rho_1=\mu_1\). In the spacetime weak formulation this means that, for every admissible \(\varphi\), the continuity equation contains the boundary contribution \(\int_\Omega\varphi(0,x)\,d\mu_0(x)-\int_\Omega\varphi(1,x)\,d\mu_1(x)\). If test functions are required to vanish at both temporal endpoints, the interior equation alone does not determine these traces; they must then be imposed separately. Free or penalized endpoints replace one or both trace equalities by optimization over the corresponding terminal measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hard endpoint constraints prescribe the initial and terminal mass measures; interior test functions alone do not encode those traces.
knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the endpoint-regimes leaf, but the assertions about temporal traces and hard, free, and penalized endpoint formulations require a specific continuity-equation or dynamic-transport source.

children.title: Spatial Boundary Regimes
children.top_down_role: Flux behavior at physical boundaries of the transport domain.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is a bounded Lipschitz domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The impermeable-boundary regime is \(m\cdot n=0\) on \((0,1)\times\partial\Omega\), understood through the boundary-free weak identity.

notation.meaning: Outward unit normal to the spatial boundary.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports spatial boundary regimes for dynamic transport.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Impermeable bounded-domain regime, contrasted with periodic and whole-space transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a bounded Lipschitz domain \(\Omega\), the impermeable spatial boundary regime requires the normal momentum trace \(m\cdot n=0\) on \((0,1)\times\partial\Omega\). Equivalently, integration by parts produces no lateral-boundary contribution, so the weak continuity identity remains valid for test functions in \(C^1([0,1]\times\overline\Omega)\). On the flat torus, periodicity cancels spatial boundary contributions. On \(\mathbb R^d\), compactly supported tests avoid a finite boundary, while suitable integrability or tightness controls flux at infinity. Allowing nonzero normal trace instead describes an open system with boundary inflow or outflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An impermeable bounded domain imposes zero normal momentum at its boundary; periodic and whole-space settings eliminate lateral boundary terms differently.
knowledge_statements.title: Spatial Boundary Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the spatial-boundary leaf, but the equivalence involving the normal trace of a measure-valued momentum and the claims for bounded, periodic, and whole-space regimes need an authoritative source.

children.title: Endpoint–Boundary Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Joint admissibility of temporal marginals and spatial flux restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) is connected and the lateral boundary is impermeable.
\((\rho,m)\) is a weak continuity-equation solution with finite endpoint measures \(\mu_0\) and \(\mu_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Necessarily \(\mu_0(\Omega)=\mu_1(\Omega)\); unequal endpoint masses are incompatible with zero boundary flux.

notation.meaning: Total mass of a measure on the domain.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports mass compatibility for the dynamic continuity equation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mass-balance compatibility between prescribed temporal endpoints and an impermeable spatial boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the spatial boundary is impermeable, then prescribed endpoints must have equal total mass: \(\mu_0(\Omega)=\mu_1(\Omega)\). Indeed, the weak continuity identity tested with the constant function \(\varphi(t,x)=1\) reduces exactly to this equality. More generally, if a normal boundary flux \(g\) is prescribed, compatibility becomes \[\mu_1(\Omega)-\mu_0(\Omega)=-\int_0^1\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,dS\,dt,\] with the sign determined by the outward-normal convention. Thus unequal endpoint masses require compensating lateral inflow or outflow and are infeasible under \(m\cdot n=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero boundary flux forces initial and final total masses to agree; any mass discrepancy must equal the signed cumulative boundary flux.
knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint–Boundary Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mass-balance condition fits the compatibility leaf, but the statement includes proof text and its boundary-flux formula and sign convention lack a supporting source with a precise locator.

children.title: Weak Flux Solutions
children.top_down_role: Distributional dynamic-transport solutions represented through weak fluxes.

assumptions_latex: \(\rho\) is a nonnegative finite measure and \(m\) an \(\mathbb R^d\)-valued finite measure on spacetime.
Finite endpoint measures \(\mu_0\) and \(\mu_1\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair is a weak flux solution exactly when the displayed distributional identity holds for every admissible test function.

notation.meaning: Mass and flux measures on spacetime.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports weak flux solutions of the continuity equation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spacetime distributional solution expressed directly through mass and vector flux measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A weak flux solution from \(\mu_0\) to \(\mu_1\) is a pair consisting of a nonnegative finite measure \(\rho\) and an \(\mathbb R^d\)-valued finite measure \(m\) on \([0,1]\times\overline\Omega\) such that, for every \(\varphi\in C^1([0,1]\times\overline\Omega)\), \[\int\partial_t\varphi\,d\rho+\int\nabla_x\varphi\cdot dm+\int_\Omega\varphi(0,\cdot)\,d\mu_0-\int_\Omega\varphi(1,\cdot)\,d\mu_1=0.\] The admissible test class determines the spatial boundary regime. Finite quadratic action additionally requires \(m=v\rho\) with \(v\in L^2(\rho;\mathbb R^d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak flux solution is a spacetime mass-flux pair satisfying the integrated continuity equation and endpoint terms against every admissible test function.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Flux Solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the weak-flux-solution leaf, but no source supports the formulation, and the admissible test class does not by itself specify which spatial boundary regime is intended.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence of Weak and Distributional Continuity-Equation Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of the spacetime distributional and timewise weak formulations in the integrable measure–velocity class, up to choosing an almost-everywhere-equal representative of the measure curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\rho_t,\mathbf v_t)$ belong to the measure--velocity class for which the weak and distributional continuity-equation formulations are defined. Every weak solution is a distributional solution. Conversely, every distributional solution admits a representative $\widetilde\rho_t=\rho_t$ for a.e. $t$ such that $t\mapsto\widetilde\rho_t$ is weakly continuous and $(\widetilde\rho_t,\mathbf v_t)$ is a weak solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every timewise weak solution is distributional. Conversely, a distributional solution can be modified on a null set of times to give a weakly continuous representative that is a timewise weak solution.
assumptions_latex: (\rho_t,\mathbf v_t)\text{ satisfies one of the two continuity-equation formulations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The weak and distributional solution notions are equivalent up to an a.e.-in-time representative of }\rho_t

children.title: Measure-Valued Solutions
children.top_down_role: Dynamic solutions permitting singular mass or momentum measures.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The curve is a measure-valued continuity-equation solution when the displayed distributional identity holds.

notation.meaning: Narrowly continuous curve of probability measures.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports measure-valued continuity-equation solutions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-disintegrated probability-measure solution with square-integrable velocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A measure-valued solution is a narrowly continuous curve \((\rho_t)_{t\in[0,1]}\subset\mathcal P_2(\Omega)\) together with a Borel velocity field \(v_t\in L^2(\rho_t;\mathbb R^d)\) satisfying \(\int_0^1\int_\Omega|v_t|^2\,d\rho_t\,dt<\infty\) and \[\int_0^1\int_\Omega\bigl(\partial_t\varphi(t,x)+\nabla_x\varphi(t,x)\cdot v_t(x)\bigr)\,d\rho_t(x)\,dt=0\] for every \(\varphi\in C_c^1((0,1)\times\Omega)\). Endpoint and spatial boundary conditions are imposed through traces and the corresponding enlarged test class. The associated momentum is \(m=dt\otimes(v_tho_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measure-valued solution is a continuous curve of probability measures transported by a square-integrable velocity field in the distributional sense.
knowledge_statements.title: Measure-Valued Solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the measure-valued-solutions leaf, but the precise curve, velocity, integrability, distributional, trace, and boundary requirements need an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Flux–Measure Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between weak flux descriptions and measure-valued solution objects.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu_t\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\) is narrowly continuous for \(t\in[0,1]\).
The nonnegative measure \(\lambda=dt\otimes\mu_t\) and vector measure \(m\) satisfy \(m\ll\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m=v\lambda\), and the flux and velocity formulations of the continuity equation coincide.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-action Eulerian solutions on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lambda=dt\otimes\mu_t\). Every vector measure \(m\ll\lambda\) has a unique density \(v\in L^1(\lambda;\mathbb R^d)\), modulo \(\lambda\)-null sets, such that \(m=v\lambda\). For every \(\zeta\in C_c^1((0,1)\times\mathbb R^d)\), the flux identity \[\int \partial_t\zeta\,d\lambda+\int \nabla\zeta\cdot dm=0\] is equivalent to \[\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^d}\bigl(\partial_t\zeta+\nabla\zeta\cdot v_t\bigr)\,d\mu_t\,dt=0.\] Moreover, the quadratic flux action equals \(\int |dm/d\lambda|^2\,d\lambda=\int_0^1\int |v_t|^2\,d\mu_t\,dt\) whenever either side is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolutely continuous space-time flux is uniquely a velocity times the mass measure, and both descriptions give the same weak continuity equation and kinetic action.
knowledge_statements.title: Flux–Measure Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the leaf, and the Radon–Nikodym correspondence, weak-equation equivalence, and action identity are mathematically coherent. No inspectable optimal-transport source or locator is supplied, so the claim cannot yet be accepted as candidate-review knowledge.

assumptions_latex: Admissible pairs \((\mu_t,v_t)\) solve the continuity equation distributionally, have endpoints \(\mu_0,\mu_1\), and have finite quadratic action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_2^2(\mu_0,\mu_1)=\inf\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^d}|v_t|^2\,d\mu_t\,dt\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic Benamou–Brenier formula on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu_0,\mu_1\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\), define \(\mathcal A(\mu,v)=\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^d}|v_t(x)|^2\,d\mu_t(x)\,dt\). Then \[W_2^2(\mu_0,\mu_1)=\inf\left\{\mathcal A(\mu,v):\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\cdot(v_t\mu_t)=0,\ \mu_{t=0}=\mu_0,\ \mu_{t=1}=\mu_1\right\}.\] The continuity equation is understood distributionally, and the infimum ranges over narrowly continuous curves with Borel velocities of finite action. Thus the static Kantorovich cost and the minimum Eulerian kinetic action have the same value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared quadratic Wasserstein distance equals the least kinetic action among continuity-equation paths joining the prescribed endpoint measures.
knowledge_statements.title: Static–Dynamic Equivalence

assumptions_latex: \(\pi\in\Pi(\mu_0,\mu_1)\) is optimal for the quadratic cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_t=((1-t)x+ty)_\#\pi\) is a constant-speed \(W_2\)-geodesic and minimizes the dynamic action.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Displacement interpolation induced by an optimal quadratic plan.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e_t(x,y)=(1-t)x+ty\) and \(\mu_t=(e_t)_\#\pi\). Then, for all \(0\le s<t\le1\), \[W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)=(t-s)W_2(\mu_0,\mu_1).\] Consequently, \((\mu_t)_{t\in[0,1]}\) is a constant-speed Wasserstein geodesic. It admits a velocity field \(v_t\in L^2(\mu_t;\mathbb R^d)\) satisfying the continuity equation and \(\|v_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}=W_2(\mu_0,\mu_1)\) for almost every \(t\). Hence its kinetic action is \(W_2^2(\mu_0,\mu_1)\), so it attains the Benamou–Brenier infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pushing an optimal plan along straight particle paths produces a constant-speed Wasserstein geodesic whose kinetic action equals the squared endpoint distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Speed Geodesic Representation

assumptions_latex: \(\rho\) is a nonnegative scalar measure and \(m\) is a vector measure on space-time.
A positive measure \(\sigma\) dominates both \(\rho\) and \(|m|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B(\rho,m)=\int f(d\rho/d\sigma,dm/d\sigma)\,d\sigma\) is domination-independent and jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-valued perspective formulation of quadratic kinetic energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the lower-semicontinuous perspective \[f(r,w)=\begin{cases}|w|^2/r,&r>0,\\0,&(r,w)=(0,0),\\+\infty,&r=0,\ w\ne0.\end{cases}\] For any positive measure \(\sigma\) dominating \(\rho\) and \(|m|\), set \[\mathcal B(\rho,m)=\int f\left(\frac{d\rho}{d\sigma},\frac{dm}{d\sigma}\right)d\sigma.\] Positive one-homogeneity makes this value independent of \(\sigma\). The functional \(\mathcal B\) is jointly convex and lower semicontinuous under weak-* convergence. If \(m=v\rho\), then \(\mathcal B(\rho,m)=\int|v|^2\,d\rho\); otherwise finite action forces \(m\ll\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing velocity by flux turns kinetic energy into the jointly convex perspective of the squared norm, valid also for measure-valued mass and flux.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Flux Reparameterization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The perspective formulation is appropriately classified as a representation and matches the flux-reparameterization leaf. A source is needed for domination independence and especially for the stated weak-* lower-semicontinuity scope and topology.

assumptions_latex: The admissible potentials belong to a class for which endpoint integrals are finite and the Hamilton–Jacobi inequality and dynamic duality are valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac12W_2^2(\mu_0,\mu_1)=\sup_{\phi}\left(\int\phi_1\,d\mu_1-\int\phi_0\,d\mu_0\right)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hamilton–Jacobi duality with one-half kinetic-action normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an admissible potential \(\phi:[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[\partial_t\phi_t(x)+\frac12|\nabla\phi_t(x)|^2\le0\] in the specified weak or viscosity sense, define \(\mathcal D(\phi)=\int\phi_1\,d\mu_1-\int\phi_0\,d\mu_0\). Then \[\frac12W_2^2(\mu_0,\mu_1)=\sup_{\phi}\mathcal D(\phi).\] Every admissible \(\phi\) gives a lower bound on every dynamic primal action \(\frac12\int_0^1\int|v_t|^2\,d\mu_t\,dt\), and the supremum equals the minimum primal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hamilton–Jacobi subsolutions provide lower bounds on dynamic transport action, and their best endpoint payoff equals half the squared Wasserstein distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Dual Potentials

children.title: Dynamic Calibrations
children.top_down_role: Dual objects aligned with candidate optimal dynamic transport paths.

assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is an admissible differentiable Hamilton–Jacobi subsolution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The calibration equalities imply equality of primal action and dual payoff, hence optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise primal–dual equality conditions for quadratic action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The potential \(\phi\) calibrates \((\mu,v)\) if, for \(dt\otimes\mu_t\)-almost every \((t,x)\), \[v_t(x)=\nabla\phi_t(x),\qquad \partial_t\phi_t(x)+\frac12|\nabla\phi_t(x)|^2=0.\] Under the weak continuity equation and valid endpoint traces, these identities yield \[\frac12\int_0^1\int|v_t|^2\,d\mu_t\,dt=\int\phi_1\,d\mu_1-\int\phi_0\,d\mu_0.\] Weak duality then certifies simultaneously that \((\mu,v)\) minimizes the dynamic action and that \(\phi\) maximizes the Hamilton–Jacobi dual problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A potential calibrates a flow when its gradient equals the velocity and its Hamilton–Jacobi inequality is saturated on the transported mass.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Calibrations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits Dynamic Calibrations, and the pointwise equality conditions are consistent with the one-half action normalization. A source is still required to substantiate the regularity, endpoint-trace, and chain-rule conditions under which the equalities certify both primal and dual attainment.

children.title: Action Optimality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Dual evidence certifying minimal dynamic action.

assumptions_latex: \((\mu_t,v_t)\) is primal feasible with finite quadratic action.
\(\phi\) is dual feasible and admits the endpoint chain rule along \((\mu_t,v_t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality between primal action and dual payoff is a verifiable certificate of optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global primal–dual certificate for dynamic quadratic transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \[P(\mu,v)=\frac12\int_0^1\int|v_t|^2\,d\mu_t\,dt,\qquad D(\phi)=\int\phi_1\,d\mu_1-\int\phi_0\,d\mu_0.\] Feasibility and the continuity-equation chain rule imply \(D(\phi)\le P(\mu,v)\). Therefore the checkable equality \[P(\mu,v)=D(\phi)\] certifies that \((\mu,v)\) is a minimum-action transport and \(\phi\) is a maximizing dynamic dual potential. More generally, a computed gap \(P(\mu,v)-D(\phi)\le\varepsilon\) certifies that the primal action is within \(\varepsilon\) of the optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matching a feasible flow's action with a feasible potential's endpoint payoff certifies exact optimality; a gap at most epsilon certifies epsilon-suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Action Optimality Certificates

children.title: Calibration Gaps
children.top_down_role: Regimes where available dual objects do not certify candidate actions.

assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is differentiable, dual feasible, and satisfies the endpoint chain rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal–dual gap decomposes into nonnegative velocity mismatch and Hamilton–Jacobi slack.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact gap identity under smooth chain-rule hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(G(\mu,v;\phi)=\frac12\int_0^1\int|v_t|^2\,d\mu_t\,dt-\left(\int\phi_1\,d\mu_1-\int\phi_0\,d\mu_0\right)\). The continuity-equation chain rule gives \[G(\mu,v;\phi)=\frac12\int_0^1\int|v_t-\nabla\phi_t|^2\,d\mu_t\,dt-\int_0^1\int\left(\partial_t\phi_t+\frac12|\nabla\phi_t|^2\right)d\mu_t\,dt.\] If \(\phi\) is dual feasible, both terms on the right are nonnegative. Thus the gap vanishes exactly when velocity matching and Hamilton–Jacobi saturation hold almost everywhere on the space-time mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The action gap is exactly the sum of squared velocity mismatch and Hamilton–Jacobi slack, so it quantifies failure of dynamic calibration.
knowledge_statements.title: Calibration Gaps

assumptions_latex: \(v\) is Borel, solves the continuity equation with \(\mu_t\), and has finite kinetic action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a path measure \(\eta\) concentrated on integral curves of \(v\) with \((e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t\).

notation.meaning: probability measure on absolutely continuous paths

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Superposition of finite-energy continuity-equation solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists \(\eta\in\mathcal P(AC^2([0,1];\mathbb R^d))\) such that \[(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t\qquad\text{for every }t\in[0,1],\] and \[\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))\qquad\text{for almost every }t\text{ and for }\eta\text{-almost every }\gamma.\] Moreover, \[\int\int_0^1|\dot\gamma(t)|^2\,dt\,d\eta(\gamma)=\int_0^1\int|v_t(x)|^2\,d\mu_t(x)\,dt.\] Thus the Eulerian solution is represented as a probability distribution of Lagrangian trajectories without changing its time marginals or kinetic energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-energy continuity-equation solution can be represented by a probability measure on integral curves having the prescribed time marginals and the same energy.
knowledge_statements.title: Path-Measure Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and the stated Eulerian-to-path conclusion fit the leaf. Acceptance requires an authoritative superposition theorem with an inspectable locator confirming the precise measurability, integrability, path-space, and energy-equality hypotheses.

assumptions_latex: \(\eta\in\mathcal P(AC^2([0,1];\mathbb R^d))\) has finite mean kinetic energy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The path measure induces an Eulerian flux solving the continuity equation, with barycentric kinetic action no larger than path energy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barycentric conversion between path measures and Eulerian fluxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the vector flux by \[\int \xi(x)\cdot dm_t(x)=\int \xi(\gamma(t))\cdot\dot\gamma(t)\,d\eta(\gamma)\] for every bounded continuous vector field \(\xi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\). Then \((\mu_t,m_t)\) satisfies \(\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\cdot m_t=0\) distributionally. Moreover, \(m_t=v_t\mu_t\) for a barycentric velocity \(v_t\) satisfying \[\int_0^1\int|v_t|^2\,d\mu_t\,dt\le\int\int_0^1|\dot\gamma(t)|^2\,dt\,d\eta(\gamma).\] Conversely, the superposition principle represents a finite-action Eulerian solution by paths with \(\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))\), in which case equality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path distribution induces its marginal mass and barycentric flux; conversely, finite-action Eulerian flows admit path representations, with equality of energies on integral curves.
knowledge_statements.title: Eulerian–Lagrangian Correspondence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eulerian equation for constant-velocity trajectories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eulerian representation of a diffeomorphic family of straight particle trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_0:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuous and differentiable almost everywhere, and set \(T_t(x)=x-tv_0(x)\). If \((T_t)_{0\le t<T_*}\) is a family of diffeomorphisms and its Eulerian velocity is defined by \(v_t=\dot T_t\circ T_t^{-1}\), then \(\partial_t v+(v\cdot\nabla)v=0\) for \(0\le t<T_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If straight constant-velocity particle trajectories form diffeomorphisms, the corresponding Eulerian velocity field satisfies the inviscid Burgers equation.
assumptions_latex: v_0:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is continuous and differentiable almost everywhere}
(T_t)_{0\le t<T_*}\text{ is a family of diffeomorphisms}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_t v+(v\cdot\nabla)v=0\quad\text{for }0\le t<T_*.

children.title: Characteristic Trajectories
children.top_down_role: Particle-path descriptions associated with sufficiently regular velocity fields.

assumptions_latex: For the path under consideration, \(t\mapsto v_t(\gamma(t))\) is integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma\) is a characteristic precisely when it is absolutely continuous and satisfies the integral ODE with its prescribed initial point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-curve definition for a time-dependent Borel velocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), a characteristic trajectory of \(v\) starting from \(x\) is a path \(\gamma_x\in AC([0,1];\mathbb R^d)\) such that \(\gamma_x(0)=x\) and \[\gamma_x(t)=x+\int_0^t v_s(\gamma_x(s))\,ds\] for every \(t\in[0,1]\). Equivalently, \(\dot\gamma_x(t)=v_t(\gamma_x(t))\) for almost every \(t\). This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of a characteristic for any specified initial point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A characteristic is an absolutely continuous path whose derivative equals the time-dependent velocity field almost everywhere, with a prescribed initial point.
knowledge_statements.title: Characteristic Trajectories

children.title: Regular Lagrangian Flows
children.top_down_role: Almost-everywhere flow representations compatible with nonsmooth vector fields.

assumptions_latex: \(v:[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) is Borel and locally integrable.
\(\mathcal L^d\) denotes Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A regular Lagrangian flow consists of almost-everywhere characteristics together with a uniform compression bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambrosio-style regular Lagrangian flow on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Borel map \(X:[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) is a regular Lagrangian flow for \(v\) if the following conditions hold: for \(\mathcal L^d\)-almost every \(x\), the path \(t\mapsto X(t,x)\) is absolutely continuous, \(X(0,x)=x\), and \[X(t,x)=x+\int_0^t v_s(X(s,x))\,ds;\] and there exists \(L\ge1\) such that \[X(t,\cdot)_\#\mathcal L^d\le L\mathcal L^d\qquad\text{for every }t\in[0,1].\] The second condition is the bounded-compression requirement and prevents the flow from concentrating positive Lebesgue mass onto null sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular Lagrangian flow follows the vector field for almost every initial point and pushes Lebesgue measure forward with uniformly bounded compression.
knowledge_statements.title: Regular Lagrangian Flows

children.title: Characteristic-to-Flow Extension
children.top_down_role: Passage from classical trajectories to measure-theoretic flow representations.

assumptions_latex: \(b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) is Borel and \(|b_t(x)|\leq a(t)(1+|x|)\) for some \(a\in L^1(0,T)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique characteristic flow, and its pushforward curve is the unique narrowly continuous measure solution of the continuity equation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Carathéodory characteristic-flow theorem under an integrable spatial Lipschitz bound
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical deterministic extension under an integrable Lipschitz bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu_0\)-almost every \(x\), the integral equation \[X(t,x)=x+\int_0^t b_s(X(s,x))\,ds\] has a unique absolutely continuous solution. The maps \(X(t,\cdot)\) form a measurable flow, and \(\mu_t:=X(t,\cdot)_\#\mu_0\) is narrowly continuous and satisfies \[\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\!\cdot(b_t\mu_t)=0,\qquad \mu_{t=0}=\mu_0,\] in distributions. Among narrowly continuous solutions satisfying \(\int_0^T\int |b_t(x)|\,d\mu_t(x)\,dt<\infty\), this solution is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrably Lipschitz velocity extends its unique characteristics to a measurable flow whose pushforwards uniquely solve the continuity equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Characteristic-to-Flow Extension

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Lipschitz characteristic and continuity-equation uniqueness theorem fits the leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no inspectable citation supports its hypotheses and uniqueness class.

children.title: Nonsmooth Velocity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Velocity-field regularity thresholds relevant to Lagrangian transport.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A path-space representation may exist even though no unique deterministic flow can be selected.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: superposition remains available below deterministic characteristic uniqueness
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes path-space superposition from deterministic flow selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The superposition conclusion can hold in a nonsmooth regime: there may exist a probability measure \(\eta\) on \(AC([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\) such that \[(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t\quad\text{for every }t,\qquad \dot\gamma(t)=b_t(\gamma(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\] for \(\eta\)-almost every path \(\gamma\). Without a spatial uniqueness hypothesis on \(b\), the conditional measure of \(\eta\) given \(e_0=x\) need not be a Dirac mass. Consequently, \(\eta\) need not be induced by any single-valued map \(X(t,x)\), and characteristic-based flow selection is not canonical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsmooth velocities may admit a superposition of characteristic paths while failing to determine one canonical path from each initial point.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Velocity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between superposition and deterministic flow selection fits this failure-boundary leaf, but the superposition theorem and non-Dirac disintegration claim require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Flow Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of admissible flows associated with the same velocity field.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete Peano-type failure of characteristic uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every waiting time \(\tau\in[0,T]\), define \[X_\tau(t)=(t-\tau)_+^2.\] Then \(X_\tau\) is continuously differentiable, \(X_\tau(0)=0\), and \[\dot X_\tau(t)=2(t-\tau)_+=2\sqrt{X_\tau(t)}=b(X_\tau(t)).\] Thus the initial-value problem has infinitely many solutions, including the stationary solution obtained by taking \(\tau=T\) on \([0,T]\). Hence the velocity field does not determine a unique characteristic starting at zero, and a deterministic flow cannot be inferred from the characteristic equation without an additional selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The field b(x)=2√(x positive part) admits characteristics from zero that wait for arbitrary times, so the characteristic equation alone does not determine a unique flow selection.
assumptions_latex: The autonomous scalar field is \(b(x)=2\sqrt{x_+}\), where \(x_+=\max\{x,0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The same initial point has infinitely many characteristics, so the characteristic equation does not determine a unique flow selection.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Peano nonuniqueness example for a non-Lipschitz vector field

children.title: Regularity Thresholds for Flow Selection
children.top_down_role: Boundaries separating uniquely selected flows from ambiguous dynamics.

assumptions_latex: \(b\in L^1(0,T;W^{1,1}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d))\cap L^1(0,T;L^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Sobolev and bounded-divergence bounds yield a unique regular Lagrangian flow up to Lebesgue-null sets.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Sobolev regularity and bounded divergence are a standard sufficient regime for regular Lagrangian flow uniqueness
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient Sobolev threshold, not a claim of sharp necessity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a regular Lagrangian flow \(X:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \[X(t,x)=x+\int_0^t b_s(X(s,x))\,ds\] for \(\mathcal L^d\)-almost every \(x\). Moreover, for every \(t\), \[X(t,\cdot)_\#\mathcal L^d\leq \exp\!\left(\int_0^t\|\nabla\!\cdot b_s\|_\infty ds\right)\mathcal L^d.\] Any two regular Lagrangian flows satisfying such a compression bound agree for \(\mathcal L^d\)-almost every initial point. Thus this regularity regime restores almost-everywhere flow selection even though pointwise classical uniqueness need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrable Sobolev regularity plus bounded divergence suffices for existence and almost-everywhere uniqueness of a regular Lagrangian flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularity Thresholds for Flow Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is an appropriate sufficient Sobolev regularity theorem for the leaf, and the stated compression estimate is conservative, but existence and almost-everywhere uniqueness require a specific DiPerna–Lions/Ambrosio-type citation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The endpoint transport cost is the infimum of the p-homogeneous kinetic action over continuity-equation paths.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The standard dynamic representation for general power \(p>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With the convention that \(|j|^p/\rho^{p-1}=0\) when \((\rho,j)=(0,0)\) and is \(+\infty\) when \(\rho=0\) but \(j\neq0\), one has \[W_p^p(\mu_0,\mu_1)=\inf_{(\rho,j)}\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^d}\frac{|j_t(x)|^p}{\rho_t(x)^{p-1}}\,dx\,dt.\] The infimum is over distributional solutions of \(\partial_t\rho+\nabla\!\cdot j=0\) with \(\rho_{0}\mathcal L^d=\mu_0\) and \(\rho_{1}\mathcal L^d=\mu_1\). Equivalently, writing \(j=\rho v\), the integrand is \(\rho|v|^p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The p-Wasserstein cost equals the minimum p-homogeneous kinetic action among density-flux paths satisfying mass conservation and the prescribed endpoints.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonquadratic-Action Transport

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The p-homogeneous dynamic representation is appropriate and internally consistent, but the general-p Benamou–Brenier formula has no inspectable supporting citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear-Mobility Transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic flux action with a Borel density-dependent mobility; no metric property is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\phi_m(r,z):=\begin{cases}|z|^2/m(r),&m(r)>0,\\0,&m(r)=0\text{ and }z=0,\\+\infty,&m(r)=0\text{ and }z\neq0.\end{cases}\] The associated extended transport cost is \[\mathsf W_m^2(\rho_0,\rho_1):=\inf_{(\rho,j)}\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_m(\rho_t(x),j_t(x))\,dx\,dt,\] where the infimum ranges over measurable densities and fluxes satisfying \(0\leq\rho_t\leq M\), \(\partial_t\rho+\nabla\!\cdot j=0\) in distributions, and \(\rho(0)=\rho_0\), \(\rho(1)=\rho_1\). The value is allowed to be \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonlinear-mobility transport is the extended cost obtained by minimizing reciprocal-mobility flux action under mass conservation; nonzero flux is forbidden where mobility vanishes.
assumptions_latex: The endpoint densities \(\rho_0,\rho_1:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]\) are measurable and integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mobility-weighted extended transport cost is defined by minimizing the weighted flux action subject to mass conservation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: quadratic generalized transport action with density-dependent mobility

knowledge_statements.title: Source-Augmented Transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A representative unbalanced dynamic action with local sources.

For \(r\geq0\), define \[\phi_p(r,z):= egin{cases}|z|^p/r^{p-1},&r>0,\0,&r=0	ext{ and }z=0,\+\infty,&r=0	ext{ and }z

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Source-augmented transport minimizes separate flux and source penalties under a continuity equation with local mass creation or destruction, so endpoint masses may differ.
assumptions_latex: The prescribed endpoint densities \(\rho_0,\rho_1\) are nonnegative and integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transport and local creation or destruction are jointly optimized under a continuity equation with source.

children.title: Degenerate Mobility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Mobility laws that vanish or lose effective transport capacity.

assumptions_latex: \(m:[0,M]\to[0,\infty)\) and the action density is \(\phi_m(\rho,j)=|j|^2/m(\rho)\) with the extended-value convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At density r-star, finite action forces zero flux; degeneracy therefore constrains admissible motion.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct consequence of the extended-value mobility action convention
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local constraint created by a zero of the mobility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every flux \(j\), \[\phi_m(r_*,j)=\begin{cases}0,&j=0,\\+\infty,&j\neq0.\end{cases}\] Consequently, if an admissible pair \((\rho,j)\) has finite total action, then \[j(t,x)=0\quad\text{for almost every }(t,x)\text{ such that }\rho(t,x)=r_*.\] Thus a zero of the mobility is not merely a large local penalty: it is a hard no-flux constraint at the corresponding density. When the zero set of \(m\) separates admissible density states, this constraint can split the finite-action state space into distinct accessibility components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Where mobility vanishes, every finite-action path must have zero flux, potentially separating the state space into inaccessible components.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Mobility Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local hard no-flux conclusion follows from the extended-value convention and fits the leaf. The further suggestion that density-state components split requires additional geometric and trace hypotheses, so a supporting source is needed.

children.title: Dynamic Action Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of finiteness, coercivity, or admissibility in generalized action functionals.

assumptions_latex: The quadratic action density is \(f(r,j)=j^2/m(r)\) for scalar flux \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The action density is not jointly convex, so standard convex lower-semicontinuity arguments fail.

notation.meaning: Hessian with respect to density and flux

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit Hessian test exhibits loss of joint convexity for a superlinear mobility
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete convexity failure for a superlinear mobility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \((0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\), the density is \(f(r,j)=j^2/r^2\). At every point with \(j\neq0\), its Hessian satisfies \[\det D^2f(r,j)=-\frac{4j^2}{r^6}<0.\] Hence \(f\) is not jointly convex in \((r,j)\). Therefore the integral action does not possess the usual convexity structure used to obtain weak lower semicontinuity, compactness-compatible relaxation, and existence of minimizers. This calculation identifies a failure mechanism: allowing a superlinear mobility such as \(m(r)=r^2\) invalidates the standard convex-action theory, although a separately relaxed formulation may still be possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For mobility m(r)=r², the flux density j²/r² has an indefinite Hessian, destroying the standard convex dynamic-action framework.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Action Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hessian determinant is correct and demonstrates loss of joint convexity for m(r)=r². A source is still required for the broader claims about the standard lower-semicontinuity and relaxation framework.

children.title: Mobility-Induced Inaccessibility
children.top_down_role: Restrictions on reachable states caused by degenerate mobility.

knowledge_statements.title: Mobility-Induced Inaccessibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A rigorously imposed no-flux separator and endpoint mass imbalance certify infinite mobility cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[M_A(t):=\int_A\rho_t(x)\,dx.\] The distributional continuity equation together with the assumed zero normal trace on \(\partial A\) gives \[M_A(t)=M_A(0)\quad\text{for every }t\in[0,1].\] Consequently, finite-action accessibility requires \[\int_A\rho_0(x)\,dx=\int_A\rho_1(x)\,dx.\] If these endpoint masses differ, no admissible finite-action path satisfying the no-flux condition exists, and therefore \[\mathsf W_m(\rho_0,\rho_1)=+\infty.\] The endpoint mass imbalance is thus an inaccessibility certificate once the zero normal trace has been established independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an admissible mobility path is subject to a genuine zero-normal-flux separator, unequal endpoint mass in either separated region certifies infinite transport cost.
assumptions_latex: \(A\subset\mathbb R^d\) is a bounded Lipschitz region whose boundary separates the relevant transport domain.
\(t\mapsto\rho_t\) is narrowly continuous, \(j\) has a well-defined normal trace on \(\partial A\), and \(\partial_t\rho+\nabla\!\cdot j=0\) holds in distributions.
The admissible mobility class imposes \(j_t\cdot n_A=0\) on \(\partial A\) for almost every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite-action admissible path satisfying the no-flux condition connects the endpoints, so their mobility transport cost is infinite.

notation.meaning: Region isolated by the no-flux separator
Outward unit normal to the separating boundary
Mass contained in region A at time t

children.title: Potential Energies
children.top_down_role: Measure functionals generated by external spatial potentials.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential Energies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: External-field energy and its smooth transport variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The potential energy generated by \(V\) is \[\mathcal V(\mu):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(x)\,d\mu(x).\] If additionally \(V\in C^1(\mathbb R^d)\), \(\xi\in C_c^1(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)\), and \(\mu_\varepsilon=(\mathrm{Id}+\varepsilon\xi)_\#\mu\), then \[\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\mathcal V(\mu_\varepsilon)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\nabla V(x)\cdot\xi(x)\,d\mu(x).\] Thus the smooth transport first-variation field of the potential term is \(\nabla V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Potential energy is the integral of an external potential against the measure; for a continuously differentiable potential, its transport first variation is the potential gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The potential energy is the expectation of the external potential under the probability measure, with transport first-variation field \(\nabla V\) in the stated smooth regime.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: potential-energy functional and its smooth pushforward variation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak regularity of potential energies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient and necessary regularity conditions for linear potential energies under weak convergence of probability measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal V(\mu)=\int_\Omega V\,d\mu\). If \(V\in C_b(\Omega)\), then \(\mathcal V\) is continuous for weak convergence on \(\mathcal P(\Omega)\). If \(V\) is lower semicontinuous and bounded below, then \(\mathcal V\) is weakly lower semicontinuous. Conversely, lower semicontinuity, respectively continuity, of \(\mathcal V\) implies lower semicontinuity, respectively continuity, of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded continuous potential induces a weakly continuous potential energy, while a lower-semicontinuous potential bounded below induces a weakly lower-semicontinuous energy. The corresponding regularity of the potential is necessary, although the stated boundedness assumptions are only part of the sufficient conditions.
assumptions_latex: For lower semicontinuity, \(V\) is lower semicontinuous and bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal V\) has the corresponding weak continuity or weak lower-semicontinuity property, and that property implies the corresponding continuity or lower semicontinuity of \(V\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real coupling of external and pairwise interaction energies on \(\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the potential energy and interaction energy by \[\mathcal{V}(\mu):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}V(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad \mathcal{W}(\mu):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d}W(x,y)\,d\mu(x)d\mu(y).\] Their potential–interaction coupling is the extended-real functional \[\mathcal{E}_{V,W}(\mu):=\mathcal{V}(\mu)+\mathcal{W}(\mu).\] Because both integrands are bounded below, the displayed integrals and their sum are well-defined in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\). When \(W(x,y)=w(x-y)\), the second term is equivalently \(\frac12\int (w*\mu)(x)\,d\mu(x)\), whenever that convolutional expression is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coupled energy is the sum of an external-potential integral and one half of the pairwise interaction integral.

knowledge_statements.title: Internal Energy Functionals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density-integral internal energy, with non-absolutely-continuous measures assigned infinite energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U:[0,\infty)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, with \(U(0)=0\) and \(U(r)\geq-Cr\) for some \(C\geq0\) and every \(r\geq0\). The associated internal energy on \(\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\) is \[\mathcal U(\mu):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb R^d}U(\rho(x))\,dx,&\text{if }\mu=\rho\,dx,\\+\infty,&\text{if }\mu\not\ll dx.\end{cases}\] The linear lower bound ensures that the integral cannot equal \(-\infty\) for a probability density.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An internal energy integrates a convex function of the density and assigns infinite energy to measures without a Lebesgue density; a linear lower bound prevents the integral from being minus infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(U:[0,\infty)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, with \(U(0)=0\).
There exists \(C\geq0\) such that \(U(r)\geq-Cr\) for every \(r\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal U(\mu)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}U(\rho(x))\,dx\) if \(\mu=\rho\,dx\), and \(\mathcal U(\mu)=+\infty\) otherwise.

knowledge_statements.title: Entropy Functionals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boltzmann entropy relative to Lebesgue measure, using the convention \(0\log 0=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With the convention \(0\log 0:=0\), the Boltzmann entropy relative to Lebesgue measure is \[\operatorname{Ent}(\mu):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho(x)\log\rho(x)\,dx,&\text{if }\mu=\rho\,dx,\\+\infty,&\text{if }\mu\not\ll dx.\end{cases}\] For a probability measure with finite second moment, the negative part of \(\rho\log\rho\) is controlled by a quadratic reference density, so the integral is well-defined in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\). This is the internal energy associated with \(U(r)=r\log r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boltzmann entropy integrates density times log density and is infinite whenever the measure is not absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Ent}(\mu)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho(x)\log\rho(x)\,dx\) for \(\mu=\rho\,dx\), and \(\operatorname{Ent}(\mu)=+\infty\) otherwise.

notation.meaning: Boltzmann entropy relative to Lebesgue measure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contraction of Relative Entropy Under Pushforward
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Data-processing inequality for relative entropy under a common Borel pushforward.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\pi:X\to X\) be Borel measurable and let \(\gamma,\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\). Then
\[
\mathcal H(\pi_\#\mu\mid\pi_\#\gamma)\le\mathcal H(\mu\mid\gamma).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying the same Borel map to a probability measure and its reference measure cannot increase their relative entropy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal H(\pi_\#\mu\mid\pi_\#\gamma)\le\mathcal H(\mu\mid\gamma)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint Lower Semicontinuity of Relative Entropy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint lower semicontinuity when both the probability measure and its reference measure vary narrowly on \(X_\varpi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\gamma^n,\mu^n\in\mathcal P(X)\) converge narrowly to \(\gamma,\mu\), respectively, in \(\mathcal P(X_\varpi)\). Then
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathcal H(\mu^n\mid\gamma^n)\ge \mathcal H(\mu\mid\gamma).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative entropy is jointly lower semicontinuous when both the probability measure and its reference measure converge narrowly on the stated space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathcal H(\mu^n\mid\gamma^n)\ge\mathcal H(\mu\mid\gamma)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Displacement Convexity of Relative Entropy Implies Log-Concavity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse implication from displacement convexity of relative entropy to open-set log-concavity of the reference measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\gamma\in\mathcal P(X)\). Assume that for every pair \(\mu^1,\mu^2\in\mathcal P(X)\) with bounded support, there exists \(\boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma(\mu^1,\mu^2)\) such that \(\mathcal H(\cdot\mid\gamma)\) is convex along
\[
\mu_t^{1\to2}:=((1-t)\pi^1+t\pi^2)_\#\boldsymbol\mu,\qquad t\in[0,1].
\]
Then, for every pair of open sets \(A,B\subset X\) and every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
\log\gamma((1-t)A+tB)\ge(1-t)\log\gamma(A)+t\log\gamma(B).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every pair of boundedly supported probability measures admits a coupling along whose linear interpolation relative entropy with respect to γ is convex, then γ satisfies the stated open-set log-concavity inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall A,B\subset X\text{ open},\ \forall t\in[0,1],\quad\log\gamma((1-t)A+tB)\ge(1-t)\log\gamma(A)+t\log\gamma(B)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Near-Identity Pushforward Approximation of Relative Entropy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of relative entropy under simultaneous pushforwards by Borel maps converging pointwise to the identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\pi^k:X\to X\) be Borel maps such that \(\pi^k(x)\to x\) for every \(x\in X\). For \(\gamma,\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\), set \(\gamma^k:=\pi^k_\#\gamma\) and \(\mu^k:=\pi^k_\#\mu\). Then
\[
\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathcal H(\mu^k\mid\gamma^k)=\mathcal H(\mu\mid\gamma).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If Borel maps converge pointwise to the identity, simultaneously pushing forward a probability measure and its reference measure preserves their relative entropy in the limit.
assumptions_latex: \pi^k:X\to X\text{ is Borel measurable for every }k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{k\to\infty}\mathcal H(\mu^k\mid\gamma^k)=\mathcal H(\mu\mid\gamma)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of log-concavity by relative-entropy convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence among Wasserstein convexity of relative entropy, displacement convexity, log-concavity, and finite-dimensional marginal representations on a separable Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a separable Hilbert space and \(\gamma\in\mathcal P(X)\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(\mathcal H(\cdot\mid\gamma)\) is geodesically convex in \(\mathcal P_p(X)\) for every \(p\in(1,+\infty)\); (ii) it is convex along generalized geodesics in \(\mathcal P_2(X)\); (iii) for every boundedly supported \(\mu^1,\mu^2\in\mathcal P(X)\), there exists \(\boldsymbol\mu\in\Gamma(\mu^1,\mu^2)\) along which \(\mathcal H(\cdot\mid\gamma)\) is displacement convex; (iv) \(\gamma\) is log-concave; (v) every finite-dimensional orthogonal projection \(\pi\) has \(\pi_\#\gamma\) representable as in (9.4.23) for a suitable convex lower-semicontinuous function \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a probability measure on a separable Hilbert space, log-concavity is equivalent to several forms of Wasserstein convexity of relative entropy and to convex exponential-density representations of all finite-dimensional orthogonal projections.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a separable Hilbert space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Properties (i)--(v) are equivalent.}
